Compute Engine Changelog

0.171.0 2026-10-27​

Behavior Changes​

  • subs() of the variable of a derivative, a series or an indefinite integral gives the value at the point (ROADMAP CE-538). Before, D(x^2, x).subs({x: 3}) gave an invalid D(…, Error('expected-a-symbol')). It is now EvaluateAt(Function(D(x^2, x), x), 3), written \left.\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x^2}{\mathrm{d}x}\right)\right|_{x=3}, which evaluates to 6 (a float under .N()).

    • This also applies inside a scoped expression: Sum(D(x^k, x), k=1..3) with x replaced by 2 evaluates to 17.
    • Integrate(a·x, x).subs({x: 3, a: 2}) evaluates to 9, and D(x^2, x).subs({x: x + 1}) to 2(x + 1).
    • Several variables are replaced at the same time, at one point that is a Tuple (|_{x=3, y=5}).
    • Only the variable itself is applied at a point. The replacement of another name is put in the derivative, the series or the integral before it is computed: D(x·y, x).subs({y: x}) is D(x·x, x), which evaluates to 2x.
    • A wildcard (_f) is still replaced inside the node. A value with no closed form stays an unevaluated EvaluateAt. The value of a Series at a point keeps its BigO remainder. A value that keeps a BigO term is NaN under .N(); Normal drops the remainder, before or after the substitution, and Normal now strips it before any numeric evaluation (Normal(Series(sin x, x, 0, 3)).N() was NaN).

  • EvaluateAt at a point has the value of Apply. The statements of the body run in order, and an If evaluates only the branch it selects. A point is never a partial application: when there are fewer points than required parameters, or more than a named callee accepts, the form stays unevaluated. A constant is its own value at any point: EvaluateAt(5, 3) is 5, and so is a named function that takes no argument.

    • A lazy callee receives the point as written, and the expression it returns is not evaluated again: EvaluateAt(p, Random()) for a lazy p that returns its operand gives Random() without a draw.
    • The form stays unevaluated only when a D, a Series or an Integrate with no closed form comes from the BODY: the identity at Series(e^{1/x}, x, 0, 3) is that series, and x ↦ x between 0 and an integral with no closed form is that integral.
    • A point that is a symbol whose value is a tuple is read at evaluation: with p := (2, 3), (x·y)|_{p} is 6.
    • EvaluateAt compiles: EvaluateAt(f, a) as the application f(a) and EvaluateAt(f, a, b) as f(b) − f(a), so the result of subs() on a derivative compiles to JavaScript. D of an EvaluateAt evaluates it first: the derivative in y of (x^2)|_{x=y} is 2y.

  • A function literal whose body is a derivative, a series or an indefinite integral of one parameter, applied to arguments that name another parameter, is a plain application. ((x, y) ↦ D(x·y, x))(3, x) is x (the derivative y at y = x of the caller); it was x + 3, a product rule mixed with the caller's x. ((x, a) ↦ ∫a·x dx)(x + 1, x) is x(x + 1)²/2; the point was lost. A function-valued parameter named like a user function no longer leaks its name: with w(x) := x + 100, (w ↦ D(w(x), x))(x ↦ 5·w(x)) is 5, and the same for Integrate and Series.

  • An indefinite integral under .N() computes its antiderivative. Integrate(Sin(x), x).N() is -cos(x) and (x ↦ ∫sin x dx)(1).N() is -0.5403…; both stayed an unevaluated Integrate (the numeric request sent the integral to the quadrature route, which has no bounds to use).

  • An evaluate handler written with anonymous parameters gets a signature with as many parameters. ce.declare('f', { evaluate: ['Function', ['Add', '_', 1]] }) is (unknown) -> unknown, not () -> unknown.

  • D(Length([x ↦ x]), x) is 0: an occurrence of the variable that a function literal binds as its parameter does not make the expression depend on the variable. Integrate(Apply(t ↦ t², x), x) is x³/3: an applied function literal in the integrand is applied before integration.

  • Canonicalizing a function literal whose raw body shares a subtree is linear in the number of distinct nodes. A body that shares the previous node twice at each level, at depth 24, took 4.9 s and takes 2 ms: the canonical form of a raw node is kept for the duration of one top-level canonicalization (ROADMAP CE-548).

  • A function literal whose body is D, Series or an indefinite Integrate of its parameter, applied to an argument that contains the parameter's name, gives the value at the argument: (x ↦ D(x^2, x))(x + 1) is 2(x + 1), not 2x. Under .N(), (x ↦ D(x^2, x))(1 + 2.5) is 7, not 2x.

  • The LaTeX of EvaluateAt parses back to the same EvaluateAt. \left.x^2\right|_{x=2} was Subscript(EvaluateAt(x^2), x = 2). The two-point form is now written with the name of the variable, \left.\left(\frac{x^3}{3}\right)\right|_{x=0}^{1}. In a bracket with no name for the variable and more free variables than coordinates in the point, the point or the bounds are for x: \left.kx\right|_{2}^{5} is 3k, while \left.\left(xy\right)\right|_{(1,2)} is 2. \left.f\right|_{A} and a bound that is a tuple keep their earlier parse.

  • Numeric integration reports an error that bounds the true error in more cases (ROADMAP CE-533, CE-376). The error reported for most integrals changes; smooth integrands use the same number of evaluations.

    • The error of a Gauss–Kronrod panel now also comes from null rules (Berntsen–Espelid), with no extra evaluations, so a kink or a jump inside a panel is counted. For the inner integral ∫₋₁₀¹⁰ n(x, 0.758125) dx of a Tycho document, the result was ± 5.7e-10 with a true error of 1.6e-5; it is now ± 9.3e-10 with a true error of 2.3e-11.
    • Far from 0, the rounding of the sample points to the doubles is counted: ∫ sin(10³·(x − a)) dx over [10⁶, 10⁶ + 0.01] was converged, ± 2.2e-13, for a true error of 2.3e-11; it is now not converged, ± 6.3e-10. Some accurate results are now reported as not converged for that reason (∫ e^(x − a) dx over [10⁶, 10⁶ + 0.01]).
    • With singularEndpoints, a singular point that is not exactly a double is found: ∫₋₁¹ |x − 0.3|^(−1/2) dx was ± 3.9e-10 for a true error of 1.3e-8 after 28,480 evaluations; it is now ± 4e-13 for 3e-14 after 6,117. A singular point a few doubles inside or outside an endpoint (for example |t − 0.1·3|^(−1/2) or |t − (0.7 − 0.4)|^(−1/2) on [0.3, 1]) now gives an error that bounds the true error.
    • An interval is no longer split at a jump, and a step next to a singular endpoint is no longer taken for a singularity: (x < 0.3 ? 0 : 1) + |x − c|^(−1/2) with c = 0.3 + 10⁻⁶ was converged, ± 3.1e-12, for a true error of 1e-6; it is now not converged, with an error that bounds the true error.
    • At a singular endpoint far from 0, the area between the endpoint and the first double above it, which no sample reaches, is now counted in the error (ROADMAP CE-552): (x − 10⁶)^(−1/2) on [10⁶, 10⁶ + 1] was ± 1.4e-5 for a true error of 2.3e-5 and is ± 5.7e-5. In a sweep of 180 such cases, the error was below the true error in 124 and is in none; the six cases that lose their converged status had a wrong error. A zero of the smooth factor a few doubles from the endpoint gets a fallback bound.
    • A step next to a slowly decaying endpoint singularity (x^(−0.95)·(x < s ? 2 : 1) on [0, 1]) no longer reports converged with an error below the true error (ROADMAP CE-547): the last panel next to the endpoint is compared with the model of the shells.
    • A pole 10⁴ to 10⁵ doubles outside an endpoint is detected (ROADMAP CE-558), and the error charged for a pole outside is the area the corner model misplaces, not the whole model area: (x − c)^(−1/4) on [10⁶, 10⁶ + 1] with c 1000 doubles below was ± 1.3e-7 and is ± 1.3e-10 for a true error of 1e-11. An exact zero of the integrand at the sample that gives the exponent of a singularity inside an endpoint no longer gives an infinite error (ROADMAP CE-557).
    • The semi-infinite oscillatory quadrature returns a finite estimate with an infinite error, not NaN, when one lobe cannot bound its error (ROADMAP CE-549).
    • The nodes of a Gauss–Kronrod panel are clamped to the panel: on a panel a few doubles wide, a node could round one double outside it, and √(x − 1) on [1, 1 + ε] gave NaN. An interval one double wide still reports 0 ± 0 (ROADMAP CE-561).

  • The interval library gives sound and tighter answers at poles, at domain boundaries and for powers (ROADMAP CE-522). These kernels are the ones that the code compiled with compile(…, { to: 'interval-js' }) calls, so every user of that target sees the change. The design review of the Enclosure value kind (see Features) found them: some answers excluded a true value, others were wider than necessary.

    • mod with a divisor interval that is not a point: mod([5, 5], [2, 4]) was [1, 1], which excludes Mod(5, 3) = 2 and Mod(5, 2.5) = 0. It is now the hull [0, 4] (a singular result with that value). When the quotient has one integer part over the whole box, the answer is the continuous range: mod([5, 5], [2.6, 4]) is [1, 2.4], rounded outward.
    • atanh at the boundary of its domain: atanh([0, 1]) was partial [0, 18.3684…], a clip of the argument to 1 − ε. It is now partial [0, +∞], and atanh([1, 1]) is empty.
    • A pole at an ENDPOINT gives a half-line. tan([0, Math.PI / 2]), cot([0, 1]), sec([0, Math.PI / 2]), csc([-1, 0]), gamma([0, 1]), powRational([-1, 0], -2, 3) and powRealBranch with a negative exponent were singular with no value (the whole line). They are now partial with the half-line beside the pole: gamma([0, 1]) is [1, +∞] and powRational([-1, 0], -2, 3) is [1, +∞]. A pole inside the interval still gives singular. A point at a pole has no value: gamma([0, 0]) and powRational([0, 0], -1, 3) are empty; tan, cot, sec and csc at a point that is their pole stay singular, because the interpreter answers ~oo there.
    • pow with a negative integer exponent over a base with a zero endpoint: pow([0, 1], -1) was partial [−∞, +∞] and is now partial [1, +∞]; pow([-1, 0], -1) is [−∞, −1], and pow([0, 0], -1) is empty.
    • powInterval with a negative base over an exponent interval: powInterval([-2, -2], [1, 2]) was empty, although (−2)^1 and (−2)^2 exist. It is now [−4, 4], the symmetric hull [−M, M] with M = max(|b|^c, |b|^d), which contains every real value of the power, also at an exponent that is a fraction with an odd denominator ((−2)^(5/3) ≈ −3.17). A base that crosses 0 takes the hull of its two parts: [-1, 1]^[1, 2] was partial [0, 1] and is [−1, 1]. At an exponent that is a POINT and not an integer, a negative base still has no value (powInterval([-2, -2], [1.5, 1.5]) is empty). Visible to Tycho's adaptive sampler (its rows 260 and 417): a box with x < 0 and an exponent interval that holds an integer is now an undecided hull that the sampler subdivides, instead of a blank region; at a non-integer point exponent the region stays blank.
    • pow with a negative integer exponent rounds outward at each step. For the double x = 1.9678349534779586e-103, pow([x, x], -3) was [1.3123025984121744e308, 1.3123025984121748e308], which excludes the true value (its nearest double is 1.3123025984121742e308). It now contains it. An exact power stays exact: pow([2, 2], -1) is [0.5, 0.5].
    • An angle in degrees, gradians or turns: the interval-js target multiplied the angle by the double nearest to the factor (Math.PI / 180, 2 * Math.PI), which can be below the true factor. In turn mode, the compiled cos(x) at the point 0.25 had two positive bounds and excluded the true value 0. The target now uses the exact factor (π/180, π/200, 2π, and its reciprocal for the inverse functions), enclosed outward as any other exact constant, also in the derivatives that the target compiles. The compiled cos and arcsin now contain the true value at a quarter turn in deg, grad and turn mode. The other targets keep the float factors.
    • fract([-1e-20, -1e-20]) was [1, 1], while the true fractional part is below 1. The subtraction x − floor(x) is now rounded outward; an exact case stays exact.
    • The other kernels with a pole now also give the half-line for a pole at an endpoint: coth([0, 1]) is [coth(1), +∞] (was singular with no value), and the same for csch, acoth, acsch and asech at 0 and for gammaln at a non-positive integer (gammaln([0, 1]) is [0, +∞]). A pole inside the interval, or a point at the pole, is still singular. asech([-1, 0]) is empty.
    • mod with a divisor interval: when the quotient has one integer part over the whole box, the answer takes no extra outward step: mod([1, 1], [2, 4]) is [1, 1] (was one ulp wider on each side).
    • Root(x, n) with a symbolic degree n, compiled to interval-js, reads the degree at run time: an integer degree keeps its exact value. With n = 6, x = [−64, −1] gives empty (was [−2, 2]); with n = 3, [−4, −1] (was [−4, 4]); a negative integer degree is the reciprocal root (n = −3, x = −8 gives −1/2). Another degree takes the power x^(1/n) as before.

  • Degrees refuses a complex number. An angle is real, and the signature of Degrees is (real) -> real. Degrees(2 + 3i) was (1/90 + i/60)·π; it is now an incompatible-type error, as Degrees((2 + 3i) ± 0.1) already was. A symbol declared complex that holds a real number still converts. NaN and the infinities are not changed.

  • The interval-js runner checks the value of an input whose type can hold an enclosure. Before, this target declined every expression with a value kind. Now, for a free symbol whose type is enclosure or a union with an enclosure arm, run() checks the value BEFORE it converts the inputs: a record { lo, hi } must have lo <= hi, no NaN and not the same infinity twice, and a number is a point. A union input is checked by arm: with y: number | enclosure, y: Infinity is accepted by the numeric arm. A refused value throws (it is not turned into an entire result). broadcast() and broadcastAsync() check every cell before the loop, so one refused cell rejects the whole call. The inputs of every other type are not changed, including the NaN that marks an absent value of a real | missing input.

  • On interval-js, a decline of an expression with an enclosure is not replaced by the interpreter, also with fallback: true: it throws with the message of the kind. The fallback of this target gives each input as the midpoint of its interval, and would give a number to a symbol typed enclosure. The other value kinds (Measurement, Quantity) keep the fallback.

Features​

  • Smoothstep(e0, e1, x) is defined in the engine. The shader targets already lowered it to the GLSL and WGSL built-in smoothstep, but the library had no definition: it stayed unevaluated, and the javascript target did not compile it. It now evaluates to t² (3 − 2t) with t = Clamp((x − e0) / (e1 − e0), 0, 1), exactly for exact operands (Smoothstep(0, 1, 1/3) is 7/27), and broadcasts over lists. The javascript and python targets compile it. When e0 = e1 the result is the step function (0 when x < e0, else 1), and when e0 > e1 the formula applies as written. The shader targets now write the formula out instead of calling the built-in smoothstep, which has no defined result when e0 ≥ e1, so every target gives the same value.

  • Enclosure, an interval value with interval arithmetic (ROADMAP CE-507 phase 3, #416). Enclosure(lo, hi) is a closed interval that holds ONE real number, whose value is somewhere in [lo, hi]. It is not the set Interval(lo, hi): Abs(Enclosure(-1, 2)) is Enclosure(0, 2), while Abs of the set is its cardinality. It is a library value kind, beside ResidueClass, Measurement and Quantity, with the kind type enclosure, and it is accepted wherever a real is accepted (admittedAs: 'real'). Its LaTeX is \mathrm{Enclosure}(a, b).

    • The canonical form orders the endpoints (Enclosure(2, 1) is Enclosure(1, 2)), reads one operand as a point (Enclosure(3) is Enclosure(3, 3)), and converts a set Interval (Enclosure(Interval(0, 1)) is Enclosure(0, 1)). An endpoint that is not an extended real, or is a value of a kind, is an incompatible-type error. A NaN endpoint, the same infinity twice and an empty set give the indeterminate value.
    • The arithmetic hooks compute with the endpoints, and keep them exact under evaluate(): Enclosure(0, 1) + Enclosure(1/3, 2) is Enclosure(1/3, 3), Enclosure(-1, 2) · Enclosure(3, 4) is Enclosure(-4, 8), and Enclosure(1, 2) − Enclosure(1, 2) is Enclosure(-1, 1) (the two operands are independent). A division by an enclosure with a zero endpoint gives a half-line (1 / Enclosure(0, 1) is Enclosure(1, +oo)), and with 0 inside the whole line.
    • A numeric function gives its image (the apply hook), with the critical points of the function: Sin(Enclosure(0, Pi)) is Enclosure(0, 1), Sin(Enclosure(0, 1)) is Enclosure(0, Sin(1)), Sqrt(Enclosure(-1, 4)) is Enclosure(0, 2) (the domain is clipped), Tan(Enclosure(0, Pi/2)) is Enclosure(0, +oo), and Ln(Enclosure(-2, -1)) is indeterminate. Under evaluate() with exact endpoints the endpoints are exact. Under .N(), the endpoints are converted to doubles OUTWARD (the largest double below lo, the smallest above hi) and the interval library computes the image: Enclosure(0, Pi).N() is Enclosure(0, 3.1415926535897936), and Sin(Enclosure(0, 1)).N() is Enclosure(0, 0.8414709848078966). The endpoints under .N() are machine doubles at every ce.precision. They are rigorous for the rational operations and best effort for the transcendental functions (ROADMAP CE-522.5).
    • The comparisons use the partial order of intervals: Enclosure(0, 1) < Enclosure(2, 3) is True, and Enclosure(0, 2) < Enclosure(1, 3) stays unevaluated. Two enclosures that touch decide only the non-strict comparison: Enclosure(0, 1) <= Enclosure(1, 2) is True and > is False, while < stays unevaluated. Enclosure(1, 1) = 1 is True; two enclosures that overlap may hold the same real, so Equal stays unevaluated.
    • Max, Min, Clamp, ElementMax and ElementMin give the hull of the extrema: Max(Enclosure(0, 2), Enclosure(1, 3)) is Enclosure(1, 3), and Max(Enclosure(0, 1), +oo) is +oo.
    • Sum, Product and Mean of a list of enclosures and numbers fold through the hooks: Mean([Enclosure(0, 1), Enclosure(1, 2), 3]) is Enclosure(4/3, 2). The other statistics stay unevaluated.
    • The code compiled for the interval-js target computes with an enclosure: an input typed enclosure is a { lo, hi } record, and the compiled code calls the same kernel of the interval library as .N() for each form, so the two give the same doubles. With x declared enclosure, compile(ce.parse('x + 1'), { to: 'interval-js' }) gives { kind: 'interval', value: { lo: 1, hi: 2 } } for run({ x: { lo: 0, hi: 1 } }). The other targets decline an enclosure with the message of the kind.
    • Measurement(Enclosure(0, 1), 0.1) and Quantity(Enclosure(0, 1), m) are incompatible-type errors.

    The rules are in doc/06-guide-augmenting.md, "Enclosures"; the design is section 4.9.2 of docs/plans/2026-10-26-value-kinds.md.

  • Two extensions of ArithmeticDefinition for a value kind that you declare.

    • The optional extremum(which, ops, context) hook gives the maximum (which is 'max') or the minimum of operands of which one at least is a value of the kind, for Max, Min, Clamp, ElementMax and ElementMin. The engine asks it before it orders the operands with compare, so a kind whose values can overlap can answer a value that is not one of the operands. undefined declines, and the engine orders the operands with compare as before.
    • compare can answer '<=' or '>=': the first value is less than (or greater than) or equal to the second, and the hook cannot say which. On a '<=' answer, LessEqual is True and Greater is False, Less and GreaterEqual stay unevaluated, and Equal asks the eq handlers. A reader that needs a total order (Sort, and Max/Min without an extremum hook) reads it as no answer.

Performance​

  • The shader targets call the built-in sin, cos, sign, max and min, and write clamp as min(max(x, lo), hi), for an operand that is finite for certain. The NaN-safe helpers that replaced them (_gpu_sin and the others) cost a bit test and a selection per call, about 10% of the frame time of a Tycho document on WebGPU, and on a finite operand they give the same bits as the built-in (measured on an Apple M5 Max over WebGPU, 39,200 inputs). An operand is finite for certain when its static type is a finite real, each symbol it reads has a declared type (a symbol declared real holds a finite value), it reads no name that the caller maps with functions or operators and no name that vars maps to other source, and it cannot overflow in f32: it uses only heads whose result does not grow past their operands (+, −, a product or quotient by a literal, sin, floor, abs, …). A name that vars maps to its own identifier (vars: { T: 'T' }, the way a host passes a uniform), with a declared type and not a constant, counts as a declared symbol. sin(x) and cos(T + 1.9k) with declared real symbols are now the built-ins, also with vars: { T: 'T' }; sin(u) with u: number, sin(x/y), sin(√x), sin(e^x), sin(xy), vars: { T: 'uT' }, a mapped constant and the parameter of a function whose type is inferred keep the helper. One limit: a sum or a product by a literal of values within that factor of the largest f32 (3.4·10³⁸) overflows, and the built-in then gives 0 on Apple GPUs where the helper gave NaN.

  • The unit of a quantity is decoded once for each boxed value. The arithmetic and the comparisons of quantities read the unit expression, its dimension and its scale from a cache on the boxed unit, and do not walk the unit again at each operation. The cache is public as decodedPayload(): the hooks of a value kind that you declare can decode the operands of a kind value once for each boxed expression in the same way.

  • The canonicalization of a binder keeps the cached types (ROADMAP CE-535). D, Sum, Integrate and the other binders declare their bound variable in a scope created for them. That declaration no longer invalidates the cached types and signs of every expression, because no name was read through the new scope before. A row of a Tycho document with D(PointY(S(u)), u), where S is a user function with a large body, typed S(u) again after each D; the replay of the canonical rebinds of the document 2ki2hjsouf went from 848 ms to 664 ms (median of 5).

Resolved Issues​

  • A sign cached during a call of a function literal is not kept after the call. With f := x ↦ …(x + 1)…, a sign of the body node x + 1 computed during f(3) (positive) was still served after the call returned, where x has no value. The removal of the call scope that holds the parameter values now invalidates the cached types, signs and values that are keyed on the engine's cache version.

  • A Block that declares a name and calls a function that reads the same name no longer prints "error canonicalizing Block: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'parent')", and the function's derived signature is correct (ROADMAP CE-542). Example: b is declared real, f is declared (real) -> unknown and assigned p ↦ sin(b·p), and Block(Declare(b), Assign(b, 1), f(0.5)) is boxed. The call reads the signature of f, which is derived by boxing f's body again in the scope where f is defined. That boxing read the names of the block being canonicalized, so the free b of f was taken for the block's local: the signature of f became (real) -> number instead of (real) -> real, and when the block was boxed in a scope from ce.createScope() the name resolution walked past the root scope and threw. The value was not affected: f reads the b of its own scope. A signature is now derived with none of the names of the construct being canonicalized, and those names shadow only inside the scopes of that construct. Found on the Tycho document g(x) with b = 1, where g calls f(x) = sin(b·x).

  • On Apple GPUs, the complex shader helpers gave a finite value for a NaN part. The built-ins sin and cos of a NaN give 0 on WebGL2 over ANGLE Metal and on WebGPU over Metal, so exp(1 + NaN·i) was (0, 0) on both shader targets, and so were sin, cos, sinh and cosh of a complex value with a NaN part (measured on an Apple M5 Max). The helpers (_gpu_cexp, _gpu_csin, _gpu_ccos, _gpu_csinh, _gpu_ccosh, and also _gpu_csqrt and _gpu_cln) now test each part first and give NaN, as the interpreter and the javascript target do.

  • A function body over a value kind keeps x/x in two more cases (ROADMAP CE-507.3 and CE-507.4). A parameter that the declared signature types with a value kind is typed so in the body, so that x/x is not folded to 1 before a kind value arrives. This did not happen with an overloaded signature: with g: ((residue) -> residue) & ((integer) -> integer) and the body x ↦ x/x, g(ResidueClass(2, 5)) was 1 and is now ResidueClass(1, 5) (the parameter is typed with the union of its types in the arms). It also did not happen for a recursive function literal assigned to a symbol declared with a function type: the literal was boxed again to bind its call to itself, and that step dropped the type.

  • N() of an integral whose integrand restricts a list gives one integral per element (Tycho row 459). With E = [0.1, 0.5], ∫_0^1 y·When(∫_{−1}^{1} 1/ElementMax(E, |x|) dx, 0 ≤ y ≤ 5) dy gave NaN, and ∫_0^1 \{0 ≤ y ≤ 5: 1/ElementMax(E, y+1)\} dy stayed unevaluated. Both now give a list, here [1 + ln 10, 1 + ln 2]. A When(L, c) or a Which with list values, alone or in a product, is distributed over the elements of the list before the integration. A condition that is a list of booleans is a mask, as before.

  • A nested numeric integral of piecewise functions converges. The body ∫_0^1 y·∫_{−10}^{10} n(x, y, ε) dx dy of Tycho's document neyret/2agcgxq87y, where n has a jump and kinks, took about 25 s under N() and stopped at a relative uncertainty of 3e-4, which did not always contain the true error. It now takes about 0.3 s and is correct to 1e-9, for six values of ε. Two causes: a Gauss–Kronrod panel did not see a jump or a kink between its last node and its end, and reported an error near zero; and the error of an inner integral was not added to the error of the outer one. A single integral now makes 15 more evaluations of its integrand.

  • The exact integral of a piecewise with a Nothing branch is no longer wrong. ∫_0^1 Which(y < 1/2, y, True, Nothing) dy gave 5/8, because the antiderivative of Nothing was taken as that of a constant. It now stays unevaluated, and N() gives NaN, as for a Which with no default clause. N() of ∫_0^1 Nothing dx is NaN, as for Missing.

  • A list combined with a piecewise evaluates to a list (Tycho row 452). [0, 1, 2, 3]·Which(x > 1, 0, True, 1) with x free evaluated to Which(1 < x, [0, 0, 0, 0], True, [0, 1, 2, 3]), which is not a List. It now evaluates to [Which(1 < x, 0, True, 0), Which(1 < x, 0, True, 1), …], the same values at each x. The same applies under Add, Abs and a bounded Sum, and to a Which or an If whose values are lists of one length, when the condition is undecided. A Which with no default clause is not changed. When such a Which is combined with an operand, the result now has a last branch for "no condition holds": 3 + Which(x > 1, 0) is Which(1 < x, 3, True, NaN), the value that substituting x first gives.

  • subs() replaces only the free occurrences of a name (Tycho row 464). Comprehension(j + 1, Element(j, Range(0, 2))).subs({j: [4, 4, 5]}) replaced the index and its binding site, and the index of a Sum, the parameter of a Function and a Block local became Error nodes. A binder now keeps its bound variables: j + Sum(j, Limits(j, 1, 3)) with {j: 10} gives 10 + Sum(j, Limits(j, 1, 3)). The occurrences replaced are exactly those that freeVariables reports, so the bounds of a Limits clause, which read the enclosing binding, are still replaced. A substitution can still capture a name: Sum(j + k, Limits(k, 1, 3)) with {j: k} gives Sum(2k, …); rename the index first to avoid this.

  • On wgsl and glsl, a call that several user functions repeat with the same arguments is computed once per pixel (Tycho row 467). Each user function was emitted as its own shader function, and the common-subexpression pass worked inside one function only. The Metal compiler under WebGPU does not merge identical calls across functions, so Tycho's voronoi-diagram drew about 2.2 times slower on WebGPU than on WebGL. The pure, non-recursive user functions of a shader are now substituted at the root, and a sum with literal bounds that calls one is written out, so the existing pass computes each shared call once. On that row, sqrt is computed 16 times per pixel (was 560) and sin 32 times (was 544). The shader text is about 50% larger. An expression that draws a random number, or a sum that stays a loop, is compiled as before.

  • A recursive function whose step passes its own call to Max or Min is no longer typed any (Tycho row 468, a regression in 0.170.0). With S(a, b) = Max(a, b) and R(i) = Which(i = 0, 0, True, R(i − 1) + S(1, R(i − 1))), R(3) was typed any. The type of a call whose body is Max or Min over numbers and tuples is now number on its tuple arm, since Max and Min read the coordinates of a tuple (Max(1, (2, 3)) is 3), so R(3) gets the same type as R without the call to S.

  • Compiling a Sum or a Product whose bounds are above 2^53 no longer hangs. compile(\sum_{k=2^{53}}^{2^{53}+2} \sin(x+k)) never returned on javascript, glsl, wgsl and interval-js, because at 2^53 the index k + 1 is k again. The compile now declines with out-of-range, the answer the interpreter gives for the same bounds.

  • Reading a chain of lazy Map/Zip collections through index lists is linear in the depth of the chain (Tycho row 453). A read such as C[1] of Map(W ↦ max(W[1], W[2]), Zip(A[I], Map(…))), nested 4 deep over 20 elements, computed 282 560 inner elements (about 17 s). It now computes 160. A pure lazy collection keeps each element that a read by index computes, until a symbol it depends on is assigned again.

  • On interval-js, run() throws a ReferenceError instead of answering entire. A ReferenceError means that the compiled code names something that is not defined, for example a helper of an operator's compileHelpers that reads a variable from outside its own body. The compileHelpers documentation says that such a read throws on every thread, and the javascript target already threw. The function that createIntervalRuntime().load() returns for a stored result does the same. Other run-time errors still answer entire ("cannot bound"). A helper of compileHelpers is defined for run() on interval-js, which is now tested.

  • On wgsl, a piecewise branch that draws a random value compiles to an if statement when the branch draws once and nothing else in the same statement draws (Tycho row 466), so only the branch that is taken draws, as in the interpreter and on glsl. \operatorname{WithRandomSeed}(s, \{x<0: \operatorname{Random}(), 0\}) compiles, and so does 1 + it. Other shapes still decline, because a hoisted if runs ahead of the rest of its statement and could change the order of the draws. 0.170.0 already used the if form, but also for a branch that draws twice, such as (\operatorname{Random}(), \cot(\operatorname{Random}())), where it drew the second value first; that shape declines again. (The 0.170.0 note that such a branch no longer compiles on wgsl describes the release before.)

  • On glsl and wgsl, a random draw bound to a temporary no longer comes before a draw written before it. A lowering that uses an operand twice (\cot, \operatorname{Remainder}, the components of a vector in \max) binds an operand that draws to a temporary ahead of its statement, and a Sum or Product hoists its loop or its terms the same way. So (\operatorname{Random}(), \cot(\operatorname{Random}())) drew the operand of \cot first, and (\operatorname{Random}(), \sum_{k=1}^{n} \operatorname{Random}()) drew the loop first, unlike the interpreter and the javascript target. Such a shape now declines, and the interpreter evaluates it; a statement whose draws are bound in their written order (\operatorname{Variance} of a list of draws, a Sum that is written first) still compiles.

  • An interval value for interval arithmetic (#416): the Enclosure value kind (see Features). With this third phase, the value kinds of #477 are complete: the mechanism and ResidueClass (phase 1), Measurement and Quantity (phase 2), and Enclosure (phase 3).

0.170.0 2026-10-26​

Breaking Changes​

  • The package is ESM only, and Node 22.12 or later is required. The UMD builds (dist/umd-min/*.cjs), the require conditions of the exports map and the ComputeEngine script-tag global are gone. A CommonJS consumer keeps calling require('@cortex-js/compute-engine'): Node loads the ESM entry through require() since Node 22.12 (and 20.19), and no entry has a top-level await. engines.node is >=22.12.0 (it was >=22.3.0). A CommonJS Jest setup that imports the package loads it through Jest's own module loader, not Node's, and needs a transform exception for the package or an ESM-capable runner. The published files drop from 61 MB to 24 MB.
  • A program that loads only @cortex-js/compute-engine/core has the javascript and interval-js compilation targets. The GPU targets (glsl, wgsl) and the source-only python target are no longer bundled in that entry (together 408 KB minified). To use one there, import the target class from @cortex-js/compute-engine/compile and register it: ce.registerCompilationTarget('glsl', new GLSLTarget()). Once the full entry, …/epsil or the epsil CLI is loaded anywhere in the program, every engine has all five targets, an engine made earlier from …/core included. An unregistered target name fails with a message that lists the registered ones.

Packaging​

  • One copy of each class across the entries. Every entry except runtime and kernel-worker is now built in one code-splitting invocation, so the engine and the modules it shares with …/numerics, …/latex-syntax and …/interval are emitted once into shared chunks. A host that imported …/core and …/compile loaded two copies of the engine (compile.js was 3.5 MB on its own), and a NumericValue made from …/numerics failed the engine's instanceof checks. One effect: a JavaScriptTarget imported from …/compile compiled n(n-1)(n-2)/6, boxed by the main entry, to 0.16666666666666666 * … (559.9999999999999 at n = 16); it is now (…) / 6, which gives 560 (#480, reported by enumeratio). runtime and kernel-worker stay single self-contained files.
  • ce.registerCompilationTarget(name, target) and ce.unregisterCompilationTarget(name) are public. The compile guide documented the first under that name, but only the internal _registerCompilationTarget existed.

Behavior Changes​

  • The code that a caller's operator compile handler writes no longer goes to the worker pool (ROADMAP CE-518, Tycho row 460). Such code can call a function that exists only on the thread that compiled it, for example globalThis.myFloorIndex(…). The result had shippable: true, so broadcastAsync() sent it to the workers, where every cell threw: each value was NaN, and the batch still reported every cell as done. Now a result with code from a caller handler has shippable: false and runs on the calling thread (reason: 'not-shippable'). This also holds for a handler attached in place to a built-in definition (ce.lookupDefinition('At').operator.compile = …). The handlers of the standard library are not affected. To send such code to the pool again, set compileShippable: true on the definition, and give the functions that the code calls in compileHelpers (see Features).
  • A point parameter accepts a list that can hold both points and lists. With k: (tuple<number, number>) -> number and y declared list<P | list<P>>, type A = list<A | P> or type B = list<B> | P (P is tuple<number, number>), k(y) maps by the depth of the value: a point gives a number, [(1, 2), (3, 4)] gives [3, 7] and [[(1, 2)]] gives [[3]]. These calls were refused for every value. A value in which one list holds both a point and a list, such as [(1, 2), [(3, 4)]], still gives an incompatible-type error (the compiled call gives NaN), and the type of the call includes error for it.
  • A point parameter accepts an empty list. k([]) is typed list<number> (it was number, for the value []), and a symbol declared list<never> that holds [] gives [] (it was refused).
  • A point beside an operand that may be a list is typed as a point or a list of points (CE-504). With L: list<unknown>, (x, y)·(2·L[1]) was typed tuple<number, number>, while L := [[1, 2]] gives [(6, 8), (12, 16)]; it is now tuple<number, number> | list<tuple<number, number> | list<any>>. With b: broadcastable<number>, (x, y)·b and (x, y)/b are broadcastable<tuple<number, number>>, and (x, y) + b is broadcastable<error>. A list of points beside a collection pairs each point with an element: p·t with t: tensor<integer> is list<broadcastable<tuple<…>>>; p·v with v: vector<integer^2> is list<tuple<…>>. Compiled JavaScript gives the interpreter's value for a list of points times or divided by a tensor of numbers (it gave wrong values for a matrix), and refuses an operand whose cells may be points.
  • A list of ranges of the same length is accepted as a matrix by the linear-algebra functions. Determinant([1..2, 3..4]) is -2, and Inverse, MatrixMultiply, Dot, LinearSolve and the other functions whose parameter is a matrix read each range as a row; they refused the list with incompatible-type. The list keeps its list<range> type, so [1..2, 3..4]^{-1} and \cdot still apply element by element.
  • A recursive alias of lists of points is accepted at a point parameter. With A = list<A> | list<tuple<number, number>> and y: A, k(y) maps by the depth of the value ([(1, 2), (3, 4)] gives [3, 7]); it was refused. A union of a list of points and a list of lists of points (list<P> | list<list<P>>) also maps by the depth of the value, and the compiled call of a point-or-point-list union now gives the same values as the interpreter (it was refused).
  • An element-wise operation over an operand of type unknown holds a ragged list or a point (CE-502). With L: list<unknown>, 2·L[1] was typed broadcastable<number>, which does not hold [[1], [2, 3]] or (1, 2) in L[1]; it is now list<list<any> | number | tuple> | number | tuple. The same holds for k(L[1]) with k: (real) -> real, and for a call of an undeclared function. A comparison over such an operand can be one boolean ([1, 2] = L[1] compares two whole lists). Compiled code is unchanged. A valueless symbol used as a number is still inferred number.
  • A function with an inferred signature, called with a string or a boolean, is typed from its body (CE-490). With f := x ↦ (-x, x), f("s") was typed tuple<number, number> and is error; with g := x ↦ x + 1, g("s") was number and is error.
  • A parameter used in arithmetic before an index read has a sound signature (CE-503). (P, t) ↦ t·P/(P[1] − 1) was (P: unknown, t: unknown) -> never and is (P: indexed_collection<number>, t: unknown) -> list<number>; applied to ([3, 2], 2) it gives [3, 2], not a list of errors.
  • A product of a list of points and a point is one no-product-between-points error at evaluation, as it already was when boxed (CE-491). With pd := x ↦ x·x[1], pd([(3, 2), (1, 4)]) was a list of two errors.
  • The terms of a sum or a product with a residue class that are not classes are combined by evaluate() (CE-507). x + x + ResidueClass(1, 5) evaluates to 2x + ResidueClass(1, 5) (it was returned as written; only simplify() combined it), and (√2 + π + ResidueClass(1, 5)).N() is 4.5558… + ResidueClass(1, 5) (the two floats were left apart). The rules for the classes themselves do not change.
  • The signatures of the arithmetic operators no longer name residue. Multiply is (number*) -> number again (it was ((number | residue)*) -> number), and Divide, Negate, Power, Root, Sqrt, Square and Subtract lost their residue arm in the same way. They accept a residue class, and a value of any kind that has the matching hook, by a rule that reads the declared kinds, not by their signature. A host that reads these signature strings sees the change, and an incompatible-type error of these operators no longer names residue as an expected type. An engine built without the ResidueClass definition no longer accepts a residue operand at these operators.
  • Two values of a kind written next to each other are a product, as two residue classes are: with GF8 a head of the kind type gf8, \operatorname{GF8}(3)\operatorname{GF8}(5) parses to a Multiply, not to a Tuple. A list of such values is typed list<gf8^2> (it was list<gf8>).
  • Sum, Product and Reduce over residue classes are typed residue. Sum([c1, c2]) was typed number and Map(Negate, [c1, c2]) vector<2>; they are residue and list<residue^2>.
  • A measurement is typed measurement, and a quantity is typed quantity (CE-507). Measurement(2.5, 0.1) was typed with the type of its nominal (real; integer, rational or complex for other nominals), and Quantity(2, m) was typed value. measurement and quantity are new primitive types of the type language. They are kind types: each one is a subtype of value and is disjoint from the number types, so ce.type('measurement').matches('real') is false. A host that compares type strings sees the change, and a host that declared a type named measurement or quantity must rename it. The result type of an operator with a measurement operand changes in the same way: Floor(2.5 ± 0.1) was typed integer and is measurement | number (a propagated uncertainty of 0 gives a plain number), 2 + (2.5 ± 0.1) is measurement, and Max(2 ± 0.1, 2) is integer<2..2> | measurement.
  • A symbol or a function with a body that is declared over a number type refuses a measurement. With s: real (or number, integer), ce.assign('s', Measurement(2, 0.1)) throws; it assigned the measurement. With f: (real) -> real and f := x ↦ x^2, f(2 ± 0.1) is an incompatible-type error; it was 4 ± 0.4, from a body that the canonical form could have changed (x/x is 1 for a real parameter). Declare the parameter real | measurement to accept one. An operator of your own declared over real with an evaluate handler (h) now leaves h(5 ± 0.1) unevaluated: the measurement does not know the derivative of h, so it does not call the handler (it gave 2 · (5 ± 0.1) for evaluate: ([x]) => x.mul(2)). An operator that handles a measurement itself names measurement in its parameter type, and its handler runs.
  • A quantity is refused at every operator that does not accept it by type. The arithmetic operators, the comparisons, Max, Min, Clamp, Sort, the operators with a value parameter (UnitConvert, List), the 24 trigonometric functions and Abs accept a quantity. Every other operator gives an incompatible-type error at boxing: Round(2.7 m), Floor(2 m), Sign(2 m), Exp(2 m), Hypot(2 m, 3) and InverseHaversine(2 m) stayed unevaluated or gave a wrong value, and Mean([2 m, 4 m]) stayed unevaluated.
  • The trigonometric functions and Abs name quantity in their signatures. The 24 trigonometric, hyperbolic and inverse functions (Sin to Arcsch) are (complex | quantity) -> number (a function that accepted infinity or signed_infinity keeps that arm), and Abs is (complex | infinity | quantity) -> number. So Arctan(2 deg) folds the angle to Arctan(π/90) as the other functions do (it stayed Arctan(2 deg)), Abs(-2 m) is 2 m, typed quantity (it stayed unevaluated, typed value), and Sin(2 m) is typed number (it was value) and stays unevaluated. The incompatible-type error of these functions names the quantity arm as an expected type (Sin("a") expects complex | quantity), and so does the type of Derivative(Sin).
  • A measurement propagates its uncertainty through every operator with a known derivative, and stays unevaluated where the rule has no answer. The rule is f(a) ± |f′(a)|·σ, and the quadrature √(Σ |∂f/∂xᵢ|²·σᵢ²) for several uncertain operands, with the modulus of each partial derivative. A propagated uncertainty of 0 gives the bare value (Cos(0 ± 0.1) is 1, as before). The rules by operator:
    • A step function (Floor, Ceil, Round, Truncate, Sign, Heaviside, PrimePi) of a real measurement gives the bare value of the function at the nominal: Floor(2.5 ± 0.1) is 2. When a jump of the function lies within one σ of the nominal, the call stays unevaluated: Floor(2.95 ± 0.1) was 2. A complex nominal at Sign stays unevaluated.
    • Mod and Fract propagate with the slope between their jumps: Mod(5 ± 0.1, 3) is 2 ± 0.1 (it was 2), and Mod(7, 3 ± 0.1) is 1 ± 0.2. A jump within one σ leaves the call unevaluated.
    • An infinite value or an infinite derivative at the nominal leaves the call unevaluated: Sqrt(0 ± 0.1) was 0, Arcsin(1 ± 0.1) was π/2; Ln(0 ± 0.1), Gamma(0 ± 0.1) and Tan(π/2 ± 0.1) are unevaluated too. A float nominal near a pole (Tan(1.5707963 ± 0.1)) gives the large finite value with its large uncertainty.
    • A real nominal whose value is not real keeps an uncertainty: Arccos(2.5 ± 0.1) is 1.5668i ± 0.0436 (it was the bare 1.5668i), and Ln(-1 ± 0.1) is πi ± 0.1.
    • Hypot, Degrees, Haversine, InverseHaversine, Factorial, Log with an uncertain base, Arctan2, Root with an uncertain index, Norm with an uncertain order, Round with an uncertain step, PreIncrement, PreDecrement, and the multilinear operators Dot, Cross, MatrixMultiply, HadamardProduct and Trace propagate every uncertain operand. Dot([2.5 ± 0.1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3]) is 15.5 ± 0.1.
    • Binomial, Choose, Pochhammer, Determinant, Inverse, Eigenvalues, ContinuedFraction, ComplexRoots, Arg, Argument and BaseForm stay unevaluated with a measurement operand, and so does an operator whose derivative the engine does not know (Zeta, Beta, the order of BesselJ). Binomial(5 ± 0.1, 2) was (5 ± 0.1)·((5 ± 0.1) − 1)/2 and Determinant([[1 ± 0.1, 2], [3, 4]]) was -2 ± 0.4: these formulas use the same measurement more than once, and the arithmetic of measurements counts each occurrence as an independent error.
    • Mean, Median, Variance, PopulationVariance, StandardDeviation and PopulationStandardDeviation of a list that holds measurements give the statistic of the nominals with the propagated uncertainty of the independent data. The other statistics (Skewness, Kurtosis, …) stay unevaluated.
    • Real, Imaginary, Conjugate and Abs keep the uncertainty of the operand: Abs(0 ± 0.1) is 0 ± 0.1.
  • A comparison of measurements uses the nominals. The uncertainties take no part: 1 ± 0.1 = 1 ± 0.5 is True, as before.
    • Max and Min decide by nominal and keep the first operand of a tie: Max(1 ± 0.1, 1 ± 0.5) is 1 ± 0.1 (it stayed unevaluated), and Max(2 ± 0.1, 2) is 2 ± 0.1 (it was 2).
    • Clamp(x, lo, hi) returns x when x equals a bound: Clamp(3 ± 0.1, 0, 3) is 3 ± 0.1 (it was 3).
    • ElementMax and ElementMin compare as Max and Min do.
    • A measurement with a complex nominal has no order: (2 + 3i) ± 0.1 < 3 is False, as 2 + 3i < 3 is, and Max of it stays unevaluated. Its equality is the equality of the nominal: Equal((2 + 3i) ± 0.1, 2 + 3i) is True.
    • A measurement is not exact: Max(3/2 ± 1/10, Indeterminate) is NaN, not Indeterminate.
  • A comparison of quantities converts to the finer unit and uses the engine tolerance there, also in Max, Min, Clamp, ElementMax, ElementMin and Sort. Max(1 m, 1.000000000001 m) is 1 m: the extrema compared with a tolerance of zero. The tolerance applies in the finer of the two units, so Equal(1 m, 100.0000000001 cm) stays False. A quantity with a magnitude that is a float is not exact: Max(1.5 m, Indeterminate) is NaN.
  • The methods .add(), .mul(), .div(), .pow(), .sub() and .sqrt() combine measurements and quantities as the evaluation does. M.add(M2) for M = 3 ± 0.1 and M2 = 2 ± 0.1 is 5 ± 0.141 (it was the sum (3 ± 0.1) + (2 ± 0.1)), and (2 m).add(30 cm) is 2.3 m (it was 30 cm + 2 m). .neg() does not call the negate hook of a kind: c.neg() is Negate(c), and Negate(c).evaluate() negates the value.
  • .re and .im of a measurement are the parts of its nominal, as before: Measurement(2.5, 0.1).re is 2.5. The numeric facts of a measurement (isPositive, sgn, isInteger) are undefined; they were the facts of the nominal (Measurement(4, 0.1).isInteger was true). So the canonical forms of the numbers do not apply to a measurement.
  • The uncertainties of several occurrences of one measurement are independent. The engine does not know that two occurrences of M are the same measurement: with M = 1 ± 0.1, Sin(M)^2 + Cos(M)^2 simplifies to 1 ± 0.13 (it simplified to 1), and M − M is 0 ± 0.141. The operators that use an operand more than once in their own formula (Binomial, Determinant, …) stay unevaluated for this reason.
  • A physical constant opens the quantity rules only when it is read. The value of SpeedOfLight and of the other physical constants is a quantity. An engine that never makes a quantity does not pay the cost of the quantity rules: the constants made while the libraries load do not count, and each constant makes its value again when it is first read.
  • Compiling an expression with a measurement or a quantity fails with a message that names the kind type ("holds a value of the kind type 'measurement'"). It failed before with "Could not compile Measurement". Neither kind has a compiled representation.

Features​

  • An operator compile handler can give the functions its code calls (ROADMAP CE-518). The new compileHelpers field of an operator definition maps a name to a function. The engine copies the source of each function into the compiled code, as const <name> = (<source>);, so the code carries its helpers to a worker of the pool and to a stored result. With compileShippable: true, the result can then run on the pool:

    ce.declare('Wrap', {
      signature: '(number, number) -> number',
      compileShippable: true,
      compileHelpers: { wrapIndex: (i, n) => ((i % n) + n) % n },
      compile: (args, compile, { language }) =>
        language === 'javascript'
          ? `wrapIndex(${compile(args[0])}, ${compile(args[1])})`
          : undefined,
    });

    A helper must not read a variable from outside its own body, and its name is an identifier that does not start with _. A built-in function, a bound function or a method has no source that can be copied, and the declaration refuses it. The compile contract of a value kind has the same field, arithmetic.compile.type.helpers (ROADMAP CE-507.1); hostNames there now names only the functions of the host that the code does not carry.

  • broadcastAsync() reports the cells that threw. The new failed field of BroadcastAsyncResult counts the cells, among the first done, whose evaluation threw, on the calling thread and on the workers. The value of such a cell is NaN, as for a cell whose value is not a number, so this count is the only way to tell the two apart. done keeps its meaning: a cell that threw was evaluated.

  • An operator can declare the arithmetic of the values it constructs: a value kind (ROADMAP CE-507, #477). With MyMod declared (integer, integer) -> residue, x + MyMod(2, 4) + MyMod(1, 4) and MyMod(2, 4) - MyMod(2, 4) stayed as they were: only ResidueClass values were combined, and no definition could give the arithmetic of another head. The new arithmetic field of an operator definition gives it:

    • The field (ArithmeticDefinition) has the hooks add and multiply (they answer folds, KindFold: the operands they combined and the value they make), negate, divide, power (also called for Sqrt, Root and Square), compare (one order for the comparisons, Max, Min, Sort, Clamp and the methods isEqual(), isLess(), …), apply (called in place of the handler of another operator that accepted the value as a number), and the fields admittedAs, resultType and compile. The new public types are ArithmeticDefinition, KindOperands, KindOperand, KindFold, ArithmeticContext and ArithmeticCompile. With MyMod declared with add, multiply and negate, x + MyMod(2, 4) + MyMod(1, 4) is x + MyMod(3, 4), and MyMod(2, 4) - MyMod(2, 4) is MyMod(0, 4), in evaluate() and simplify().
    • The result type of an operator with an arithmetic field must be a kind type: residue, or a nominal type defined as exactly value and declared with { mint: false }, such as ce.declareType('gf8', 'value', { mint: false }). Such a nominal type is a subtype of value and expression, and is disjoint from every other type, as residue is: the engine keeps the number rules (x - x = 0, x/x = 1, like terms) away from its values and from a symbol declared with it. Any other result type (integer, value, residue | integer, a nominal type with another definition) is refused when the operator is declared, with an error that names the rule.
    • The mint option of ce.declareType() is public. { mint: false } declares a type without a constructor of the same name; a kind uses it, because its values are made by its own operator.
    • admittedAs: 'real' or 'number' lets every operator that accepts a real (or a number) accept the values, and apply then computes the result: a measurement kind can propagate its error through Sin and Floor. admittedAs: 'none' (the default, and the rule of residue) admits the values at the arithmetic operators only.
    • compile gives a compiled representation to a kind type (compile.type) and to the literals of a head (compile.value). Code compiled with it reports the kind types in the new CompilationResult.valueKinds, and the bindings of a kind type in StoredEntryPlan.kinds; it is returned without the number conversion of run(), and createJavaScriptRuntime().load() refuses it, because the run-time check of a kind is a function of the host. Without compile, an expression with a value of a kind declines, as a residue class does.

    ResidueClass now declares its arithmetic with this field. The design, which also covers Quantity, Measurement and an interval value (#416) in later phases, is docs/plans/2026-10-26-value-kinds.md. The guide is doc/06-guide-augmenting.md, "Declaring a Value Kind"; the type rules are in doc/08-guide-types.md, "Kind Types".

  • Measurement and Quantity are value kinds (ROADMAP CE-507 phase 2, CE-508, #477). Their arithmetic, their order and their propagation of an uncertainty are now the hooks of their arithmetic field, and the operators no longer test the names Measurement and Quantity. The visible changes are listed under Behavior Changes and Resolved Issues.

    • Measurement has the kind type measurement and is accepted where a number is accepted (admittedAs: 'number'). An operator that accepted the measurement as a number calls the apply hook of the kind, which computes the value at the nominal and propagates the uncertainty.
    • Quantity has the kind type quantity and is accepted only by the arithmetic operators, the comparisons, the operators that name quantity and the operators with a value parameter (admittedAs: 'none'). Its add hook makes one sum for each physical dimension, in the unit with the largest scale, and reads how each term was written to add temperatures with an offset: 20 degC − 5 degC is 15 K, and 20 degC + 5 degC is 571.3 K, as before.
    • ArithmeticDefinition.compare can answer 'unordered': the two values are known and have no order (a measurement with a complex nominal). The order operators then answer False, Equal and NotEqual ask the eq handlers, and Max, Min and Sort stay unevaluated.
    • ArithmeticDefinition.isExact(value) says whether a value of the kind is exact, for the rule that an inexact operand turns Indeterminate into NaN. Absent: the values are exact.
    • ArithmeticDefinition.isNaN(value) says whether a value of the kind stands for no value, as the number NaN does (a measurement with a NaN nominal, a quantity with a NaN magnitude). Such a value follows the rule of NaN: Max, Min, ElementMax, ElementMin and Clamp give NaN, the order operators give False, and Equal gives False, also for the value and itself. Absent: no value of the kind is NaN.
    • KindOperands.written holds the operands as they were written on every route: under simplify(), the operands before their simplification. So a kind whose negate gives a value and whose add reads Negate(b) in written gives the same difference under evaluate(), .N() and simplify().
    • ArithmeticDefinition.numericValue(value) gives the number that a value of the kind stands for. re, im, bignumRe, bignumIm and valueOf() of the value read it. The fact queries (isPositive, sgn, …) do not.
    • ArithmeticContext.tolerance gives the compare hook the tolerance of .is(): the tolerance argument of the call, or engine.tolerance. So M.is(2.6, 0.2) for M = 2.5 ± 0.1 uses the tolerance 0.2. It is undefined for the other comparisons.

    The rules are in doc/06-guide-augmenting.md, "Measurements and Quantities"; the decisions are in section 13 of docs/plans/2026-10-26-value-kinds.md.

  • factor() accepts variable and generator options, and a new factorDetailed() returns a structured result. factor(p, { variable, generator }) factors over an explicit number field, as Factor(p, x, generator) does. factorDetailed() returns the exact factors with their multiplicities, the scalar content, whether the factorization is complete, and the reason and stage of a refusal; with statistics: true it also returns the work counts of each step. Both are exported from the main and the core entry points. No MathJSON operator is added.

  • Number-field factoring lifts at unramified prime ideals of any residue degree. It used to need an inert prime, and ten inputs of the extended number-field corpus were refused because none was found. The factors are recovered with an exact lattice reduction and the recombination is certified. A weighted scaling of the generator and the variable and tighter bounds on the coefficients of a divisor reduce coefficient growth. When the coefficients are rational, the norm fallback skips the unshifted norm, which is always repeated. The statistics keep the reason the direct method failed before a norm fallback.

  • Number-field factoring reads x^n monomials directly when it converts an expanded polynomial of high degree, and no longer refuses such an input because the conversion went over its budget.

Resolved Issues​

  • A coordinate of a list of points inside PointList compiles to a list (CE-514, Tycho row 447). On the javascript target, (v ↦ PointList(PointY(v), PointX(v)))([(1, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6)]) compiled to [NaN, NaN]; it now gives [[2, 1], [5, 4]], as evaluate() does. The same holds for a named function called with a list of points. A PointX/PointY/PointZ component whose operand is not provably one point is a zip source when its value is an array and one slot otherwise, decided at run time. The type of the call is now a list of points too: f(L) for a list L of two points with integer coordinates is a list<tuple<integer, integer>^2>, where it was tuple<unknown, unknown>.
  • A call of a function whose signature was inferred is typed from its body with each parameter typed as its argument, when the type inferred for the result does not describe the call (CE-514). The result inferred for v ↦ PointList(PointY(v), PointX(v)) is one point, and a call with a list of points evaluates to a list of points. The call was typed one point; it is now typed from the body. This applies only when the inferred result is not a scalar and the walk of the body bounded by it gives no type, and only for arguments that are numbers or lists of numbers or points. A result type that the host declares, or that the literal writes, stays the bound, and a function that reads a symbol from outside its parameters keeps its inferred result, so a call after that symbol changes type is still refused (CE-473).
  • Five shader fixes found by comparing WebGL2 and WebGPU on a GPU (CE-509 to CE-513, Tycho rows 454 to 458).
    • On wgsl, tanh calls a helper that answers sign(x) when |x| > 10. On WebGPU over Metal the built-in returned 0 at x = 44 and NaN from x = 45, where the value is 1. Coth is 1.0 / tanh(x) on both targets: the quotient cosh(x) / sinh(x) was NaN above about 89 in f32.
    • On wgsl, a constant above the f32 maximum (\exp(100) + x, 10^{40} + x) is written _gpu_inf(), and a constant that rounds to the maximum is written as the maximum. WebGPU rejected the whole shader for such a literal.
    • On glsl, Mod stays in the range of the divisor. The built-in mod gave mod(1e8, 3.0) = -2 and mod(-1e6, 1000.0) = 1000 on WebGL2 over ANGLE Metal; they are now 1 and 0. On both targets Mod(x, 1) is fract(fract(x)), so a tiny negative x gives 0 instead of 1.0.
    • On both targets, Mod calls a _gpu_fmod helper, which receives each operand once. On wgsl the inline formula wrote the dividend three times and the divisor five times.
    • On wgsl, a piecewise arm that calls a user function, or a special function with a loop (Zeta, HurwitzZeta, PolyLog, LerchPhi, BesselJ, Mandelbrot, …), becomes a branch of an if statement. select computes both arms: with g(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{300}\cos(ix), \{x<0 : g(x), 0\} took 5.05 ms on WebGPU against 2.36 ms with an if.
  • sin, cos and tan of a quotient π·u / d compile to the exact half-turn forms (sinpi, cospi, tanpi) on every target, as π·u already did. \sin(2\pi s / P) at s = 2, P = -2 is now exactly 0 in the compiled code; it was 2.4e-16 in JavaScript, so a test \sin(…) > 0 was true in the compiled code and false in the interpreter. e^{i\pi u/d} and the hyperbolic functions of i\pi u/d take the exact forms too.
  • On wgsl, a piecewise branch that draws a random value no longer compiles (it is evaluated by the interpreter instead). WGSL select computes every branch, so a draw in a branch that was not taken still advanced the random stream and changed every later draw in the shader. glsl is unchanged: its ?: evaluates only the branch that is taken.
  • On glsl, Mod of a scalar by a vector compiles (Mod(1, v) broadcasts the scalar); the built-in mod has no such overload, and it was refused.
  • On glsl and wgsl, Sin, Cos, Sec, Csc, Cot, Sign, Smoothstep and Heaviside give NaN when the operand is NaN (CE-520), as the javascript target does. On Apple GPUs the built-ins sin, cos, sign and smoothstep of a NaN gave 0 (so \sec x gave +∞), and the GLSL Heaviside gave 0.5. They now call helpers that test the bit pattern of the operand, as Max and Min do (CE-519). \tan(\pi x) on the shader targets is now +∞ at every pole, as on the other compiled targets; it was +∞ or −∞ depending on the sign of the zero cosine, and not the same on WebGL2 and WebGPU.
  • On glsl and wgsl, Max, Min, Clamp, ElementMax and ElementMin give NaN when an operand is NaN (CE-519, Tycho row 465), as the interpreter and the javascript target do. The shader built-ins return the other operand on Apple GPUs, so \max(0, \sqrt{1 - x^2}) at x = 2 was 0. The targets now call helpers that test the bit pattern of each operand (a test a != a was removed by the compiler on WebGPU over Metal) and return the NaN operand itself. Clamp(x, lo, hi) with lo > hi now gives hi on glsl as on the other targets (the built-in clamp left it undefined). A vector Clamp with scalar bounds, and an ElementMax or ElementMin of a vector and a scalar in any position, now compile on both targets: the scalar is broadcast, as in the interpreter. They were refused on wgsl, and on glsl when the scalar came first.
  • A part of a loop body printed or evaluated outside its operator keeps its index (CE-498). ReplaceAt([1,2,3], i, 9) taken from Loop(…, Element(i, Range(1, 3))) printed an incompatible-type error, with i read as the imaginary unit; it now prints ReplaceAt([1,2,3], i, 9).
  • An undeclared recursive pair that builds a list is typed -> list<number> in every install order (CE-38). Assigning G := (n, K) ↦ F(n, K) before F gave -> list<any>.
  • A symbol declared list<residue> is accepted by the arithmetic operators (CE-507). With L: list<residue>, L + L, -L and L · 2 were incompatible-type errors when boxed, while a list literal of classes was accepted. They are typed list<residue> and are computed element by element.
  • A boxed function literal mapped over residue classes keeps the rules of the classes (CE-507). ce.function('Map', [ce.box(x ↦ x/x), [ResidueClass(2, 4), ResidueClass(3, 4)]]) gave [1, 1]: the body was simplified to 1 before the type of the elements was known, and 2 has no inverse modulo 4. It now gives [ResidueClass(2, 4) / ResidueClass(2, 4), ResidueClass(1, 4)], as ce.box() and ce.parse() of the same expression do.
  • Measurements and quantities: wrong values and wrong types (CE-508, fixed by making Measurement and Quantity value kinds, CE-507).
    • Quantity(2, m) − Quantity(2, m) simplifies to 0 m. It simplified to the number 0, without the unit.
    • Quantity(2, m) + Quantity(30, cm) simplifies to 2.3 m, and Quantity(2, m) · Quantity(3, s) to 6 m·s. simplify() returned them unchanged.
    • x + Quantity(2, m) + Quantity(3, m) evaluates to x + 5 m. It stayed unchanged, because one operand was not a quantity.
    • Measurement(2, 0.1) − Measurement(2, 0.1) simplifies to Measurement(0, 0.141…), as it evaluates. It simplified to 0.
    • ResidueClass(2, 5) + Quantity(3, m) is typed quantity | residue. It was typed list<list<any> | residue> | residue.
    • A comparison that is not decided keeps the measurement: Less(Measurement(2, 0.1), x) evaluates to itself. It evaluated to Less(2, x), without the uncertainty, and Equal did the same.
    • A measurement with a complex nominal at an operator whose parameter is real is an incompatible-type error at evaluation: ContinuedFraction((2 + 3i) ± 0.1) was [2], and Floor, Mod, Hypot, Degrees and the other operators with a real parameter read the real part.
    • A unit is no longer read as a free symbol: InverseHaversine(Quantity(2, m)) evaluated to 2·arcsin(√2·√m). A quantity at an operator that does not accept it is now an incompatible-type error at boxing.
    • Measurement(2, 0.1).isLess(3) is true and .isEqual(2) is true. The methods answered undefined, while Less and Equal answered True.
    • A complex nominal keeps its uncertainty through every operator with a derivative: Arctan((2 + 3i) ± 0.1) is (1.4099 + 0.2291i) ± 0.0079. The uncertainty was dropped for some operators and kept for others, depending on how the derivative was printed.
    • Log2(Measurement(2 + 3i, 0.1)) is (1.8502 + 1.4179i) ± 0.0400. It was 1, a wrong value: the logarithms read only the real part of a complex nominal.
    • Two uncertain complex operands add the moduli of their contributions: Measurement(1, 0.1) · Measurement(i, 0.1) is i ± 0.1414. The two contributions cancelled, and the result was the bare i.
    • Power(-2, Measurement(2, 0.1)) is 4 ± 1.3, propagated with the principal logarithm of the base. It was the exact 4, without an uncertainty. An uncertain exponent of the base 0 leaves the power unevaluated.

0.169.2 2026-10-26​

Behavior Changes​

  • An open record type is no longer a dictionary of its listed field types (CE-4, CE-10). record{a: integer} was a subtype of dictionary<integer> and is not now, because the record can hold other fields; the relation is now transitive. A dictionary value such as {a: 1} still matches dictionary<integer>. A read by a key known only at evaluation on an open record is typed any.
  • A declared type with unknown at a nested position refines from each assignment (CE-3.5): t: tuple<unknown, integer> := ("x", 2) was tuple<unknown, integer> and is tuple<string, integer>.
  • The static type of a block local no longer depends on statement order (CE-43): mutate(v); v = [1.5, 2] typed v as list<real>; it is vector<real^2>, as in the other order. An assignment inside a match case or a while let body widens the local: let xs = [1,2,3]; while let [h, ...] = xs { xs = Rest(xs) }; xs was typed vector<integer^3> for the value [], and is list<integer>.
  • A let-bound function literal's effects follow a later conformance (CE-62.2), and so do its callers.
  • A numeric tuple at a scalar parameter is a tuple of numbers (CE-47): h((1, 2)) with h := x ↦ 2x was any and is tuple<number, number>. A tuple with a tuple or string component is any; h(((1, 2), 3)) was typed number for the value ((2, 4), 6).
  • Map over elements whose depth the type does not state admits nested lists: Map(k, L) with k: (real) -> real and L: list<unknown> (or list<any>, list<list<unknown>>) was typed list<real>, which did not hold a ragged or nested element, and is list<indexed_collection<any> | real>. An operand typed any at a declared scalar parameter types the same on the box and derived routes (CE-485).
  • A nominal list-of-points type is not read through its definition (CE-488): k(x) with k: (tuple<number, number>) -> number and x of a nominal list<tuple<…>> type was typed list<number> and is error, as its value is.
  • An access proved to be out of range is typed by its marker alone (CE-42.3): At(["a","b"], 9) was missing | string and is missing; M[7][1] over a matrix was integer | nan and is nan. Arithmetic over a proved-absent row or point is Missing.
  • A local declared any keeps its type (CE-444), and an operand typed any at a generic collection parameter no longer fixes the element type from the other operands: ReplaceAt(ys, 2, "z") with ys: any was list<string> and is list<any>.
  • An absent value of a symbol declared any gives NaN in arithmetic on every route: with p: any assigned Missing, p + 1 was Missing and is NaN, as subs and compiled code already gave.

Resolved Issues​

  • subs() on a structural expression that is a lone symbol keeps a constant name in the replacement. With x declared real, the structural x with x replaced by the structural t + i gave t + (0 + 1i) in 0.168.0 to 0.169.1, so a sum with an index i over an inlined f(x) = x gave complex values: with X = [1, 2, 3], Σ_{i=1}^{3} f(X + i) gave [3+3i, 6+3i, 9+3i]. It gives [9, 12, 15] again. A requested form (subs(…, { canonical: true })) is still honored.

  • The count of a comprehension matches its cells when a clause can fail. [j for i in 1..3 if bad(i), j in []], where the guard gives an error, had a count of 0 but yields 3 error cells; its count is now 3.

  • Testing whether a comprehension is finite no longer runs user code. The test does not evaluate a guard or an impure domain, so let r = [i for i in 1..3, j in filter(1..i, keep)] no longer calls keep.

  • A Map, Filter or Reduce callback follows a reassignment of its source. With L := [1, 2] and m = Map(x ↦ x + 1, L), a later L := [["a"]] made m.evaluate() a list of incompatible-type errors; it now gives the value that a fresh Map gives.

  • Range(n) with n < 1 counts down from 1 on every route. A raw Range(0) and the compiled JavaScript Range(0) were empty; they are now [1, 0], as the canonical form already was.

  • A coefficient times an ellipsis product keeps the product whole. 3(2·4·…·2n) evaluated, expanded and simplified to 3·2·4·…·2·n or 48·…·n; it now stays 3·(2·4·…·2n). The same holds in a sum: x + 3(2·4·…·2n) was x + 48·(…·n), and like terms still collect ((2·4·…·2n) + (2·4·…·2n) is 2(2·4·…·2n)).

  • The type of Negate, Sqrt and the other element-wise functions of a list of range rows holds its value. Negate([1..3, 4..6]) was typed list<range> for a matrix of integers; it is now list<list<integer>>. Sum([1..2, 3..4]) is typed integer | list<integer> (it was number, for the value [4, 6]).

  • An undeclared recursive pair that builds a list is typed -> list<number> (CE-38), and a function literal boxed before the function it calls is typed once that function is assigned: g := (n, K) ↦ f(n, K) boxed before f := (n, K) ↦ n + K was -> unknown and is -> number.

  • A polymorphic callback over rows (CE-30): Map(k, [[x ↦ x + 1]]) with k: ((integer) -> T) -> T was matrix<unknown^(1x1)> and is matrix<number^(1x1)>.

  • The meet and overlap of chains of list, set and tuple aliases (CE-449) finish in under 0.25 s at depth 32; they took several seconds, or did not finish.

0.169.1 2026-10-25​

Behavior Changes​

  • references and referencedFunctions list a name that already has a value or a definition. They give the dependencies of an expression, for example the edges between the cells of a notebook, and they lost an edge as soon as the cell it points to was evaluated. After ce.assign('a', 5), g(x) := x + a references a (it gave []). Once f is defined by f(x) := …, by ce.assign('f', …) or declared with { signature: … }, g(x) := f(x) + a references a and f (it gave ["a"]), and referencedFunctions is ["f"]. A user function passed as an operand is referenced too: Map(L, f) references L and f. The names of a library (Add, Sin, Pi, …: the standard library, a library given to the constructor, or one loaded with ce.loadLibrary()) and constants are still left out. unknowns and freeVariables are unchanged: they list only the symbols with no value.

Resolved Issues​

  • subs() on a structural expression keeps a constant name in the replacement. With x declared real, the structural x + 1 with x replaced by the structural X + i gave X + (0 + 1i) + 1 in 0.168.0 and 0.169.0: a declared symbol of a structural expression is bound, and its replacement was boxed canonically. It gives X + i + 1 again, in the structural form. An undeclared x was not affected.
  • A function that reads a function declared with an unknown result compiles. With f declared (real | signed_infinity | nan) -> unknown and assigned x ↦ x + A cos(x) + d, the compile of a function whose body reads f as a value (g(t) := f'(t) + 1) was refused: "the symbol 'f' that its body reads holds a value of type (ceArg_0: unknown) -> number". The check now reads the signature that the definition derives with the declared parameter types, -> nan | real | signed_infinity, which is the type ce.assign() accepted. A later change of the type of a symbol that f reads (A assigned 2i) is still refused.

0.169.0 2026-10-25​

Behavior Changes​

  • A finite range of integers and the list of its integers are the same element of a collection. Set(Range(1, 3), [1, 2, 3]) has one element, [1, 2, 3] is an element of [Range(1, 3)], and IndexOf, Unique, Tally, Union and Contains treat the two as one. Range(1, 3), Range(1, 3, 1) and [1, 2, 3] are the same for isSame and have the same hash. The rule applies to a range whose bounds and step are integer literals and that has at most 10,000 elements. Equal is unchanged.
  • A range that is an element of a collection stays a range. [1..3, 4] evaluates to [Range(1, 3), 4] (it was [[1,2,3], 4]), and Tuple(Range(1, 3), 4) to (Range(1, 3), 4), so the value agrees with the type tuple<range, integer>. A symbol declared list<range> holds [Range(1, 3)] (it held [[1, 2, 3]], which is not a list of ranges). The same applies to a Set element, a cell of a broadcast result (g(s) = 1..s; g([2, 3]) is [Range(1, 2), Range(1, 3)]) and a spread element. A range on its own is unchanged, and Length, At, Flatten, Sum and Map give the same values. Other lazy elements, such as a Map or a comprehension, are still listed.
  • LUDecomposition, QRDecomposition and CholeskyDecomposition of a matrix of exact rational entries give exact factors under evaluate(). The LU of [[4, 3], [6, 3]] is ([[0,1],[1,0]], [[1,0],[2/3,1]], [[6,3],[0,1]]) (the lower factor held 0.6666666666666666), and the QR of [[3, 4], [4, 3]] is ([[3/5,4/5],[4/5,-3/5]], [[5,24/5],[0,7/5]]). .N() and a matrix with a float entry still give floats, with the same permutation. A matrix with an exact entry that is not rational, such as √2, now stays unevaluated under evaluate() (it gave floats); .N() decomposes it. The result types state the exact cells: rational for the LU factors, real for QR and Cholesky.
  • The R factor of QRDecomposition has a non-negative diagonal on the exact and the float route. The float route gave R[0][0] = -5 for [[3, 4], [4, 3]], with Q negated to match; it now gives 5.
  • CholeskyDecomposition of a matrix that is not symmetric is the error expected-symmetric-matrix. It read only the lower triangle, so [[4, 0], [2, 3]] gave a factor L with L·Lᵀ = [[4, 2], [2, 3]]. A float matrix that is symmetric within rounding error is accepted.
  • Inverse, MatrixPower and Determinant no longer claim rational cells. A float that holds a whole number (2.0) is typed as an integer, so the claim was wrong for Inverse([[2.0, 1], [1, 3]]), typed matrix<rational^(2x2)> with float cells. The inverse of an integer matrix is now typed matrix<real^(2x2)>, and the determinant of a rational matrix real. The values do not change.
  • A type alias with no fixed point is refused when it is declared. ce.declareType('nn', '!nn', { alias: true }) throws the error alias-without-fixed-point, and the DeclareType and Epsil type alias routes give an invalid-type-declaration error. Recursive aliases such as tree = list<tree> | integer, and aliases that have a fixed point such as !a | any, are still accepted.
  • An Epsil program whose result is a finite comprehension gives a List. [do { k * 2 } for k in 1..3] and let xs = [if k > 1 { k } else { 0 } for k in 1..3]; xs gave an unevaluated Comprehension; they give [2, 4, 6] and [0, 2, 3]. An infinite comprehension stays as it is.
  • \operatorname{implies} and \operatorname{iff} parse as Implies and Equivalent. p \operatorname{implies} q was a product of the symbols implies, p and q. \mathrm{…}, \text{…} and \keyword{…} spellings of the two words parse the same way.
  • The type of a call checks the arguments against a declared signature on every route. With k declared (tuple<number, number>) -> number, the type of a function whose body calls k(3) is error, as the value is; it was number. A list of points at a declared point parameter maps on that route too, so the derived type of k(P) is list<number>.

New Features​

  • A type handler can read whether the engine is strict. The engine view that a type handler receives (PureEngineView) has a strict property, the same value as ce.strict.

Resolved Issues​

  • The structural form keeps a constant name as written again. In 0.168.0, ce.box(['Power', 'i', 2], { form: 'structural' }) gave Power(Complex(0, 1), 2), e became ExponentialE, and Half became 1/2, so M(i) = i^2 read structurally had no parameter named i. A symbol whose canonical form is another expression (i, ImaginaryUnit, e, Half) now keeps its name and is unbound, typed unknown, as in 0.167.0. Every other symbol still binds to its definition: ["Add", "t", "t"] with t: tuple<integer, integer> is typed tuple<integer, integer>. The canonical form and the value are unchanged: the canonical form of the structural i^2 is -1.
  • A compile refused because a captured symbol changed type names that symbol. The message gives the symbol and both of its types, for example "the symbol 'd' that its body reads has the type real, but the body of 'x_0' was typed when 'd' had the type integer".
  • A partial application keeps its argument inside a held operand. With f(a, b) := If(b, a[1] + a[2], 42), f((1, 2)) gave (_) => If(_, At(a, 1) + At(a, 2), 42), and applying it to True gave a[1] + a[2] instead of 3. With m(a, b) := a + b, m(b) applied to 1 gave 2 instead of b + 1: the free parameter was renamed by name and captured the argument b.
  • The type of a call holds its value in more cases.
    • The derived type of At is error for a base that cannot be indexed (a number, a boolean, a set, an interval), as the boxed At is. So with h(a, t) := a[1] + a[2] + t, the partial application h(3) is typed error, as its value is, not (t: unknown) -> number.
    • With k declared (tuple<number, number>) -> number and U(L) := k(First(L)), U([[(1, 2), (3, 4)]]) was typed number for the value [3, 7]. A call whose argument is outside an inferred parameter type is now typed from the body.
    • A union of lists of points maps at a declared point parameter, so Map(L ↦ k(L), [[(1, 2), (3, 4)], [(5, 6)]]) is typed list<list<number>> (it was list<number>).
