    • The type of a call in the body of a function refuses a matrix at a declared list<integer> parameter, as the boxed call does.
  • A Text run whose words are a keyword round-trips through LaTeX. Text(p, "and", q) was written p\text{and}q, which parses as And(p, q). It is now written p\text{{}and}q, which prints the same and parses back as text.
  • An intersection with a never arm is a subtype of never. integer & never was not a subtype of never, nor of itself, so ce.declareType('q', 'integer & never', { alias: true }) threw signature "(integer & never) -> integer & never" does not match.
  • A product with a scalar factor of inferred or unknown type has number cells (CE-481). L·u with L: list<integer> and u inferred number was list<integer> and is list<number>; x ↦ a·x with a := [1, 2, 3] was (x: unknown) -> vector<integer^3>, which did not hold [0.5, 1, 1.5], and is (x: unknown) -> vector<3>.
  • A call over a captured symbol of type unknown no longer claims a scalar result (CE-478). With g := s ↦ 2s and f := t ↦ g(y), f was typed (t: unknown) -> number, and after y := [1, 2, 3] the value of f(1) was [2, 4, 6]. It is now (t: unknown) -> any, which holds a list, a tuple or a ragged list in y.
  • The signature of a function that calls itself from a Map callback holds its values (CE-479). m(n) := Map(x ↦ If(x < 1, 0, m(x − 1)), [n]) was -> list<number> (m(1) is [[0]]) and is -> list<integer | list>. The same holds for a mutually recursive pair, in either assignment order.
  • Epsil: a function called before a later let of a name its body reads is typed for both bindings (CE-480). In let a = g(); let i = 2; function g() { i^2 }, g was typed () -> integer<0..> for the value -1 (the first call reads the constant i); it is now () -> number.

0.168.0 2026-10-25​

Breaking Changes​

  • The complexPromotion compile option is removed. It was deprecated in 0.115.0 as an alias of mode: 'complex', with a one-time console warning. The option is no longer on CompilationOptions, CompileTarget or the options of compile(), and a JavaScript caller that still passes it gets no warning: the key is ignored and the compilation runs in the default mode: 'auto'. That mode promotes an unknown-sign Sqrt, Ln, Log or Power through the complex kernels, but unlike mode: 'complex' it does not treat every wide numeric binding as complex, so the emitted code and the reported mode can differ from what complexPromotion: true gave. Pass mode: 'complex' to keep the old behavior, or mode: 'strict' to forbid promotion.

  • The warning for the removed realOnly compile option is gone. The option itself was removed earlier. A JavaScript caller that still passes the key no longer gets a console warning; the key is ignored.

  • Deprecated type aliases are removed. Use the name on the right:

    RemovedUse
    BoxedExpressionExpression
    SemiBoxedExpressionExpressionInput
    ExpressionComputeEngineComputeEngine

    The three were identical to their replacements, so a rename is the whole migration.

  • The fractionalDigits serialization option is removed from toMathJson(), toLatex() and the LaTeX number format (JsonSerializationOptions, NumberSerializationFormat and the options of LatexSyntax). Use digits instead: fractionalDigits: n becomes digits: { fractional: n }, and 'auto' and 'max' keep their names.

    With toMathJson(), the replacement gives the same output as before. With toLatex(), it does not:

    CallBefore (fractionalDigits)Now (digits)
    π, toMathJson, 6 digits3.1415933.141593
    π, toLatex, 3 digits3.141\ldots3.142
    2.0, toLatex, 2 digits22.00

    toLatex({ fractionalDigits: n }) cut the digits after the nth, wrote a \ldots marker when a digit was cut, and dropped trailing zeros. toLatex({ digits: { fractional: n } }) rounds to exactly n digits after the decimal point and writes no marker. The truncationMarker option is now read only by the parser.

    An engine-wide digits (ce.latexOptions = { …, digits: { fractional: 2 } }) now applies to .latex and toLatex(), as an engine-wide fractionalDigits did. Before, only fractionalDigits was read from the engine-wide settings.

    A standalone LatexSyntax serializer (one used without an engine) now accepts digits, in its constructor and per call: new LatexSyntax({ digits: { fractional: 3 } }) writes { num: "3.14159265" } as 3.142. It rounds a float and writes an exact number in full. With "auto" or "max" it writes every digit, since it has no engine precision to round to.

  • A bare number is no longer a digits value. toLatex({ digits: -4 }) and toMathJson({ digits: 6 }) were accepted at runtime, although the DisplayDigits type does not allow a number: n ≥ 0 meant { fractional: n } and n < 0 meant { significant: -n }. Such a call now throws an error that names the accepted values, in toMathJson(), toLatex() and a standalone LatexSyntax. An invalid digits set on ce.latexOptions throws when it is set. Write { fractional: n } or { significant: n }.

  • The canonical option of replace() is removed. Use form: canonical: true becomes form: 'canonical', canonical: false becomes form: 'raw', and a canonical form or a list of forms is passed to form unchanged.

  • The broadcast() batch body is built on request (ROADMAP CE-423, user decision 2026-10-25). Since 0.166.0, compile() of an expression that reads a shared list of numbers at a scalar index (F_{i+1} with F: list<number>) also compiled the batch body that makes broadcast() up to 15 times faster, a second compilation of the same size as the first (about 45 % of the compile time of such a kernel). It is now compiled only with compile(expr, { broadcast: true }). Without the option the result has no batch field, and broadcast(), broadcastAsync() and a kernel worker run the ordinary body for every cell, with the same values. A caller that broadcasts such a kernel over many cells passes the option; a caller that only calls run() saves the second compilation. A consumer that reads both run() and broadcast() from one result (Tycho's plot rows) passes the option at its compile site, or its implicit plots lose the 0.166.0 speed.

  • A product written by juxtaposition now types its symbols as numbers (ROADMAP CE-32). ce.parse('2t'), ce.parse('x y') and ce.box(['InvisibleOperator', 2, 't']) left a symbol with no value and no declaration unknown, where 2\cdot t types it number. They now type it number too. The product itself (its factors, their order and its LaTeX) is unchanged, and a function application such as f(x) keeps its reading. Types derived from such a product change: t ↦ (t, 2t) is (unknown) -> tuple<number, number> (it was (unknown) -> tuple<unknown, number>) and t ↦ [t, 2t] is (unknown) -> vector<2>. The inferred type stays for the lifetime of the engine, so in an engine used for several expressions, a symbol used as a factor is a number in later expressions: after \mathrm{B}x, \mathrm{B}(x+1) is a product, and after EG, x \in G \setminus H reports an error, as it already did after E\cdot G. Use a fresh engine, or declare the symbol, when a name has two roles.

  • Compiled Python reads a None input as NaN in arithmetic (ROADMAP CE-395 and CE-460, user decisions 2026-10-25). None is the Python spelling of Missing; p + 1, 1 / p, np.sin(p) and r^2 + 1 raised TypeError for it, and now give nan, as the interpreter and compiled JavaScript do. The conversion applies to an input whose type admits missing (number | missing, any), is unknown (a free symbol of a parsed expression, r in 2\pi r), or was inferred as number (r in \sin(r)). The generated code changes for those inputs: each read is (float('nan') if r is None else r), which costs about 6 to 15 % in a hot loop. An input declared number (ce.declare('r', 'number')) compiles to the same code as before and pays nothing; declare an input to keep the previous code. A comparison still reads the absent value (p ≠ 0 stays undecided). A vars source that is a number literal is not wrapped.

Resolved Issues​

  • A float plus a fraction was written as a mixed number (CE-471). ["Add", {"num": "2.0"}, ["Rational", 1, 3]] was written 2.0\frac{1}{3}, which reads back as a product (0.666…). It is now 2.0+\frac{1}{3}. Add(2, 1/3) is still 2\frac{1}{3}.

  • A point function with a second argument was typed any (CE-469). With f: (broadcastable<tuple<real, real>>, tuple<real, real>) -> real, f([[(1,2),(3,4)],[(5,6),(7,8)]], (1,1)) is typed matrix<real^(2x2)>, and f((1,2), (1,1)) is real.

  • A function literal with a rest parameter is accepted as a callback. Map((a, ...xs) => …, …) was refused with a callback-arity error that counted the rest parameter as required.

  • The interval target wrote a constant list out one term per element at any width, and Max, Min, Sum or Reduce over a list of 2,000 numbers overflowed the stack of the compiler. A list wider than 100 numbers is now one table read at run time: Sin(x + 4·L) over 2,000 numbers compiles to 135 characters, where it was 60,876.

  • Compiled Reduce and Scan used the library kernel for a combiner that only had the same name. With a user-declared Max(a, b) = 2a + b, Reduce([1, 2, 3], Max) compiled to Math.max and gave 3, where the interpreter gives 11; the same held for a parameter or a block-local function named Max, for a Max given in the functions option, and on the Python and interval targets. Such a fold now takes the route of a custom combiner or declines.

  • A function literal that passes a list to a function with an inferred point parameter was typed -> error. With d(a) := a[1] + a[2], x ↦ d([x, x]) is now typed (unknown) -> number; it evaluates. A signature that the engine inferred is not a contract, so the derived type of a call no longer checks the arguments against it. A call that passes a list of lists there is typed from the body: d([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) evaluates to [4, 6] and is now typed vector<integer^2>, not number. Compiled code accepts a number or a list of numbers at such a parameter (d(S(x), [1, 1]) on interval-js), and the message of a call that still fails says whether the point type was inferred or declared.

  • The type of a broadcast over a list whose elements have different ranks repeated an element arm. M + C with M: list<list<integer> | number> and C: broadcastable<number> was typed list<list<integer> | list<list<integer> | number> | number>; an arm that another arm holds is now dropped, and a union inside the element union is flattened: list<list<list<integer> | number> | number>.

  • Compiling nested Sum and Product was exponential in the nesting. The unrolled form of a clause is now limited to 10,000 nodes in total, and a larger clause is emitted as a loop: Σ_{a=1}^{60}Σ_{b=1}^{60}Σ_{c=1}^{60} abcx compiled in 12.7 s to 18 MB of code, and now in a few milliseconds. A body shared by a Sum and a Product at each of 10 levels compiles in 1.7 s instead of 55 s.

  • Compiled Python gave another absence value than the interpreter for an element read of an absent tuple. With b: list<tuple<number, string>> and b = [], At(At(b, 1), 1) was None (Missing); it is now nan, as in the interpreter. A read past the end of a tuple with an unknown slot picks the value from the elements, as the interpreter does.

  • Compiled Last declined an operand that First compiles, such as At(tup(x), 1) with x: any. It now compiles as At(…, -1).

  • The ASCII toString() of a Limit left out the variable: lim_(a) …. It now prints lim_(x -> a) ….

  • NLimit of a function that decays to 0 gave a tiny residue such as −2e-22 for 7t/(t² + 9) at infinity. A result whose magnitude is below its error estimate is now extrapolated again with a tighter tolerance and snapped to 0 when it stays below the estimate; a small true limit such as 1e-20·(1 + 2/t) is kept.

  • simplify() did not collect like terms of a numerator over a sum denominator: (t − t + 1)/(y + z) stayed as written; it is now 1/(y + z).

  • simplify() did not collect constant cofactors of like terms: π(√2 − 1) + π(√2 + 1) is now 2π√2, so the integral ∫ (x² − 1)/((x − 1)(x⁴ + 1)) dx over the real line gives π/√2.

  • Infinite sums and products: a two-term body whose second term is not a Negate now telescopes (Σ 1/(k+x) − 1/(k+x+1) from 1 to ∞ is 1/(x+1)); evaluate() and .N() now give the limit of a divergent or vanishing infinite product of a rational body (Π k and Π (k+1)/k are +∞, Π k/(k+1) is 0); the shifted-factorial rule no longer simplifies Π_{k=1}^n (k − 3) to 0.

  • An unevaluated Solve from a parse kept InvisibleOperator and Delimiter in its MathJSON. It now holds the canonical equation, so the parse route and the box route give the same result.

  • simplify() of −(2·4·…·2n) distributed the sign into the product and folded it to −16·…·n. An ellipsis product is no longer expanded, and −(1 + 2 + … + n) keeps its pattern order.

  • Map(x ↦ x + 1, [[(1, 2)], Missing]) gave [NaN, NaN]. The first cell is now a list holding the incompatible-type error, as without the Missing.

  • Mean, Median, Variance and StandardDeviation of an exact Range under .N() walked the float range and gave -8.50000000000000060577 for Mean(Range(-17, 0, 1/3)). They now read the held operand and use the closed form: -8.5.

  • The display preview of an unevaluated Dedup, Reverse or Filter of a string-typed symbol printed a list, while the value was a string. The preview now evaluates its source.

  • A base case assigned in a closure could record a pending sequence definition under a discarded scope, which stayed in the map and in every checkpoint. A discarded scope is now skipped.

  • A qualified call on an unknown protocol name (Comparable.compare("a", "b") with Comparable undeclared) gave an arity error. It now gives a protocol-unknown error that names the symbol.

  • IdentityMatrix(n), ZeroMatrix(2, n) and OnesMatrix(n) with a symbolic extent gave an expected-positive-integer error; Kernel(n) for a valueless n: integer gave []; Shape(m) for an unassigned m: matrix<integer> gave (-1, -1), and Shape(q)/Rank(q) of a free symbol gave ()/0. Each now stays unevaluated.

  • Sum(Rest(g(3))) and Reduce(Rest(g(3)), Add, 0) with g(t) = [t, 2t] stayed unevaluated. A lazy view over a held call is now resolved before the reduction; Most, Reverse, Filter and Join over g(3) too.

  • The entry type of a declared open record left out its undeclared fields, so FlatMap(ra, x ↦ [At(x, 2)]) with ra: record{a: integer} holding {a: 1, b: Missing} was an incompatible-type error. A declared record now reads tuple<string, any> entries and Values(ra) is list<any>; a dictionary literal keeps its field types.

  • Tabulate(w, 3) with w holding an error gave three copies of the error; it is now the error once, as Map(w, …) is.

  • Static types that did not hold the value of the expression. In each case the type is now a type of the value:

    • Length([1, Error("x")]), Count and IsEmpty over a list with a failed cell were typed error for the value 2; First, Last, At, IsError, Element, Contains and IndexOf over such a list are now unknown, and Sin([1, err, 3]) and [1, err, 3] + 1 are typed as lists over the valid cells.
    • PointY([(1, Missing), (2, 3)]) keeps its length: list<integer | missing^2>.
    • A type derived from operand descriptors now refuses what boxing refuses: derive('Add', [string, integer]) is error, so Map((a, b) ↦ a + b, ss, ys) over strings and integers is list<unknown>; Simplify(Sin(r)·P) with P: boolean is error; Sin over a list<string> is error.
    • Map(Abs, [1, Missing, 2]) and Map(Negate, …) are list<integer | nan^3>, as the lambda form is; Abs(w) with w: nan is nan.
    • An undeclared self-recursive numeric function (fact := n ↦ If(n ≤ 1, 1, n·fact(n − 1))) is typed (unknown) -> number, as when declared.
    • A conditional with a branch typed unknown from a parameter is typed unknown instead of by its other branch: f := (n, s) ↦ If(n = 0, s[1], [1, 2]) applied to (0, [7]) gives 7, which vector<integer^2> did not hold.

  • A component read of a tuple local did not type the parameter: g(s) = do { let q = (s, 0); take(q[1], 2) } applied to [1, 2, 3] gave element-wise errors. q[1] now aliases s, which is read as a list.

  • \keyword{if} x > 0 \keyword{then} x without else parsed to text next to the operands and reported no error. It now parses to the two-operand If, which is Missing when the condition is false, and it stops at an outer comma or semicolon.

  • \int dx and \int (dx) were an unexpected-command error. They now parse to Integrate(1, x).

  • LaTeX parser cases that were marked @fixme: a chained \over (1\over 2\over 3) now gives a non-associative-operator error, as TeX rejects it; \tan(90-0.000001)\degree applies the degree sign to the argument; a differential inside a denominator (\int\frac{3x}{5dx}, also inside a sum, a product or a function argument) gives an unexpected-differential error.

  • The compiled Map element function found the functions its callback calls by name in the drain scope. With an outer h(x) = sin(x) + 1.5, a callback f(x) = N(h(x)) and a block that declares h(x) = sin(x) + 2.5, the compiled sum used the inner h. The callees of a named or literal callback are now resolved through the callback's lexical binding, and the drain falls back to the interpreter when they differ.

  • A sum or product with one bound (\sum_{k=1} k) failed to compile with a message about Nothing; it now declines on every target with a message that says the form has no value.

  • Python target: Power with a float exponent was emitted as t ** 0.3 in auto mode while the analysis read it as promoted. It is now np.emath.power(t, 0.3), as the analysis says.

  • Shader targets: a trigonometric argument with a constant term that calls a library function (\sin(x + \Gamma(20))) was not reduced by whole periods, so its float32 value was far from the JavaScript value. A pure constant term is now folded for the reduction unless it reaches a function mapped through the functions option or a vars input.

  • Compiled JavaScript gave another absence value than the interpreter for an element read of an absent tuple. With tup := t ↦ (t, 2t), x: any and x = [], compiled At(At(tup(x), 1), 2) gave Missing; it now gives NaN, as the interpreter does. The compiled code now takes the value from the slot types of the tuple, so a slot typed unknown is no longer read as a number (Missing, not NaN), and a numeric slot of tuple<number, string>, or a position outside the tuple, gives NaN.

  • Compiled JavaScript over a symbol declared any that holds a list gave wrong values: with p = [1, 2] and q = [3, 4], p + q was the string "1,23,4", p·q was NaN, Max(p, q) was NaN, and p < q was one boolean. Such an operand is now tested at run time, and a list takes the list code ([4, 6], [True, True], 4). A value that is not a list runs the same code as before, and other types are not affected. Multiply and Power of such a list are entry-wise, as for a bare list.

  • Compiled PointX, PointY and PointZ of a value that is not a point (a number, a boolean, a string) gave NaN. They now throw a RangeError, as the interpreter gives an incompatible-type error. An absent value or NaN still gives NaN.

  • The type of a call that maps a function with a list result over an operand of unknown depth did not hold its value. With h := (t: number) ↦ [t, 2t] and x: any, h(x) was typed broadcastable<vector<2>>, which does not hold the list of matrices that x = [[1, 2], [3]] gives. It is now R | list<R | list<any>> over an operand of a top type and R | tensor<cells of R> over a tensor operand (R is the result for one element). A function with a boolean, string or tuple result over an operand typed any is typed the same way. A compiled Max or Min of h(x)[1] now declines, as for any operand that may hold Nothing.

  • interval-js: ≠ with an operand that has no value over the whole cell (\sqrt{x} \ne 0 over x = [-1, -1]) gave 'maybe'. It now gives 'true', as the interpreter and the other targets give True for NaN ≠ 0.

  • .N() did not check a value assigned to a callback parameter. The parameter of a Map callback is typed from the source elements, and evaluate() refuses an assignment of another type. Under .N(), evaluate({numericApproximation: true}) and N(…), the check was skipped: Map(q ↦ (q := q + 0.5; q + 1), 1..3).N() gave [2.5, 3.5, 4.5], and a list or a string was accepted too. It now gives an incompatible-type error for each element, as evaluate() does.

  • Static types that did not hold the value of the expression. In each case below the type of the expression was not a type of its value; it now is.

    • Map(g, t) with g := x ↦ x + 10 and t := ([1, 2], 3) is typed list<number | vector<2>> (it was list<number>, for the value [[11, 12], 13]) (CE-5). A function literal with an untyped parameter over a list<any> gets a list<any> arm in its result: (x ↦ (x, x))(A) is list<list<any> | tuple<…>> (CE-16).
    • (1, 2) + q and (1, 2)·q with q: unknown have number components (they kept integer, and the value for q = 0.5 is (1.5, 2.5)) (CE-373).
    • With tv: tuple<number, number> | vector<number^2>, Sin(tv), Sqrt(tv) and Power(tv, 2) are typed tuple<number, number> | vector<2> (they were number) (CE-7).
    • Sort(tu) with tu: tuple<unknown, missing> := (1, Missing) is typed list<missing | unknown> (it was list<missing>) (CE-3).
    • A tuple whose coordinate is a list with a failed cell has the same type inside a list as alone (it was error inside a list) (CE-367).
    • A Fold whose body assigns its accumulator is typed unknown, not from its seed alone (CE-11).
    • Any and All are typed boolean | missing when a cell can be absent: Any([1, Missing], x ↦ x > 2) evaluates to Missing (CE-8).
    • With the alias cyc = cyc | list<integer> and k: cyc := [1, 2], Map(x ↦ x + 10, k) is typed list<integer> and evaluates to [11, 12]. It was typed collection<integer> and evaluated to Set(11, 12) (CE-31).
    • If(c, 1, 0) with c of unknown type is typed integer | list<integer | list<any>>: c can hold a mask. A condition that can be undecided ([1, 2] = [1, Missing]) adds missing to the type of If and Which (CE-22).
    • MatrixMultiply of two vectors is typed as a scalar (integer for integer vectors). A lazy IdentityMatrix(101) is typed matrix<integer^(101x101)>, and Tabulate with literal extents has a shape. TrigExpand, TrigToExp and TrigReduce of Missing or of an untyped symbol keep the operand's type, not value (CE-39).
    • With f(n, s) = s if n == 0 else f(n - 1, [1, 2]), f(1, [0]) keeps the declared result; it was typed vector<integer^1> for the value [1, 2] (CE-34).
    • ce.box(expr, { form: 'structural' }) binds symbols to their definitions, as ce.function() does: with t: tuple<integer, integer>, Add(t, t) is typed tuple<integer, integer> (it was unknown) (CE-29).

  • More precise static types.

    • An operand that may be absent adds nan to a numeric result type, instead of widening the type to number: Length(At(xs, 1)) is integer | nan | signed_infinity, and Sin(m) with m: real | missing is nan | real (CE-41). [-2, NaN, Missing] is typed list<integer | missing | nan^3>.
    • v / g(1) with v: vector<integer^2> and an integer-valued g is typed vector<rational^2>, as the tuple route gives (CE-59).
    • A list literal of points of different tuple types keeps its length: [(1/2, 1), (~oo, ~oo)] is list<(tuple<…> | tuple<…>)^2> (CE-28).
    • First(Rest(xs)) and First(Take(xs, 2)) over a list literal have no absent member, and a numeric position proved not to exist (At([7, 8, 9], 99)) is typed nan (CE-42).
    • Map(Sqrt, x) over a union of vector types is typed arm by arm, and Map(Add, xs, ys) over two list<integer> is typed list<integer> (it was list<value>) (CE-31, CE-45).
    • An undeclared self-recursive function that builds a list is typed -> list<number>, and so is a declared mutually recursive pair (they were collection<number> or -> unknown) (CE-37, CE-38).
    • Simplify and the other lazy operators type the operands of a held application from their bindings (CE-40).
    • assume(t ∈ ExtendedRealNumbers) types t as real | signed_infinity (it left t typed unknown); the other extended sets work the same way (CE-50).
    • q: integer := uu, with uu an undeclared symbol, narrows uu to integer (CE-39).

  • Arguments and values that were admitted and now are refused when boxed.

    • g(S) with g: (integer) -> integer and S: list<string> (declared, no value) is an incompatible-type error, and so is f(S) with f: (matrix<2x2>) -> integer. h(S) with h: (list<integer>) -> integer stays valid, because the empty list is a value of both types (CE-24).
    • Map(h, s) with h: (T) -> T where T: number and s: list<string> is refused; it failed on each element (CE-30).
    • Q + M with Q a list of lists of points and M a list of lists of integers is one incompatible-type error, not a nested list of errors (CE-28).
    • After ce.declareType("Row", "vector<integer^3>", {alias: true}), ce.declare("R2", "list<Row^2>") is refused with the same message as list<vector<integer^3>^2> (CE-17).

  • A value-bounded type variable accepts its own literal (CE-52). With f: (x: T) -> T where T: 5, f(5) is typed 5; it was an incompatible-type error. In the same way where T: real<0..10> accepts g(3).

  • Setting .value follows the rules of ce.assign() (CE-49). n.value = 5 types n as integer (it stayed unknown), a value that does not fit a declared type is refused, and m.value = "hi" on an inferred integer symbol changes the type as ce.assign does (the type stayed integer). On a boxed symbol whose name a nested scope declares again, the setter writes the symbol's own binding, not the inner one.

  • A destructured local aliases the parameter it came from (CE-35). g(s) = do { let (a, b) = (s, 0); take(a, 2) } gave three incompatible-type errors for g([1, 2, 3]); it gives [1, 2].

  • A value-bound function with a declared effects contract refuses a rebuild that makes it effectful (CE-62). With g: (number) pure -> number bound to x ↦ 2h(x) and then h := x ↦ x + Random(), the body of g was silently rebuilt into a random call; the rebuild now throws EffectContractError and keeps the old body.

  • Epsil: an alias of a binding that holds a function literal is checked like the binding (CE-61). After let k = (n: integer) => n + 1 and let g = k, g(1.5) is reported by the static check, as k(1.5) is.

  • A float coefficient times a power of a reciprocal was written with a factor 1\times (CE-439). Multiply(0.5, y, Power(Divide(1, x), 2)) was written \frac{1\times0.5y}{x^2}, and its prettified MathJSON had the numerator ["Multiply", 1, 0.5, "y"]. The numerator of 1/x is 1, raised to the power 2, and the split of the product into a numerator and a denominator kept that 1^2 as a factor, which does not fold with a float coefficient. It is now \frac{0.5y}{x^2}. A long numerator over a single power of x is still written with a solidus, (0.5\vert x\vert x^{n})/x^2, as before.

  • The LaTeX of a function whose parameter is _1 showed an empty parameter list (CE-417). ["Function", ["Divide", "_1", "n"], "_1"] was written ()\mapsto\frac{\operatorname{\_1}}{n}, which looks like a function of no argument. A function literal whose parameters are the wildcards of its body now writes them: \operatorname{\_1}\mapsto\frac{\operatorname{\_1}}{n}, and (\operatorname{\_1}, \operatorname{\_2})\mapsto\operatorname{\_1}+\operatorname{\_2} for two. Both read back as the same function, as before. A body that uses a bare _ keeps ()\mapsto.

  • The type of a call whose argument may be absent did not hold the value of the call (CE-422). The type of a call of a user function is derived from its body, a second time with the parameter typed missing when the argument may be absent. The parameter is now typed as the call binds the absent value. With P: tuple<number, number> | missing:

    • At a parameter declared broadcastable<tuple<number, number>>, a string, a boolean or a list, an absent argument is an incompatible-type error, and it adds nothing to the type. With f := a ↦ (a.x + 1, a.y + 1), f(P) was typed tuple<missing, missing> | tuple<number, number> and is now tuple<number, number>, as at a parameter declared tuple<number, number>.
    • At a parameter declared real or integer, the absent value is read as NaN. With f := a ↦ (a, 1) and f: (real) -> unknown, the call was typed tuple<real, integer>, and its value (NaN, 1) did not fit. It is now typed tuple<nan, integer> | tuple<real, integer>, and f(Missing) is typed tuple<nan, integer> (it was tuple<missing, integer>).

  • Compiled Digamma, Trigamma and PolyGamma gave NaN at a pole. The interpreter answers ~oo at a non-positive integer, and compiled code spells that pole Infinity, as it does for Gamma. With a variable argument the compiled JavaScript gave NaN; it now gives Infinity. Compiled PolyGamma(-1, x) gave NaN; it is now LogGamma(x), as in the interpreter, for x > 0 and at a pole.

  • The GPU LerchPhi and PolyLog gave ±Infinity for some finite values at a large negative order, for example Φ(−0.5, −30, 10) = 8.0e28. They now give the value.

  • The colour reference showed wrong results. Color returns an Oklch expression, not a tuple, and ColorFromColorspace returns the colour expression of its space (Hsl(0, 1, 0.5)). doc/86-reference-colors.md now shows the real results.

  • GLSL and WGSL: a product with a derivative or with a one-operand function lost its grouping. 3·h'(x) with h(x) = x³ + sin x compiled to 9.0 * (x * x) + cos(x), not 9x² + 3cos x, and 3·Binomial(x + 1, 1), and ElementMax, ElementMin or Median with one operand, compiled to 3x + 1. The substituted body is now in parentheses, so the code of a derivative at the root is also in parentheses, for example (-sin(t)).

  • GLSL and WGSL: Oklch and Oklab with an infinite or NaN channel gave the raw channels. They now give the NaN colour, as compiled JavaScript does.

  • WGSL: ContrastingColor with a tuple background and colour candidates (ContrastingColor((u, 1, 1), Rgb(1, 0, 0), Rgb(0, 0, 1))) declined. It now compiles, as on GLSL.

  • GLSL: a loop-invariant declaration that no code reads is no longer emitted.

  • Compiled Python: And, Or and Not over a list of booleans read the list as one truth value (And(L, q) gave True for L = [True, False]). They are now computed element by element, as in the interpreter. Other list shapes are not compiled.

  • Compiled Python: \arg(x - iy) at y = 0 gave −π for a negative x. It now gives π, as the interpreter does.

  • Compiled Python: a string at a parameter of a list type was read as a list of code points, so Length counted "e\u0301x" as 3 where the interpreter counts 2 characters. The compiled function now refuses a string there with a TypeError, as compiled JavaScript does.

  • A one-operand Subtract, ElementMax or ElementMin from raw MathJSON compiled to a wrong value: 3·Subtract(x + 1) was 3 * (-x + 1), and 3·ElementMax(x + 1) was 3 * x + 1 on Python. A one-operand Divide or Power, and a Clamp with fewer than three operands, gave invalid code or NaN. They now compile to the operand, or are not compiled, as the interpreter gives an error for them.

  • Compiled Max and Min of a nested list of unknown type gave NaN (Max(g(x)[1], 1) with g := t ↦ [t, 2t] and a matrix element). They now flatten every level, as the interpreter does.

  • Compiled JavaScript added a number to a point: At(P, 1) + 1 with P: broadcastable<tuple<number, number>> gave [4, 5], where the interpreter gives an incompatible-type error. It is now not compiled.

  • A compiled power with a list exponent with a fractional cell gave NaN for a negative base (p^[2, 0.5] for (-4)^0.5). It now takes the complex lane, as a scalar exponent does, and gives 2i.

  • A compiled Root whose degree is known only at run time (Root(p, 3) over a list, or Root(x, n)) gave NaN for a negative radicand. It now gives the real root where the interpreter does (Root(-8, 3) is -2).

  • A compiled complex function of NaN (√ of a sum with an absent cell) gave {re: 0, im: NaN}. It now gives NaN.

  • A compiled user function read a free name of its body in the scope of the compilation. With a global a := 2, G := x ↦ x + a, and a assigned 1000 in a new scope, compiled G(1) gave 1001; the interpreter gives 3. Compiled code now declines a call whose body reads a name that the scope of the compilation binds to a different definition.

  • vars: { g: '…' } did not replace a user function g at its calls in compiled code. It now does, on JavaScript and interval-js. On GLSL and WGSL a vars entry names a uniform, which cannot be called, so a user function keeps its own definition there; the functions option replaces it.

  • A list of points at a parameter with no type annotation declined, and two forms gave the string "1,21": a list held by a let local at a point parameter, and the same call of a function assigned in the engine. They now compile and give the interpreter's value.

  • Compiled arithmetic on a function value (g + 1 with a block-local g) gave a string or null. It is now not compiled.

  • Compiled code did not check some parameter types. An argument at a list or tuple parameter is now tested for its shape, and the arguments of an annotated function literal applied directly are tested too; a failed test gives NaN, as the test of an integer parameter does. An assignment to a typed parameter of a value outside its type is now not compiled.

  • freeSymbols listed names that the program binds: a library function passed by name (reduce(1..20, lcm, 1)), the index of a comprehension read by its condition, and the names of a destructuring loop index. The compiled Epsil programs that read them now run.

  • Evaluating a dictionary that holds the same dictionary under several keys took exponential time (30 levels did not finish in 25 s). Each shared value is now evaluated once: 30 levels take about 1 ms.

  • A compiled power read a symbol in its exponent as unknown. With k = 1, y^{k/2-1} stayed on the real lane and gave NaN for a negative y, where y^{-1/2} gives the complex value. The value of an assigned symbol in the exponent is now used, so the two forms agree; the interpreted integral of such an integrand is complex too. A free symbol keeps the real lane.

  • A compiled ordering with a constant pole (x < 1/0, x < (-1)!) was true at x = 1, because 1/0 compiled to IEEE infinity. The interpreter gives False, and compiled code now does too, on every target.

  • When(v, C) with a mask of rank 2 or more now selects cell by cell at every level, as If and Which do, in the interpreter and in compiled code. Before, compiled JavaScript read each row as one condition and gave [NaN, NaN], and the interpreter kept the When unevaluated.

  • A compiled selection whose arm is a point or a list of points read one point as a list. One point is now lifted whole, as in the interpreter.

Improvements​

  • A comparison over a string or a tensor of strings (S: broadcastable<string>, matrix<string>) compiles again on JavaScript.

  • When(B, B < 0) with B: broadcastable<number> compiles.

  • mode: 'complex' compiles an operand that may be a number or a list (broadcastable<number>, number | list<number>). Before, it declined.

  • A function declared with a real result stays on the real lane in mode: 'complex' when its definition is emitted, and when it reads an assigned value that is complex only by promotion.

  • Compiled code calls a function returned by a call: let a = mk(2) then a(1), when mk returns a function literal on every path.

  • interval-js compiles an index into the tuple that a block-local function returns (At(f(x), 1) with f := (u) ↦ (u + 1, 2)).

  • Compiled Python: Equal and NotEqual with one list of numbers compile to a list of booleans, as the interpreter answers. Before, they were not compiled.

  • Compiled Python: a function defined in a block (const h = (k) => k + 1, function h(k)) can be called when its arguments are numbers, booleans or strings.

  • GLSL and WGSL: Mod(v, 1) and 2^v over a vector compile to fract(v) and exp2(v). Before, these forms applied to a scalar only.

  • GLSL and WGSL: GCD and LCM of any number of operands, a vector or a literal list included, compile as a fold over the components. Before, GCD took exactly two scalars and LCM did not compile.

  • GLSL and WGSL: a Match whose case body holds a loop-form Sum or Product compiles to an if … else chain. Before, it declined.

  • GLSL and WGSL compile Digamma, Trigamma and PolyGamma (order 0 to 24) of a real argument. Before, these heads fell back to the interpreter (#340). The relative error in float32 is about 1e-6 for Digamma and Trigamma and 1e-5 for PolyGamma.

  • The GPU Zeta(s) answers down to s = −63. It answered NaN below s = −24.5.

New Features​

  • epsil --workers <n> (also in the REPL and in epsil mcp) gives the engine a pool of n worker threads (at most 256) and runs each program asynchronously, so a findFit with a global search scans on the workers and gives the same values. Without the option, nothing changes. --workers auto picks the default pool size (the count of cores minus 1, from 1 to 8). With a pool, Ctrl-C in the REPL stops the entry that runs and gives the prompt back; the declarations of the session stay, and a second Ctrl-C ends the process if the entry does not stop.
  • IsPrime compiles to JavaScript.

Performance​

  • Derivatives of order 3 or more of nested expressions are faster and shorter: each intermediate derivative is simplified before it is differentiated again. The third derivative of √(x+√(x+√(x+√(x+x)))) takes about a third of the time and prints 37% shorter.

  • A coordinate of point arithmetic over a list of points held by a symbol (PointX(4·P + 0.3·(t, t)) with P: list<tuple<number, number>>) is compiled as 4·PointX(P) + 0.3·t on the JavaScript and interval targets, so the points are not built. Reduce(L, Add) (also Multiply, Max, Min) compiles on the interval target when L is not written out but its width is known from its structure.

  • A Map whose element function is a tree of integer operations is compiled with exact results when the bounds prove that no step leaves the safe integers: sum(map(x => x^2 + 1, 1..100000)) takes 0.12 s, it took about 10 s. map(f, xs) with a named user function f uses the same compiled element function as a lambda: exact results for an integer body, and machine floats for an N(…) body when the engine runs at machine precision.

  • A list or a tuple of string literals evaluates to itself, as a list of numbers already did. A recursion that passes a list of 3,000 strings at each call is about 30 times faster, and the cost of a call no longer grows with the length of the list.

  • A symbol that holds a tuple expression, such as a point (f(u), g(u)), evaluates its elements once and gives the remembered value at the next reads, until a name it reads changes.

  • A symbol assigned a seeded random draw is memoized again (WithRandomSeed(…), also inside other arithmetic). Each element read drew and computed the whole list again.

  • evaluateAsync() of a list or a tuple of numbers returns the same expression at once, as evaluate() does: about 2 ms in place of 180 to 350 ms for 20,000 points. The data preparation of FindFit.evaluateAsync() is 2 to 3 times faster, and the asynchronous evaluation of a large list gives the event loop a turn about every 8 ms: a timer can run, and an AbortSignal aborted during the evaluation rejects it with a CancellationError.

  • The compile-time constant fold no longer walks more than 10,000 elements or iterations, and CountIf, Any, Reduce and Fold are priced per element: sum(filter(1..99999, isPrime)) compiles in about 0.1 s (it took 6.9 s) and runs as compiled code.

  • Compiling in degree, grad or turn mode no longer resets the caches of the engine for each constant subexpression that is folded (about 30% faster for 60 angular constants).

  • Compiled JavaScript: Min/Max of a scalar and a list, or of two lists, no longer copies the lists (7 to 9 times faster at 10,000 elements); Re, Im, Abs and Arg of the square or the cube of x + iy read the parts directly, with no complex object; a block-local function that the block only calls has no broadcast wrapper; a loop that replaces elements of a local list (xs = ReplaceAt(xs, i, v)) copies the list once and then writes in place, O(n) in place of O(n²), with no change to the array of the caller (#386). Map(Sin, [a, b, c, d, e]) and other one-parameter library operators over a written-out list of five or more elements compile to separate calls on every target, glsl, wgsl and interval-js included.

  • .N() of an infinite sum whose convergence cannot be established declines in milliseconds, not in up to 30 seconds: the walk first evaluates the terms with the compiled body (#326). Values above machine precision are unchanged.

  • The Python target computes the index-independent collection work of a Sum or a Product once, not at each iteration (n = 10,000: 34 → 1.4 ms).

  • A misordered nested call of a callback operator (Map(Map(xs, f), g), Filter(p, …), Fold(xs, f, 0), TakeWhile, DropWhile, FlatMap, MaxBy, MinBy) takes a time linear in its depth (it was exponential: 5 s at depth 10). Canonicalizing deeply nested function literals is faster (a Map 80 levels deep: 434 → 156 ms), and arithmetic on symbols of type real | +oo | -oo no longer builds that type again for each result.

  • The test suite runs 6 to 9 times faster: a custom jest environment (config/jest-environment.cjs) makes the vm context of each test file with an ordinary global object, so a read of Math or Number is no longer a proxy trap.

Behavior Changes​

  • A Map of a named function whose body is in N(…) compiles at machine precision also when the body holds a loop or an inner collection, as the same body written as a lambda already did. map(g, 1..200) with g(x) = N(h(x) + 1) and h(x) = Sum(x/k, k = 1..10) is now compiled; its values can differ from the interpreted values in the last digits. A body whose nested loops do more than 100,000 turns in total stays interpreted.
  • Σ 1/(n (ln n)^p) with p ≤ 1 evaluates to +∞ under evaluate() and .N(), and so do other series that diverge as slowly as Σ 1/(n ln n) (a limit comparison with Σ 1/(n ln n)). They stayed symbolic.
  • Compiled JavaScript Arg of a square or a cube now gives a zero imaginary part as +0, so arg((0 − i)^2) is π, as in the interpreter (it was −π).
  • Setting .value on a symbol checks the value as ce.assign() does. n.value = "hi" for n declared integer now throws a TypeCompatibilityError; before, the value was written and the type stayed integer.
  • A numeric result whose operand may be absent keeps its handler's type and adds nan, instead of becoming number. Sin(m) with m: real | missing is typed nan | real; Length(At(xs, 1)) is integer | nan | signed_infinity. Code that compares a type string with number sees the narrower spelling.
  • Any and All can be typed boolean | missing, when a cell can be absent or the predicate can answer Missing.
  • The declared result of MatrixMultiply is matrix | vector | number. The product of two vectors is a number, which the old signature matrix | vector did not admit.
  • More calls are refused when they are boxed, where they failed on each element at evaluation: a declared function applied to a symbol whose type shares no value with the parameter (CE-24), and Map with a polymorphic callback whose type-variable bound refuses the element type (CE-30).
  • An inferred signature keeps its parameter names (CE-60). (x) => x + 1 has the type (x: unknown) -> number; it printed (unknown) -> number. A wildcard parameter (_, _1) and a destructuring pattern have no name. The names do not change how types compare. So a named call to an unannotated function literal held in a binding works: f := (a, b) => a - b; f(b: 2, a: 10) gives 8 (it was argument-name-unknown), and in Epsil ns.D(k: 1, x: 10) with const ns = {D -> ((x, k) => x - k)} no longer reports argument-names-unavailable. When a call names a parameter that the function does not have, the error lists the declared names.
  • A library operator given by name to Map is typed by its own type handler (CE-45.2), as x ↦ f(x) is. With xs: list<integer>, Map(Abs, xs) was list<number> and is list<integer<0..>>; Map(Sin, xs) was list<number> and is list<real>; Map(Conjugate, xs) was list<unknown> and is list<integer>. A function you declare keeps its declared result. A more precise type can change a value: with L: list<vector<number>>, Map(Reverse, L) · Map(Reverse, L) was an entry-by-entry product and is now the matrix product, as L · L and the lambda form Map(x ↦ Reverse(x), L) give.
  • A free symbol in a list literal is inferred as a number (CE-39.4), as in x + 1. With L := [u, v], the value of At(L, 1) was typed unknown and is number. A symbol used in a list literal and later used as a boolean condition gives an incompatible-type error. A parameter of a function literal is not affected (x ↦ [x] keeps the result list<unknown>). Arithmetic over free symbols in a list literal is read as a number too (CE-39.6): AdjugateMatrix([[x, y], [z, w]]) evaluated to a value typed list<list<unknown>> and is a matrix<2x2>.
  • A function with a point parameter maps over a matrix or tensor of points (CE-448). With g: (tuple<real, real>) -> real and P := [[(1,2),(3,4)],[(5,6),(7,8)]], g(P) was an incompatible-type error and is the 2×2 matrix of g at each point, as PointX and Abs give. For P: broadcastable<tuple<real, real>>, g(P) was typed list<real> | real and is broadcastable<real>; for T: tensor<tuple<real, real>>, g(T) was typed error and is tensor<real>. Compiled JavaScript maps the same calls; it threw "not a point" at rank 2.
  • A captured free symbol of a function literal is inferred on its outer binding, and a call checks the captured values (CE-473). In g := x ↦ [-x, y], y was left unknown outside the literal; it is now inferred number where it is declared. After y := "abc", a call of a named function whose captured value no longer fits the type its signature relied on (g(3) was [-3, "abc"], typed vector<2>) gives incompatible-type; Apply of the literal is typed from the current value; compiled JavaScript refuses such a call. A symbol read as the head of a provisional product ((g)(t) before g is a function) is not narrowed outside the literal.
  • A call never maps over the arguments of a rest parameter. h(...xs) = Length(xs) with h([1,2,3]) gave [1,1,1] and is 1; h([1,2],[3]) gave [2,2] and is 2. A fixed parameter before the rest parameter still maps a list. The same holds for Apply and Map.
  • A rest parameter is typed tuple in the body (CE-470), and Length and Count of a tuple are integer: h(a, ...rest) = Length(rest) was typed -> integer | signed_infinity and is -> integer.
  • A point-function call over a collection symbol with no value stays symbolic (CE-468). With g: (tuple<real, real>) -> real and a valueless L: list<tuple<real, real>>, g(L).evaluate() gave incompatible-type and is now g(L); after L has a value, it maps.

0.167.0 2026-10-24​

Behavior Changes​

  • FixedPoint(f, x) stays unevaluated when the default iteration limit is reached without converging (#474, contributed by enumeratio). FixedPoint(x ↦ 1 - x, 0.3) cycles between 0.3 and 0.7, and used to return whichever it held after ce.iterationLimit applications, a value that is not a fixed point. The call now stays unevaluated, as the divergence guards of FixedPoint and Any over an unbounded source already do. This also applies to an iteration that converges too slowly for the limit: at a precision of 200 digits, FixedPoint(Cos, 1.0) needs about 1170 steps, and it used to return a value correct to about 175 digits. A larger ce.iterationLimit lets such an iteration converge. With an explicit maximum, the last value is still returned, as in Wolfram's FixedPoint[f, x, n].

New Features​

  • A worker pool for a kernel loaded with the runtime entry (CE-436, Tycho row 445). The light entry @cortex-js/compute-engine/runtime now exports createKernelPool, and its runtime has loadBroadcastAsync(stored, { workers }): the broadcastAsync() of the compilation result, for code that a host stored and loads without an engine. It takes the same options (out, deadline, signal, chunk, inline, …) and gives the same result (done, route, reason); the function also has willUsePool(cells) and shippable. Only stored code that keeps the shippable: true field of its compilation result goes to a worker; other code runs on the calling thread (reason: 'not-shippable'). A worker that loads stored kernels can now run them on a pool of its own without importing the engine bundle. The runtime entry grows by about 15 KB minified (5 KB gzipped).

    import {
      createJavaScriptRuntime,
      createKernelPool,
    } from '@cortex-js/compute-engine/runtime';
    const workers = createKernelPool({
      create: () =>
        new Worker(
          new URL('@cortex-js/compute-engine/kernel-worker', import.meta.url),
          { type: 'module' }
        ),
    });
    const run = createJavaScriptRuntime().loadBroadcastAsync(stored, { workers });
    const { out, done, route } = await run({ x: xs }, { deadline: 100 });

  • Index axes in the grid layout of broadcast (ROADMAP CE-421, Tycho row 440). The indexes option names the inputs that are index axes: the input of each is the axis length n, and at each cell the variable is the cell's position along that axis, 0 to n − 1. f.broadcast({ m: 64, n: 64, F }, { layout: 'grid', indexes: ['m', 'n'] }) gives the values of the same grid with the columns 0 … 63, with no column to build, send to a worker or read. On a marching kernel that reads eight values of a shared list per cell, a 64 × 64 × 64 grid takes 3.5 ms instead of 4.05 ms.

  • executeEpsilAsync() (ROADMAP CE-314.1, Tycho row 441). Runs an Epsil program as executeEpsil() does and returns a promise of the same result. Each top-level statement is evaluated with evaluateAsync(), so a findFit whose search runs on the worker pool, or an operator with only an evaluateAsync handler, takes its asynchronous route. The signal option stops the program: the promise rejects with a CancellationError. A withTimeLimit() span around the call applies to the whole program.

Bug Fixes​

  • A chain of mixed comparisons serializes as a chain (CE-433). Since 0.166.0, 0 < M \le 5 parses to ["And", ["Less", 0, "M"], ["LessEqual", "M", 5]], and the serializer wrote that And as 0\lt M\land M\le5. It now writes 0\lt M\le5, which parses back to the same MathJSON. An And is written as a chain only when the chain spelling parses back to it: each link starts with the term the previous link ends with, and two adjacent links have different operators (a<b \land b<c keeps its \land, since a<b<c is one Less). A chain inside an \land needs no parentheses: 0\lt x\le1\land y\gt2.

  • broadcastAsync() with a deadline settles when the workers never start (CE-434). A batch that waited for a worker that never posts ready (for example a worker that fails only when it gets a message) never settled, even with a deadline: the pool started to watch the deadline only when it sent the task to a worker. A task that still waits at its deadline now settles with no cells done, and the batch resolves at about the deadline.

  • ReplaceAll in a function body reads a parameter as its argument (#476). ReplaceAll holds its target, so in x ↦ ReplaceAll(x, a → b) the rules were matched against the symbol x, and the call returned its argument unchanged: FixedPoint, Map or a call over a rewriting step did nothing. A parameter of a running call, in the target or in a rule, now means the value the call bound to it, as Function[x, x /. a -> b][a] does in Wolfram:

    const f = ['Function', ['ReplaceAll', 'x', ['List', ['Rule', 'a', 'b']]], 'x'];
    ce.box(['Apply', f, ['Add', 'a', 1]]).evaluate();
    // Before → a + 1    Now → b + 1
    ce.box(['FixedPoint', f, 'a']).evaluate();
    // Before → a        Now → b

    Outside a function nothing changes: a held target keeps a symbol with an assigned value as the symbol (x := 5; ReplaceAll(x^2, x → 3) is 9), and so does a let local of a function body.

  • Assign and Declare evaluate their value on the asynchronous route. With evaluateAsync(), x = FindFit(…) and let x = FindFit(…) ran the synchronous FindFit, and an operator with only an evaluateAsync handler stayed unevaluated in the value. Both now await the asynchronous evaluation of the value; the results of the synchronous route do not change.

Performance​

  • expr.latex keeps its string, and prettified serialization is cheaper (ROADMAP CE-438, Tycho row 444). A second read of .latex on the same boxed expression returns the string of the first read while nothing that can change it has changed (a declaration, an assignment, an assumption, the precision or another engine setting, the LaTeX options or dictionary): about 0.3 µs instead of about 200 µs for a 20-node expression. The prettified MathJSON that .latex and toLatex() use no longer splits a product with no factor that can go to a denominator into a numerator and a denominator, which built and canonicalized new expressions: a first .latex of such an expression takes about 180 µs instead of 280 to 360 µs. The output does not change. toLatex({ prettify: false }) stays the fastest form for a string used as a key; expr.digest is the key to use for a cache.

  • The sum of a compiled Map is computed on doubles (ROADMAP CE-432). At machine precision, Sum(Map(f, xs)) whose element function the auto-compilation compiles now adds the doubles of the elements, with the rules of the element-by-element sum, instead of boxing each element: sum(map(x => N(sin(x) + x^2), 1..100000)) takes about 45 ms instead of about 190 ms, with the same value. The asynchronous route takes the same path in steps that give the event loop a turn. A Map over a set, an impure Map, and any element that the interpreter must compute keep the element-by-element sum.

  • FindFit.evaluateAsync() no longer blocks the calling thread for long (ROADMAP CE-429). One grid point of the separable scan and the setup (the data rows, the compilation of the model and of its derivatives) now give the event loop a turn, about every 8 ms, and an abort during the setup stops it. For an interpreted model over 200 rows, the longest block went from about 110 ms to 12 ms; the results do not change.

  • A product of decimal values no longer keeps every digit (ROADMAP CE-319.4 and CE-319.5). The product of two decimal values is rounded to twice the working precision plus 20 digits when it has more. It kept every digit of the exact product, so a value multiplied by itself at each step of a loop doubled its digits at each step: at precision 50, FixedPoint(x ↦ 2.8·x·(1 − x), 0.2) did not finish in 2 minutes, and now takes about 40 ms. .N() of a product of 64,000 factors went from 43 s to 0.9 s. The digits past the working precision are kept as guard digits, so the printed values do not change.

  • A product of many distinct factors takes a time proportional to its size (ROADMAP CE-319.3). A product looked for each new factor among all the factors it already held, and .N() also built a new product for each factor. A product of 2,000 distinct symbols took 18 ms on evaluate() and 8.6 s on .N(); it now takes 12 ms and 7 ms, and 64,000 symbols take about 250 ms on both routes. This also fixes the float coefficient of such a product under .N(): the coefficients were multiplied from the right, so 10⁻²⁰⁰·10⁻¹²³·10²⁰⁰·x went through a subnormal value and gave 9.88·10⁻¹²⁴·x, and some orders of large and small factors gave a coefficient of 0. It is now 10⁻¹²³·x.

  • Compiling an expression with shared subexpressions and constant folding on takes a time proportional to its distinct parts (ROADMAP CE-319.1). Before it folds a constant, the compiler checks the whole expression for a name bound by the compilation, a Sum or Product with a non-finite bound, and a free symbol reached through an assigned value. Each check visited a shared subexpression once for each place it appears, so e = e + e repeated 24 times over 2 + √3 took 3.9 s to compile. Each check now visits a subexpression once: the same expression compiles in about 110 ms, and at 60 levels in about 200 ms. The compiled code does not change.

  • A more deeply nested expression compiles (ROADMAP CE-320.2). The compiler is recursive, and each level of a nested expression uses stack. A chain of Sin and Cos compiled up to a depth of about 280, and a polynomial in Horner form, a₀ + x(a₁ + x(a₂ + …)), up to a degree of about 120; past that, compile() answered success: false and the call ran in the interpreter. Each level now uses less stack, and the two limits are about 420 and 205. The compiled code does not change.

0.166.0 2026-10-24​

Breaking Changes​

  • A parsed comparison chain is no longer a nested tree (ROADMAP CE-411, Tycho row 433). The LaTeX and Epsil parsers wrote a < b \le c as LessEqual(Less(a, b), c), and a = b = c as Equal(a, Equal(b, c)). A run of one operator is now one n-ary node, Equal(a, b, c), and a run of mixed operators is an And of links that share their boundary term: a < b \le c is And(Less(a, b), LessEqual(b, c)), in the raw form too. MathJSON input that nests a comparison inside another comparison, such as ["Less", "a", ["Less", "b", "c"]], now means a comparison of the inner truth value, not a chain. The serializers put parentheses around a comparison inside a comparison.

Behavior Changes​

  • A declared type of a batch input is trusted (ROADMAP CE-410). In the batch body, a read At(F, i) whose index type proves an integer of at least 1 (for example i + 1 with i declared integer<0..>) is a direct read with no run-time test; a read past the end still gives NaN. When an input breaks its declared type (a fractional i for integer, a string in a list declared list<number>), the result is not defined. A plain array that passed the check once is not checked again while its length is unchanged.

  • A list at an untyped parameter beside a point parameter maps (ROADMAP CE-414.2). A parameter with no type (unknown, any, no annotation) of a function that also has a point parameter now follows the rule of a one-parameter function: its type is refined from the body, and it maps a list unless the body uses it as a collection. With f := (P, t) ↦ (P.x + t, P.y) declared (tuple<number, number>, unknown) -> unknown, f((1, 2), [0, 1, 2]) is [(1, 2), (2, 2), (3, 2)], typed list<tuple<number, number>>; it was ([1, 2, 3], 2). With (P, L) ↦ Length(L), L is refined to collection and the list is still taken whole. Compiled JavaScript gives the same values.

  • An absent point at a broadcastable<tuple<…>> parameter gives Missing (ROADMAP CE-420), as at a tuple<…> parameter. With f := (a, b) ↦ (a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y), f([(1, 2), (3, 4)], [(10, 20), Missing]) is [(11, 22), Missing] for every mix of the two declarations; with broadcastable<…> parameters the second element was an incompatible-type error. A list of only absent points, [Missing, Missing], now gives [Missing, Missing] for every declaration; at a tuple<…> parameter the call was an incompatible-type error. A list of points that is absent as a whole (P: list<tuple<…>> | missing holding Missing) now gives Missing at a broadcastable<tuple<…>> parameter too, and the call's type has the missing option; it was an incompatible-type error. Compiled JavaScript gives undefined for an absent point, and for an absent list, at a broadcastable<tuple<…>> parameter; it declined.

  • A time limit applies to an asynchronous evaluation (ROADMAP CE-424, Tycho's CE-314 feedback). ce.withTimeLimit(20, () => { p = expr.evaluateAsync(); }) had no effect: the limit was removed when the callback returned, before the evaluation went on after its first await. A FindFit global search ran to its end (270 ms). The evaluation now keeps the limit (and a withStepBudget budget) that is in force when evaluateAsync() is called, until it ends. A timeout is reported as by evaluate(): the FindFit search answers its best point so far with timedOut: True after 21 ms, and the time left is given to the workers of a kernel pool.

  • broadcastAsync() evaluates no cell before it returns (ROADMAP CE-425.2, Tycho's CE-314 feedback). A batch that stays on the calling thread (no pool, a result that cannot run on a worker, or fewer cells than the inline threshold) ran its first slice, up to 16 384 cells, before the call returned. The batch now yields to the event loop (a macrotask turn) before its first slice, as it already did between two slices. A signal aborted right after the call now stops the batch before its first cell.

New Features​

  • The record of FindFit.evaluateAsync() says where the search ran (ROADMAP CE-428, Tycho's CE-314 feedback). The record of the asynchronous route of FindFit and FindRoot has a route entry: "pool" when the workers of the engine's kernel pool solved the grid points, or "calling-thread". With "calling-thread", a reason entry says why the pool did not take the search: "no-pool", "no-global-search", "not-separable", "not-compilable", "pool-declined" (the pool rejected every slice), "no-points-to-ship" or "setup-timeout". The record of evaluate() has neither entry.

  • broadcastAsync({ …, inline: false }) refuses the calling thread (ROADMAP CE-426). When the batch would not go to the worker pool, the call resolves at once with done: 0 and evaluates no cell; when a worker fails during the batch, the call keeps the cells that the workers did and does not complete the rest on the calling thread. result.willUsePool(cells) of a compiled result says before the call whether a batch of that many cells would go to the pool now.

  • result.shippable says whether a compiled result can run on a worker (ROADMAP CE-427). It is false when the compiled code draws random numbers from the engine, names a host global (a vars or functions entry given by name), or has a caller preamble; such a result always runs on the calling thread. It is present where broadcastAsync is.

  • The result of broadcastAsync() says where the batch ran (ROADMAP CE-428). route is 'pool' or 'calling-thread', and reason, present when the pool did not take the whole batch, is one of 'no-pool', 'pool-unusable', 'not-shippable', 'below-threshold' and 'pool-declined'. The types BroadcastAsyncRoute and BroadcastAsyncReason are exported. route is a required field of BroadcastAsyncResult: code that builds such an object itself (a mock, for example) must set it.

Bug Fixes​

  • FindFit.evaluateAsync() lets timers run during a search on the calling thread (ROADMAP CE-425.1, Tycho's CE-314 feedback). With no kernel pool, or when the pool does not take the search (a model that does not compile, a search that is not separable, no global option), the whole search ran in one piece: a 5-point fit of a cos(b x + c) + d LogGamma(x + c) blocked the thread for more than 4 s, so a page did not respond and an AbortSignal aborted by a timer was not seen until the end. The search now gives the event loop a turn about every 8 ms (between grid points, solver starts, solver iterations and groups of 8 data rows); the longest block of that fit is now about 25 ms. The results do not change; a short fit is up to about 5 % slower, near the noise of the measurement.

  • Equal and NotEqual of two relations compare their truth values (ROADMAP CE-411, Tycho row 433). ["Equal", ["LessEqual", "a", 0], ["LessEqual", "b", 0]] was boxed as the chain a ≤ 0 = b ≤ 0, and the LaTeX (a\le0)=(b\le0) evaluated as that chain after a substitution: both gave False for a = b = 1. Both now give True when the two conditions are both true or both false.

  • A negated relation in a comparison chain negates only its own link (ROADMAP CE-411). a < b \not\le c is And(Less(a, b), Not(LessEqual(b, c))); it was Not(And(Less(a, b), LessEqual(b, c))). The LaTeX commands \nleq, \nleqslant, \ngeq, \ngeqslant, \not\lt and \not\gt are now parsed; they gave an unexpected-command error.

  • A call of a function with a broadcastable<tuple<…>> parameter over a list of points compiles (ROADMAP CE-412, Tycho row 437). With f := a ↦ (a.x + 1, a.y + 1) and P a list of points, or a point or a list of points, compile(f(P)) declined. It now compiles to one call per point, as a bare tuple<…> parameter does, and gives the interpreter's values.

  • A bare tuple<…> parameter maps a list of points of unknown length (ROADMAP CE-413, Tycho row 438). With n unbound, a call over Map((u, v) ↦ (u, v), \frac{1}{n}[0...n], \frac{1}{n}[0...n]) was an incompatible-type error. It now maps one point per call, lazily, as for a list of known length.

  • A list in a scalar slot beside a point parameter maps (ROADMAP CE-414, Tycho row 439). With h := (P, t) ↦ P.x + t and t declared real, h((1, 2), [0, 1, 2]) was an incompatible-type error. It is now [1, 2, 3], typed as a list, in the interpreter and in compiled JavaScript. This applies when the slot's type cannot hold a list (real, number, boolean, string); for a slot typed unknown, see Behavior Changes.

  • A compiled call with an argument declared broadcastable<tuple<…>> that holds one point compiles (ROADMAP CE-415). It declined; it now gives the interpreter's value.

  • Printing a function whose parameter is _1 no longer defines _ (ROADMAP CE-416). toString() renamed the parameter with a substitution that created the symbol _ in the engine's scope, so a later lazy Map printed Error(incompatible-type …) in place of a call.

  • broadcastAsync reads an input that shares memory with out as it was given. When an input array was a view of the output buffer, each slice read it after earlier slices had written their results there: with Tuple(x + 1, 10x), x = [1, 2, 3, 4] in the first half of out and chunk: 1, the result was [2, 10, 11, 100, 12, 110, 101, 1000] instead of [2, 10, 3, 20, 4, 30, 5, 40]. broadcast was correct. Such inputs are now copied once before the first slice.

Performance​

  • A broadcast kernel runs up to 15 times faster (ROADMAP CE-410, Tycho row 432). For a kernel that reads two values of a shared list<number> and returns a tuple, 250 000 cells take about 0.55 ms instead of 8.3 ms when the index is declared integer<0..>, and about 0.95 ms when it is declared integer. A kernel that reads a shared list gets a second compiled body for batches: the list is checked once per batch (a Float64Array, or a plain array of numbers) and then read directly, and the inputs are passed as arguments. A shared Float64Array is read in place; it was copied into a plain array on every batch. The cell loop is generated for each compiled body, And/Or of plain comparisons compile to a conditional, and the per-cell call is direct.

0.165.0 2026-10-24​

Breaking Changes​

  • The IntervalValue type includes the answer strings of a comparison (ROADMAP CE-210, Tycho row 411). A compiled interval-js runner returns 'true', 'false' or 'maybe' for a boolean expression, but the public type IntervalValue was IntervalResult | Interval | IntervalValue[]. It is now IntervalResult | BoolInterval | Interval | IntervalValue[]. Code that narrows an IntervalValue with a check on kind must first test for a string.

Behavior Changes​

  • Compiled JavaScript keeps an absent value whose type is not known through a point accessor and arithmetic (ROADMAP CE-229). With W = (p, s) ↦ (s·PointX(p), s·PointY(p), s·PointZ(p)) and L a list of two points, the interpreter gives (Missing, Missing, Missing) for W(L[5], 2), and compiled JavaScript gave [NaN, NaN, NaN]. The interpreter answers the marker of the codomain for an absent operand: NaN when the operation is provably a number, Missing otherwise. Compiled code now does the same: a coordinate accessor whose type is any or unknown gives undefined (the compiled spelling of Missing) for an absent point, and an element-wise Add, Multiply (and the other arithmetic) whose type is not provably a number keeps an undefined operand of type any or unknown. W(L[5], 2) compiles to [undefined, undefined, undefined]. Beside an operand that is a list at run time the absence lands in each cell, as in the interpreter: [1, 2] + PointX(p) with p absent is [NaN, NaN]. A numeric operation, such as 2·x with x absent, is still NaN.

  • A parameter declared broadcastable<T> maps to the cells when T cannot hold a list (ROADMAP CE-405, Tycho row 434). With f: (broadcastable<number>) -> number and f := x ↦ x + 1, f([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) is [[2, 3], [4, 5]], typed matrix<2x2>. It was a list of two incompatible-type errors, one for each row, while the call was typed matrix<2x2>: the declared parameter mapped exactly one level down and checked each row against number. Since 0.162.0 broadcastable<T> is T | tensor<T>, and an undeclared function and the compiled targets already map to the cells. This applies when T is a number, a boolean, a string or a tuple; a tuple is not mapped into, so a list of points maps one point per call. A parameter declared broadcastable<value> keeps the one-level rule, and so does a call that maps such a parameter. An element that is neither a T nor a collection is an incompatible-type error that names broadcastable<T>. Such a function now compiles to JavaScript through the element-wise call, with each cell checked against T, where it declined. A call that maps a broadcastable<value> parameter is typed with one list level around the result (list<value>; it was typed from the whole shape of the argument).

  • Every result of the MCP server says which engine computed it (ROADMAP CE-406). A server loads the engine when it starts and keeps it, so after an upgrade a running server answered with the old engine, and nothing in its results showed it. A JSON result now has engineVersion, and an error message ends with a line Engine version: …. When the package installed on disk has another version, the result also has an engineWarning (or a line in an error message) that says to restart the server.

  • The interval-js fallback answers a comparison, and does not read a wide input as its midpoint (ROADMAP CE-210). When the target cannot compile an expression (Greater(Fibonacci(x), 0): Fibonacci has no interval lowering), the result runs the interpreter at the midpoint of each interval input. A boolean value was { kind: 'entire' }; it is now the answer string, 'true' or 'false', as compiled code gives it. When an input is wider than a point, the value at its midpoint does not bound the values over it, and was returned as if it did: Fibonacci(x) over [1, 10] was { kind: 'empty' } (no value at 5.5), although it takes the values 1 to 55 there. Over such an input a boolean expression is now 'maybe' and a number is { kind: 'entire' }. At a point the answers are exact, as before.

  • A declared collection that shares only the empty collection with a collection parameter is refused when the expression is boxed (ROADMAP CE-402). With R: list<list<number>> or B: list<boolean>, Mean(R) and Mean(B) were valid and were refused only when evaluated, while Histogram(R, 2) was refused when boxed: the empty list is both a list<list<number>> and a collection<number>. A collection argument is now admitted at a collection parameter only when their element types can match, so Mean(R), Mean(B) and Mean([Missing, "a"]) are refused when they are boxed. A collection whose elements are not known yet (list, list<any>, set<unknown>, tensor) is still admitted.

Resolved Issues​

  • A compiled call with an argument that is one point or a list of points gave a wrong value (ROADMAP CE-407, Tycho row 435). With f: (tuple<number, number>) -> tuple<number, number>, f := a ↦ (a.x + 1, a.y + 1) and L: tuple<number, number> | list<tuple<number, number>>, the interpreter maps f(L) over the points when L holds a list, and gives one point when L holds a point. The call was typed tuple<number, number>, and compiled JavaScript called f once on the whole list: for [(1, 2), (3, 4)] it gave ["1,21", "3,41"] and reported success. The call is now typed list<tuple<number, number>> | tuple<number, number>, and compiled JavaScript tests the value at run time: it maps over a list of points and gives a point whole. The same applies to an argument declared broadcastable<tuple<number, number>>, which was typed and compiled as a list of points only, so compiled code read one point as a list; a matrix of points there throws at run time, as the interpreter gives an incompatible-type error. An absent argument of such a type (… | missing) gives Missing, as an absent list of points does; it was an incompatible-type error. A union that also admits another collection (… | list<list<tuple<…>>>, … | list), and a parameter with a coordinate that is not a number, a boolean or a string (tuple<list<number>, number>), are now declined by the compiler: a point and a list of points cannot be told apart at run time there.

  • A generic parameter declared broadcastable<T> with a number bound refused a matrix (ROADMAP CE-409). With w: (x: broadcastable<T>) -> list<T> where T: number and w := x ↦ [x], w([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) was the error incompatible-type when boxed, while the same declaration without a type variable, broadcastable<number>, maps to the cells (ROADMAP CE-405). The type solver read the matrix one level down and bound T to the rows. It now binds T to the cells when the bound cannot hold a list, also for a list with rows of different lengths: w([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) is [[[1], [2]], [[3], [4]]], typed list<list<list<integer>>>, and compiled code gives the same value. A type variable with no bound (where T) now maps each row whole, as where T: value does; each row was an incompatible-type error naming T.

  • A parameter named Return can be called in the body of Sum, Integrate and the other operators that take an expression (ROADMAP CE-401). Since 0.164.0 a Return statement in such a body is the error return-in-expression-body. The check also refused a call of a parameter of the enclosing function literal named Return: ["Function", ["Sum", ["Return"], ["Limits", "k", 1, 3]], ["Typed", "Return", "() -> real"]] was invalid. The call is now allowed, with or without a type on the parameter, and the function applied to () ↦ 2 gives 6. A Return that calls a bare parameter, of the function or of an enclosing function, also no longer adds nothing to the result type of the function: Return ↦ 1 + Return() is typed (unknown) -> broadcastable<number>, not (unknown) -> broadcastable<number> | nothing.

  • The result of a function whose parameter is declared broadcastable<T> was typed for a whole collection (ROADMAP CE-408, Tycho row 436). With l: (broadcastable<tuple<number, number>>) -> unknown and l := A ↦ √(A.x² + A.y²), the signature was refined to -> broadcastable<number>, so l(P) over a list of points was typed list<broadcastable<number>> and P / l(P) had a tensor arm. Each call of the body receives one T, so the result is now typed with the parameter read as T: -> number, and l(P) is list<number> | number.

  • The LaTeX serialization of Reduce and Fold keeps the initial value (ROADMAP CE-292). Reduce([1, 2], Add, 10) serialized as \sum of the list without the seed, so the LaTeX parsed back as an expression whose value is 3, not 13. A seeded reduction now writes its third operand, and the \sum/\prod shorthand is used only when there is no seed.

  • A symbol declared with the type error parses (ROADMAP CE-294). With w: error, w, w+1 and \int_0^1 w\,dw gave an unexpected-symbol error. They now parse as terms. A symbol of type never also parses now.

  • In lenient mode, ab√x..5 reports ambiguous-radical (ROADMAP CE-298), as ab√x and 5..ab√x already did. The line-level ambiguity checks now read the tree after the range-precedence repair.

  • Declare with a type string that does not parse returns an error (ROADMAP CE-101). ["Declare", "r", {str: "integer<<"}] threw when it was evaluated. It now gives Error("invalid-type-declaration", …) with the message of the type parser.

  • Hold around a Function with no body does not throw (ROADMAP CE-106). Reading the type of Hold(Function()), or evaluating it, threw from the signature of the function literal. The bodyless function literal is now typed error.

  • A ce.declare() of a value that is refused leaves no placeholder (ROADMAP CE-116, issue #394). When the value does not fit its type, a new name stays undeclared and a redeclaration keeps its previous binding, as the operator route already did.

  • More boolean identities fold beside an unknown (ROADMAP CE-119). Nand(True, A), Nor(False, A), Nand(A, A) and Nor(A, A) evaluate to ¬A, Implies(True, A) to A, Implies(A, False) to ¬A, and Implies(A, A) and Equivalent(A, A) to True. An absent operand gives the same results as before.

  • isEqual() of a symbol reads the bounds that pin it to a value (ROADMAP CE-104). With b ≥ 0 and b ≤ 0 assumed, b.isEqual(0) is true; it was undefined, and ce.number(0).isEqual(b) agrees. The Equal operator does not read bounds.

  • Limit of a function whose body is Return(v) (ROADMAP CE-400) gives the limit of v. It gave a Return expression as its value. A Return inside a statement block or a branch leaves the limit unevaluated.

  • A divergent improper integral with a symbolic exponent stays unevaluated (ROADMAP CE-383). ∫₀^∞ xⁿ dx gave a value under the condition 0 < n ∧ n < 0, which no n satisfies.

  • The limit at infinity of a ratio of logarithms (ROADMAP CE-147). ln(3x)/ln(x) and ln(3x)/ln(x^π) give 1 and 1/π; they stayed unevaluated. A ratio that is not an indeterminate form, such as (2 + sin x)/(3 + sin x), still has no limit.

  • Determinant and CharacteristicPolynomial of a matrix with float entries fold their constants (ROADMAP CE-145). Determinant([[x + 1.5, 1], [1, 2]]) is 2x + 2; it was 2x - 1 + 3.

  • A telescoping sum with an infinite bound and a parameter (ROADMAP CE-142). \sum_{k=1}^\infty ((x+k+1)^2-(x+k)^2) is +oo; it was (x + 1 + oo)^2 - (x + 1)^2. The product \prod_{k=1}^\infty (x+k+1)/(x+k), whose sign depends on x, stays unevaluated. A sum whose term at the finite bound is a pole stays unevaluated.

  • Reducers over a Range held by a symbol use the closed form (ROADMAP CE-80). With r := Range(1, 10^20), Sum(r), Mean(r), Median(r), Variance(r), Max(r) and Min(r) return at once; they walked every element.

  • Dot of two empty lists (ROADMAP CE-220) is 0 for two numeric vectors and [] for two lists of points, as the compiled code gives. It stayed unevaluated.

  • Compiled Max, Min and the ordering comparisons decline an operand of type color, regexp or object (ROADMAP CE-393). The compiled code read such a value as a number, while the interpreter leaves the call unevaluated. With a fallback, the interpreter now runs. A custom compile handler of the operator still takes precedence.

  • The WGSL Mod keeps the sign of the divisor when the quotient underflows (ROADMAP CE-246). floor(r / b) gave -0 for a tiny remainder of the opposite sign, so the divisor was not added.

  • NLimit of a function that rises before it decays (ROADMAP CE-184). NLimit(t ↦ 7t/(t² + 9), ∞) is about 0 (−2e-22); it was NaN. The numeric limit retries from a start closer to the target when the first extrapolation is rejected.

  • narrow() of two collection types of different kinds that share values (ROADMAP CE-12). matrix<number> and collection<vector<integer>> narrow to matrix<integer>; the result was never. A pair that cannot be reduced is kept as an intersection.

  • The empty tuple type prints as tuple<> (ROADMAP CE-23), which parses back to the empty tuple. It printed as the bare tuple, which means a tuple of any length.

  • Abs of a list or a matrix of numbers is typed from its cells (ROADMAP CE-18). Abs([1, 2]) is typed list<integer<0..>^2>; the type had a signed_infinity arm that the value cannot take.
