  • Epsil: the hint of a type error in an annotation is shown (ROADMAP CE-307). let v: vector<integer^(2x3)> now says to write matrix<…> for two dimensions.

  • Epsil: an error in the body of a match case is underlined on that case (ROADMAP CE-308), not on the whole statement. The error frame names the case (in Match argument 3).

  • Epsil: a loop over a range whose bound is an unassigned local reports the error (ROADMAP CE-309). In a function, for k in 1..t { t = 2 } gives read-before-declaration, as compiled code does; it ran zero times. A lambda in a pipe stage that assigns a new name, (1..3) |> map((k) => do { t = k * 2; t }), no longer needs the scope effect.

  • Faster type checks and set operations (ROADMAP CE-315, CE-316). isSubtype on a union whose arms are the same type node took exponential time in the nesting depth. Duplicate removal in a set comprehension, in Intersection and in SymmetricDifference compares an element only with the elements of the same hash: 3,604 comparisons in place of 812,704 for a comprehension over Range(1, 900).

  • The structural hash of a deeply nested expression does not repeat (ROADMAP CE-318). The hash of a function expression, and of a dictionary, repeated every 32 or 64 levels of nesting, so different deep expressions fell into one hash bucket. Hash values of all function expressions change.

  • Compiled code: seven more corrections (ROADMAP CE-224, CE-226, CE-230, CE-243, CE-251, CE-262, CE-282).

    • GLSL and WGSL decline a point component typed indexed_collection or collection, as they decline a list; such a value was put in a vecN.
    • A comprehension whose term assigns its own index declines to compile, and the interpreter runs it. The compiled code threw "Assignment to constant variable".
    • A branch of If or Which behind a condition that is constant by its type no longer moves the compiled result to the complex lane: x + Which(1 > 0, y, True, √(y − 1)) compiles to real code.
    • The GLSL and WGSL integer-power helpers of a vector give +∞, not NaN, for a zero component under a negative odd exponent, as the scalar helper does.
    • A one-operand Add, Multiply, And or Or, and Power(x, 1), from non-canonical input compile with correct grouping on JavaScript and the GPU targets. 3·(x+1)^1 compiled as 3·x + 1.
    • Compiled JavaScript \arg(x − iy) is π at y = 0 and a negative x, as the interpreter gives; it was −π.
    • compileShader on GLSL and WGSL converts the arguments and results of trigonometric functions in degree, grad and turn modes, as compile does.

  • Evaluation: six corrections (ROADMAP CE-99, CE-105, CE-108, CE-115, CE-121, CE-129).

    • A dictionary that holds an Error value reports isValid === false, as a list and a tuple do, and has() of an object reads its field values.
    • A symbol that holds an error gives that error when it is called: w(1), Apply(w, 1) and Pipe(3, w) stayed unevaluated, while Map(w, …) gave the error.
    • An error passed to a function declared with a typed signature carries the frame of that call.
    • Sum and Product with several Limits clauses, where a bound depends on another index, evaluate in either clause order: Sum(k, Limits(k, 1, n), Limits(n, 1, 10)) is 220.
    • The .mul() method no longer stores the current value of a variable in a point or a list: with w := 4, 2·(w, 2) keeps (2w, 4) and follows a later assignment of w.
    • A callback written InverseFunction(f) or Derivative(f, n) is accepted by the lazy collection operators: Map(InverseFunction(Sin), xs).

  • Numeric evaluation: more values and better accuracy (ROADMAP CE-180, CE-185, CE-189, CE-192, CE-197).

    • .N() of a divergent integral next to a singular bound, ∫₀¹ t⁻³⁰⁰ dt, is +oo; it was a Measurement of +oo with a NaN error.
    • A Measurement whose error is below 1e-100 prints in exponential notation; it printed the text of a RangeError.
    • Gamma and Factorial at an argument whose value is past the exponent range stay unevaluated, and no longer give 0 to internal callers.
    • Arcoth, Arcosh and the other inverse functions with a branch point at ±1 read an exact sum next to ±1 (1 + 10⁻¹⁰) exactly at machine precision: Arcoth(1 + 10⁻¹⁰) is 11.8594990552752; it was 11.8594990139, the value at the double.
    • The complex Gamma is about 100 times more accurate for an argument with Re z above 2 (relative error 1.6e-15 on the real axis, it was 2e-13), so Hypergeometric2F1 with a complex z is more accurate too.
    • PolyGamma(m, z) of an order from 100 to 400 close to a half-integer on the real axis has a value: PolyGamma(120, -1/2 + 10⁻⁵i).
    • GammaRegularized(n, z) for an integer n up to 200 and a negative z has a value under .N().

  • More precise static types (ROADMAP CE-17, CE-44).

    • The meet of a fixed-length list with a plain list of lists is never (the empty list for an open length). It was a type such as list<list^3>, which the type parser refuses.
    • An element-wise comparison over a list that can be absent as a whole, L < 3 with L: list<integer> | missing, is typed list<boolean> | missing; it was list<boolean | missing>.

  • Symbolic computation: nine corrections and capabilities (ROADMAP CE-137, CE-138, CE-141, CE-152, CE-154, CE-155, CE-156, CE-157, CE-158).

    • Solve finds the roots of equations with sines and cosines of multiples of the unknown: sin x + sin 2x = 0, cos 2x + cos x = 0, sin 2x = cos x.
    • D and Integrate over a parameter of a user function use the argument of the call: with g(f) := \frac{d}{dx} f, g(x^2) is 2x; it was 0. This also holds when a global symbol has the name of the parameter, and for an argument that holds it: with g(f) := \int f\,dx, g(f + x) is f·x + x²/2.
    • The definite integral of sin(x − Round(x))/(x − Round(x)) is no longer evaluated through an antiderivative that ignores the jumps of Round; it gave 0. .N() gives 63.1177… on [0, 64].
    • A definite integral of |u| or sgn(u) with a quadratic u is split at the real roots of u: \int_{-1}^{1} |x^2 - 1/4|\,dx is 1/2.
    • TrigReduce reduces each element of a list and each side of an equation (it rewrote them in exponential form), and TrigReduce(Missing) stays Missing.
    • Sum and Product over Element(j, Range(1, k)) read the value of k, as Limits does.
    • simplify() rationalizes a quotient by a constant inside a sum or a product: 1/(2−√2) − 1/(2+√2) is √2.
    • simplify() reads a negative imaginary literal as a negation, so sin(−i) + sin(i) is 0, and simplifies the numerator of a quotient as a term of a sum: (Si(1) − Si(−1))/y is 2Si(1)/y.

0.164.0 2026-10-23​

Behavior Changes​

  • The structural form of ce.parse() leaves out a spacing command between the operands of a juxtaposition (ROADMAP CE-403, Tycho row 431). ce.parse("\\,d=2", { form: "structural" }) was ["Equal", ["InvisibleOperator", ["HorizontalSpacing", 3], "d"], 2], a product of a space and d on the left side, while d=\,2 was ["Equal", "d", 2]: the shape depended on where the space was. It is now ["Equal", "d", 2], as d\,=2, \quad d=2 and x\,+\,y (["Add", "x", "y"]) are. The canonical form already left the spacing out. The raw form keeps it, and so does the structural property of a raw expression. A space still separates two tokens: x\,.75e2 is x times 75.

  • Mean and the other statistics refuse a matrix when the expression is boxed (ROADMAP CE-13). Mean([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) was a valid expression that failed only when it was evaluated. The data parameter of Mean, Median, Mode, Variance, PopulationVariance, StandardDeviation, PopulationStandardDeviation, Kurtosis, Skewness, Quartiles, InterquartileRange, Histogram, BinCounts, Covariance, PopulationCovariance and Correlation is now a collection of numbers, collection<nothing | number> (collection<nothing | number | tuple> for the first operand of the bivariate statistics, which also take a collection of (x, y) pairs), in place of collection<any>. A matrix, a symbol declared matrix, a ragged list, a collection of booleans, strings or residue classes, and a dictionary are now invalid when they are boxed, with an incompatible-type error that names the data parameter. Vectors, sets, ranges, tuples, data with Missing or Nothing cells, measurements and symbolic data are accepted as before. The validation now reads the rank of a collection<T> parameter whose elements cannot be lists as 1, so any operator with such a parameter refuses an argument of rank 2 or more. Related changes:

    • A symbol with no value used as statistics data (Mean(q)) is inferred collection<nothing | number> | distribution | number.
    • In Histogram(P + 0.5, 1/100) with P of unknown type, P is inferred list<number> (it was matrix).
    • The inferred parameter of a user function xs ↦ Mean(xs) is collection<nothing | number> | value.

  • A Return in an operand of Sum, Product, Integrate, D, ND, NIntegrate, Limit or NLimit is an error (ROADMAP CE-96). These operands (the body, a bound, a variable) are expressions, computed once per index value or integration point, not statement blocks of the enclosing function, so a Return there has no function to end. It stayed in the value: Sum(1 + Return("q"), (k, 1, 2)) was 2 + 2Return("q"), and D(Return(x^2), x) was 2x·Apply(Derivative("Return", 1), x^2). The expression is now invalid, with the error return-in-expression-body naming the operator. A Return inside a function literal in the body ends that function, as before, and a Return inside Hold is data.

  • x/0 waits for the value of x (ROADMAP CE-95, Tycho row 413). With x: real and no value, x/0 was canonicalized to ComplexInfinity, so \{x/0 > 0: 1, 0\} compiled to (0 < Infinity) ? 1 : 0 and gave 1 at every x, including x = 0, where the value is 0/0. A quotient by the number 0 now folds to ComplexInfinity only when the numerator is provably not zero: a number other than 0 (5/0, π/0, i/0), or an expression whose sign is known from its type and the assumptions ((x^2+1)/0, e^x/0). Otherwise the quotient stays x/0 through evaluate(), .N() and simplify(), and the value decides: Indeterminate at x = 0, ComplexInfinity elsewhere. A numerator that reads a variable with an assigned value is not folded when it is boxed, so the answer follows a later assignment. The compiled branch above now gives 0 at x = 0. A limit does not take such a quotient as its value: lim_{x→a⁺} x/(x−a) with no assumption on a stays unevaluated.

  • A vector plus a matrix adds the vector to the rows (ROADMAP CE-399). A sum of tensors whose shapes nest (the shape of each one is the start of the shape of the deepest) adds element i of the vector to row i of the matrix: [1, 2] + [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] is [[2, 3, 4], [6, 7, 8]], typed matrix<integer^(2x3)>. It was Error("incompatible-dimensions", "2 vs 2x3") for two list literals, while the same sum of symbols that held these values gave the matrix, as compiled JavaScript and Less did. The value is now the same on every route; a compiled Sum over a list that holds a matrix and a row gives it too, where it threw. Shapes that do not nest ([1, 2, 3] + [[1, 2], [3, 4]], a 2 by 2 plus a 2 by 3 matrix) are still an incompatible-dimensions error. A product is not changed: a vector times a matrix is the matrix product.

New Features​

  • couldMatch(other, { nonEmpty: true }) (ROADMAP CE-397, Tycho row 429). couldMatch() answers true for two list types with no dimensions whatever their elements, because the empty list is a value of both. With the option, it answers whether a value that is not an empty collection has both types, so it tells a list of numbers from a list of points: ce.type('list<number>').couldMatch('list<tuple<number, number>>', { nonEmpty: true }) is false, and couldMatch('list<integer>', { nonEmpty: true }) is true. Only the outer collection must be non-empty: [[]] is a value of both list<list<number>> and list<list<string>>. The couldMatch documentation no longer says that list<integer> could not be a list<string>.

Resolved Issues​

  • FindFit with global: true searches an even function of a periodic term on a fine enough grid (ROADMAP CE-176, Tycho row 407). The grid spaces a searched frequency by the period of the expression around the periodic function. An even outer function (Cos, Sec, Cosh, Sech) of a term that changes sign under a half-period shift has half the period of the term: cos(cos θ) and sec(sin θ) have the period π, cos(sin θ cos θ) has π/2. The grid recorded 2π (or π), so it was twice as coarse as the basins of the residual. cos(sin θ + 1), cos(sin² θ) and sin(cos θ) keep their period.

  • The type of an element-wise operation over a list of tensors or a broadcastable operand (ROADMAP CE-398, Tycho row 430). Three kinds of static type did not hold the value, or said less than they could:

    • A list whose elements are each a number or a tensor (list<broadcastable<number>>, list<tensor<number>>) is not one tensor, because two elements can have different ranks ([1, [2, 3], [[4]]]). An element-wise operation over it is now typed list<broadcastable<…>>: with U: vector<real^3> and M: list<broadcastable<number>>, U + M is list<broadcastable<number>>. It was list<broadcastable<number> | list<any>>, an arm with no layout on the compiled routes. Sin(T) with T: list<tensor<number>> was typed tensor, which [[sin 1, sin 2], [[sin 3]]] is not.
    • An operand declared broadcastable<number> may hold a matrix. Beside a vector, the result was typed as if the operand was a number: with B: broadcastable<number> holding a 3 by 2 matrix, U + B, U^B and U < B evaluate to 3 by 2 matrices, but were typed vector<3> and list<boolean^3>. They are now typed tensor and tensor<boolean>. A union with a broadcastable arm (broadcastable<real> | integer) is read the same way.
    • U·B was typed broadcastable<real>, the cells of U: with B = i it is [i, 2i, 3i]. A product with a broadcastable<E> factor beside a collection now takes the tier of E (tensor here). A product of a list literal and such a factor ([1, 2]·b) is broadcastable<number>, not vector<2>: when b holds a matrix the product is a matrix product ([1, 2]·[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] is [9, 12, 15]).

    A comparison of an element-wise application over an abstract collection with a list (Sin(P) < [1, 2] with P: collection<number>) is now typed tensor<boolean>, not list<boolean^2>: Sin(P) is typed broadcastable<number>, which admits a matrix.

0.163.0 2026-10-23​

Breaking Changes​

  • Residue classes have a type of their own, residue (ROADMAP CE-136, #471). A residue class, an element of ℤ/nℤ, had the type value, and the engine kept the number rules (c/c is 1, c - c is 0) away from it by looking for an operator named ResidueClass. A head with another name got no protection: with MyMod declared (any, any) -> value, MyMod(2, 4)/MyMod(2, 4) simplified to 1, although 2 has no inverse modulo 4. The type now does what the name did:

    • ResidueClass(k, n) is typed residue, arithmetic over classes too (c · [1, 2] is a list<residue^2>, NaN + c is nan | residue), and ℤ/nℤ is a set<residue>. residue is a value, not a number: it is disjoint from every numeric type, residue | integer is a union, and a symbol declared residue refuses an integer (ce.assign('r', 2) throws; an integer is a representative of a class, not the class).
    • The arithmetic operators that have residue arithmetic (Add, Subtract, Multiply, Divide, Negate, Power, Square, Sqrt, Root) name residue in their parameter types. Every other operator refuses a class at boxing with an incompatible-type error: Sin(c), Floor(c), Mod(c, 5) were admitted and stayed unevaluated. The incompatible-type error of these nine operators names the new parameter type: Sqrt("banana") reports "expected complex | infinity | residue", where it reported complex | infinity. Max(c, x) and Min(c, x) refuse a class too, as an operand, an element of a list or an element of ℤ/nℤ: classes have no order. The call is typed error when it is boxed and evaluates to an incompatible-type error (Max(c, x) was typed number and stayed unevaluated).
    • The protection reads the type: an operator declared to return residue (ce.declare('MyMod', { signature: '(any, any) -> residue' })), a function whose inferred signature returns it (g := k ↦ ResidueClass(k, 4) is (unknown) -> residue), and a symbol declared residue, which is protected before it has a value (r/r stays r/r). A head with another name gets the admission and the protection, not the arithmetic of ResidueClass: a sum or a product of its values stays unevaluated (a hook for the head to supply that arithmetic is planned, ROADMAP CE-507). A symbol typed value or left undeclared is still read as a possible number: w/w is 1 for it.
    • A juxtaposed class is a product: \overline{3}_{7}x parses to Multiply, not to a tuple. compile() declines an expression typed residue or one that holds a class; an expression that only may hold one (a parameter typed number | residue) compiles. The documentation lists the type in doc/08-guide-types.md, the rules in docs/TYPE-SYSTEM.md, and how an operator declares it in doc/06-guide-augmenting.md.

  • A comparison with an absent number is absent (ROADMAP CE-93, Tycho row 411). With w: number | missing holding Missing, w > 0 was False: a numeric slot read its absent value as NaN. But If(w > 0, 1, 0) had no value (the absent-condition error), so the two forms disagreed. A comparison (<, ≤, >, ≥, =, ≠, chained or not) with an absent operand is now Missing, in a numeric slot too, and it is typed boolean | missing. The broadcast form agrees: [1, 2] < w is [Missing, Missing]. A NaN is a value, and a comparison with it keeps the IEEE answer; arithmetic still reads an absent number as NaN (w + 1 < 2 is False). Compiled JavaScript and Python give the absent value (undefined, None) when such an operand is passed absent, where JavaScript gave false and Python raised a TypeError; a chain is read link by link, so 5 < 0 < w is false. On GLSL and WGSL an absent number can only be NaN, and these comparisons compile as before, with the IEEE answer. A chained comparison with an operand that has an effect (0 < w < Random()) and an operand that may be absent no longer compiles; with fallback (the default) compile() runs the interpreter. One case compiled numeric code cannot tell apart: a local variable that holds the NaN of an If with no else branch is read as a value. Rule: docs/ERROR-MODEL.md.

New Features​

  • Factoring over a number field (contributed by KingArth0r, #469). Factor(polynomial, variable, generator) factors over the algebraic extension of the rationals that generator selects. The generator can be an exact radical (√2, ∛2), ImaginaryUnit, or the new AlgebraicGenerator(List(c₀, c₁, …)): a root of the irreducible polynomial with these rational coefficients in ascending order, with no numerical embedding chosen. Factor(x^2 - 2, x, √2) is (x - √2)(x + √2); over the rationals, x^2 - 2 stays irreducible. The result is exact, also under .N(). A request that the engine cannot answer within its limits (a coefficient it cannot read, an unsupported generator, the operation budget) stays unevaluated; it is never factored over the rationals instead, and an unevaluated result is not a proof of irreducibility. A power of a generator at or above the degree of its polynomial is reduced, as (√2)^2 is 2: for α a root of t² - 2, α^2 is 2 and Expand((x - α)(x + α)) is x^2 - 2. The one- and two-argument forms of Factor are unchanged. Examples and limits: number-field factoring.

Performance​

  • Solve of a polynomial whose roots have closed forms is about 4 times faster (ROADMAP CE-385). x^4 + x^2 - 1 = 0 takes 1.0 ms, where it took 4.1 ms in 0.162.0 and 1.9 ms in 0.133.0. The roots that the closed-form formulas give for the equation itself (a quadratic, a pure power a·xⁿ + b, or a polynomial in xᵍ that reduces to one of these) are exact by construction, so they are no longer substituted back into the equation, and repeated roots among them are found by comparing the expressions. Before, each root was substituted and the residual, an exact constant such as (-1/2 + √5/2)^2 + (-1/2 + √5/2) - 1, was proved zero by refining it at increasing precision. The roots of every other route (squaring, a change of variable, the rational-root search, the numeric root finder) are still checked.
  • Symbolic operations are 10% to 30% faster (ROADMAP CE-385). Compared with 0.162.0: D(x^3, x) and Expand((x + 1)^3) take about 0.7 of the time, evaluate() and simplify() of small expressions about 0.8, and antiderivatives and definite integrals 0.7 to 0.8. The type of a new expression is derived with less work when its operands are numbers: the check for an element-wise application over a list is skipped, and fewer objects are created for each operand. A product with no sum, no Negate, no Divide and no matrix among its factors is built once instead of twice. An indefinite integral no longer prepares the residue method, which applies only to some definite integrals, and the check of a function type is done once per type. The results are the same.

Behavior Changes​

  • A branch on NaN ≠ x takes its first arm (ROADMAP CE-125). NaN ≠ 2 is True, but If(NaN ≠ 2, 1, 0) and, with b holding NaN, Which(b ≠ 2, 1, True, 0) took no arm: Missing in the interpreter, NaN in compiled JavaScript and Python. A statement-form If ran neither branch. The element-wise form gave the IEEE answer, so Which([1, b, 3] ≠ 2, 1, True, 0) was [1, 1, 1] and its second element did not match the scalar form. A branch now uses the value True of a ≠ with a NaN operand, as it already used the value False of <, ≤, >, ≥ and =: the examples give 1 on the interpreter, JavaScript and Python. An absent operand (Missing, an input the caller leaves out) still leaves the branch without an arm. Rule: docs/ERROR-MODEL.md.

  • A chained comparison with a NaN pair is False (ROADMAP CE-94, Tycho row 413). 0 < NaN < Missing was Missing, while 0 < i < Missing was False: a pair with no order stopped the chain, but a NaN pair did not, and the absent operand won. A pair with a NaN operand now makes the chain False, wherever the absent operand sits (Missing < 0 < NaN is False too), on the interpreter and in compiled JavaScript and Python, which gave undefined/None. A chain whose every pair has the absent operand stays absent: NaN < Missing < 0 is Missing. Undefined is read as absent in a chain as Missing is: NaN < Undefined < 0 and i < Undefined < 0 are Missing, where they were False. Also fixed: compiled code decides a branch over a chain link by link, as the interpreter does, so with x = 1 and w (number | missing) absent, If(x < 0 < w, 1, 2) gives 2, where it gave NaN. Rule: docs/ERROR-MODEL.md.

  • .N() of an integral whose integrand has no value is NaN (ROADMAP CE-177, Tycho row 411). Integrate(Which(t > 5, 1), Limits(t, 0, 1)).N() stayed unevaluated: no sample of the integrand was a number, and the integral was kept as if the integrand held an unknown symbol. NIntegrate and the compiled routes gave NaN. When every sample is the undefined value (NaN, a selection with no selected arm, arithmetic with Missing), the integral is now NaN under .N(), also for a double integral; ∫₀¹ t·Missing dt is NaN too. An integrand that still holds a free symbol (∫₀¹ t·D dt, an undeclared g(t)) stays symbolic.

Resolved Issues​

  • A product over a list of elements of unknown type, or over rows, was typed unknown (ROADMAP CE-374). Product(L) of an operand that is not a list literal becomes Reduce(L, Multiply, 1) at canonicalization, and the type of a Reduce is the reducer's own result type, which is unknown for Multiply over an element of unknown type: with L: list<unknown>, Sum(Rest(L)) was a broadcastable<number> and Product(Rest(L)) was unknown; with V: list<vector<2>>, Product(Rest(V)) was unknown too. A seeded Add or Multiply fold with the identity as its seed is now typed as Sum or Product type the collection when the elements are of unknown type or are numbers or rows: Product(Rest(L)) is a broadcastable<number> and Product(Rest(V)) is integer | vector<2> (the seed for an empty list, or a row). A tuple arm keeps the reducer's typing, and Scan keeps its running values.

  • Compiled Equal and NotEqual read a NaN operand as absent and answered Missing where the interpreter answers False or True (ROADMAP CE-386). With g := t ↦ [t, 2t] and x: any, the element g(x)[5] at x = 3 is NaN (an index past the end of a list of numbers), and the interpreter answers False for g(x)[5] = 1 and True for g(x)[5] ≠ 1. The compiled equality over an operand that may hold an object-domain absence (here typed missing | number | vector<2>) carried a guard that read NaN as absent, and answered Missing. The guard now tests the object absence only (undefined): a NaN operand compares as IEEE says on both routes, and g(x)[5] = 1 at x = "a", where the element is the object absence, still answers Missing on both. IsMissing and Coalesce keep reading NaN as absent. The guard is also emitted for an element read or a call typed any or unknown, which admits the absent value without a missing arm (a declared symbol of such a type stays the scalar the host passes): with g: (unknown) -> list, the element g(x)[1] is typed any, and g(x)[1] = 1 at x = [] answered NaN where the interpreter answers Missing. Each operand of the guarded comparison that is a call or an element read, or that is impure, is now evaluated once: Equal(g(x)[1], Random()) drew twice, in the absence test and in the comparison.

  • .N() of an integral that diverges at an infinite bound gave a random value or NaN (ROADMAP CE-391). evaluate() gives +∞ for ∫₀^∞ eˣ dx, but .N() gave a Monte-Carlo estimate that changed at each run (5007912 ± 2900000), and NaN for ∫₀^∞ x dx. When the integrand has one sign on the interval and does not decay faster than 1/x (or overflows) on the infinite tail, .N(), NIntegrate and a compiled integral now give +∞ or −∞. When the sign changes, .N() and NIntegrate take the answer of the exact route, as compiled code already did with the closed form: ∫₀^∞ (x − 1) dx is +∞ and ∫₀^∞ (eˣ − 5) dx is +∞ (it was a Monte-Carlo value). An integral with no value (∫₀^∞ sin x dx, ∫_{−∞}^∞ x dx) still gives NaN.

  • .N() of ∫₀^∞ x¹⁰⁰·e⁻ˣ dx was wrong by 45 orders of magnitude (ROADMAP CE-394). It gave 1.9·10¹¹² ± 1.8·10¹¹²; the value is 100! ≈ 9.3·10¹⁵⁷. In double precision x¹⁰⁰ is ∞ and e⁻ˣ is 0 past x ≈ 1200, so the integrand was NaN on the tail, the quadrature did not converge, and Monte Carlo missed the peak. Where a product of powers and exponentials is not finite, it is now computed again as exp(100·ln x − x), on .N(), NIntegrate and compiled code: the result is 100! to 10 digits. An integral too large for the change of variable of the quadrature (170!) is NaN, not a random value.

  • A definite integral over a half-infinite interval with a pole at its finite bound was ComplexInfinity (ROADMAP CE-391). ∫₀^∞ (x − 1)/x³ dx and ∫₀^∞ −1/x³ dx gave ComplexInfinity, which is not the value of a real integral. They are now −∞: the sign of the integrand next to the pole decides, and the antiderivative at the infinite bound tells whether the tail adds a divergence of its own. When it adds one of the other sign (∫₀^∞ (x − 1)/x² dx), the integral has no value and is Indeterminate.

  • A function that receives itself as an argument and recurses through a lazy Map stayed unevaluated (a regression in 0.160.0, #470, ROADMAP CE-387). With G = (self, t) ↦ If(Length(t) = 0, 0, Max(Map(c ↦ self(self, c), t)) + 1), the height of a tree given as nested lists, Apply(G, G, [[[], []]]) gave the Apply(…) back, where 0.159.0 gave 2; Reduce and Sum in place of Max failed the same way. The body scope of a function literal is shared by its applications, and an application hides its parameters there, so that the body reads the values of its call frame. A nested application of the same literal put the parameters back when it ended, and a canonicalization of the literal during an application declared them again, while an enclosing application still read its parameters through that scope: the next element of the lazy Map then read self with no value. The parameters now come back when the last application ends, and a canonicalization during an application uses the hidden bindings.

  • The signature of a function literal read a captured parameter as a number cell in a nested literal (ROADMAP CE-379). With g := x ↦ (() ↦ [x]), the signature was (unknown) -> () -> vector<1>: the nested literal has a type of its own, and its own typing read the captured x as a number cell, while x ↦ [x] is (unknown) -> list<unknown> since 0.162.0. The value ["a"] of g("a")() does not fit a vector<1>. The derivation of a signature now types a nested literal again with the parameters of the enclosing literals added to its own: g is (unknown) -> () -> list<unknown>, x ↦ (() ↦ [[x]]) is (unknown) -> () -> list<list<unknown>>, and a parameter of the nested literal that shadows the captured name is read as its own (x ↦ ((x: real) ↦ [x]) keeps (real) -> vector<real^1>). A use that narrows the parameter keeps the number cell (x ↦ (() ↦ [x + 1]) is (unknown) -> () -> vector<1>). An ascribed result of the nested literal is kept, and so are the arms of an early Return of its body; a call of the nested literal inside the body is typed from the derived result.

  • Solve of a polynomial with large terms gave a root that is not a root, or lost a root. The rational-root search tested each candidate by the value of the polynomial at 21 digits, and a candidate was taken for a root when the terms were large: x³ − 10¹²x² + 10¹² = 0 gave the root 10¹², whose value is 10¹², and the true root next to it was then removed as its duplicate, so the list held 2 of the 3 roots; x⁹ − 1000x⁸ + 1000 = 0 held 8 of its 9 roots. A candidate is now an exact rational, tested with exact arithmetic. A root found by the numeric root finder whose value is an integer is now a float (1000000000000.0), not an exact integer, so the exact check no longer rejects the root that it approximates. A rational root of a polynomial of degree 3 or more is now exact: 2x³ − 3x² − 3x + 2 = 0 gives −1, 1/2 and 2 (it gave 0.5).

  • Compiled code declined a call of a user function whose argument is an untyped free input (ROADMAP CE-377). With g := t ↦ [t, 2] and x free, the signature of g is (unknown) -> list<unknown>, so the engine types g(x)[1] as unknown, and the complex lane of the JavaScript target declined g(x)[1] + g(x)[2] ("scalar arithmetic over a list-valued operand"); Trace(m(x)) + 1 with m := t ↦ [[t, 1], [2, 3]] declined the same way, and Sum(1 + v(x)[2], k from 1 to 3) with v := s ↦ [s, k] and k = i declined in every mode. The emitted code reads an untyped free input as one scalar (x + 1 is _.x + 1), so the compiler now types an operand with each such input read as a number, with the engine's own derivation: g(x) is a vector<2>, g(x)[1] is a number, and the operand is a scalar. The three expressions compile in every mode, with the interpreter's values; a call keeps its run-time broadcast, so an input that holds a list at run time still maps the call over it. The shader targets read the static length of such a call's result the same way: v(x)[2] + 1 with v := s ↦ [s, 2s] compiles to (_fn_v(x)).y + 1.0 on GLSL and WGSL, where it declined ("the base (type list<unknown>) has no statically known length"); a list with a complex element still has no shader value, and the decline now names that element. The decline of an operand that only may be a list at run time, h(x) + 1 with h: (unknown) -> unknown and no body, names the operand and its type ("a possibly list-valued operand (h(x), of type unknown)"), where it said "a list-valued operand".

  • Compiled JavaScript gave NaN or false for an absent element where the interpreter gives Missing (ROADMAP CE-368). With g := t ↦ [t, 2t] and x: any, the element g(x)[5] is absent at x = [1, 2, 3] (the index is past the end) and at x = [], and the interpreter answers Missing for g(x)[5] + 1, Sin(g(x)[5]), -g(x)[5], g(x)[5]·g(x)[5] and g(x)[5] < 1. The compiled code spelled the absent element undefined and applied the scalar function to it: NaN, or false for the comparison. The run-time broadcast (_SYS.bcast) and the checked product (_SYS.mulChecked) now answer undefined when an operand is absent beside scalars only, and a compiled comparison answers undefined for an absent cell. Beside a present list the absent operand is still NaN in each cell (g(x)[5] + [1, 2] is [NaN, NaN] on both routes, and so is g(x)[5] + g(x)[1] at x = [1, 2]), and a comparison with a list answers an absent cell for each (g(x)[5] < [1, 2] is [Missing, Missing]). The compiled Sum of a list with an absent element is unchanged (NaN, a numeric slot, as in the interpreter). The ten tests of tycho-row-425-index-of-broadcastable-call.test.ts that recorded the divergence are agreement checks again.

  • A surplus tuple operand of Numerator, Denominator or NumeratorDenominator gave a tuple of errors (#467, contributed by enumeratio). A call with an operand past the declared arity is one unexpected-argument error when the surplus operand is a tuple, as it is for a list: Numerator(3/2, (1, 2)) was (Error, Error), a tuple of two errors, and is now the one error. The type of the call is no longer lifted over a surplus list or tuple (it was list<…> or tuple<…>): it keeps the declared result type of the operator, nothing | number for Numerator and Denominator and nothing | tuple<number, number> for NumeratorDenominator.

  • simplify() gave False for a relation whose two sides are the same function call. f(a) = f(a), sin(a) = sin(a) and g(x) + 1 = g(x) + 1 simplified to False, and f(a) ≠ f(a) to True; evaluate() gave the correct values. The simplifier rewrote the relation as f(a) - f(a) = 0, that is 0 = 0, and the factoring step then divided both sides by their common coefficient, 0, which gave NaN = NaN. Such a relation now stays as it is, as x = x does, and Factor(0 = 0) is 0 = 0 (it was NaN = NaN). The same error made Equal(c, c) False for a value c of an extension head (#471).

  • Compiled folds over elements of unknown type, absent elements, and booleans (ROADMAP CE-380, CE-381, CE-382). Three kinds of compiled JavaScript folds (Sum, Product, Reduce, Scan, and Max, Mean and the other statistics) disagreed with the interpreter:

    • With L: list<unknown>, Sum(L) + 1 and Product(L) · 2 did not compile, although L usually holds real numbers. They now compile, and a complex entry of the fold is added as complex: over [[1, 2], [i, 3]], Sum(L) + 1 is [2 + i, 6] and Reduce(L, Add, 0) + 1 is [2 + i, 6]; the second gave ["[object Object]1", 6]. In the complex mode, the same parents over list<list<number>> compile too, and a bare list is read as a list whose cells may be complex, as list<unknown> is: L + 1 over [i, 2] gave ["[object Object]1", 3]. In the default mode, a complex entry in a list input that the code reads as real is still the host's responsibility.
    • JavaScript reads null as 0 in +, * and Math.min. With L: list<number | missing> and [2, null, 3], Scan(L, Multiply, 1) gave [2, 0, 0], Reduce(L, Add, 0) gave 5 and Reduce(L, Min) gave 0; Reduce(L, Multiply, ImaginaryUnit) threw. Each is now NaN from the absent element on, as in the interpreter ([2, NaN, NaN], NaN). The Product and Sum of rows with an absent entry ([[2, null], [3, 4]]) are [6, NaN] and [5, NaN] (they were [6, 0] and [5, 4]), and a matrix product reads an absent cell as NaN.
    • The Sum and Product of a list of booleans or strings (list<boolean>, list<list<string>>), the Reduce and Scan of a list of booleans with Add, Multiply, Min or Max, and the Max, Min and Mean of a list of booleans no longer compile; the interpreter gives an incompatible-type error or leaves Max(True, False) unevaluated. The compiled Sum of [[true], [false]] was [1]. With fallback (the default), compile() runs the interpreter for these.

  • Compiled Multiply of a fold and a matrix did not compile (ROADMAP CE-388). With M: matrix<number> and L: list<matrix<number>> (or list<tensor<number>>, or list<unknown>), Sum(L)·M, M·Reduce(L, Add, 0) and 2·Sum(L)·M were refused at compile time, so compile() ran the interpreter. They now compile to the matrix product, decided on the shapes of the values as in the interpreter: Sum(L)·M is [[2, 2], [5, 3]] for L = [[[1, 2], [3, 4]], [[1, 0], [0, 1]]] and M = [[0, 1], [1, 0]]. With complex entries (L: list<matrix<complex>>, or an At(P, 1) of complex matrices) the product is computed as complex; such products were refused too. A factor that may hold points (Sum(L) over a list of lists of points, or over list<list<unknown>>) beside a matrix is still refused: compiled code holds a point as an array, and the interpreter scales the matrix by the point.

  • Multiply of a lazy collection and a matrix paired their elements (ROADMAP CE-390). The value of Scan, Reverse or Map is a lazy collection, and Multiply read it as a plain collection: beside a matrix, it paired each element with a row of the matrix. With L holding the vectors [1, 2] and [3, 4] and M = [[0, 1], [1, 0]], Reverse(L)·M was [[0, 4], [1, 0]]; it is now the matrix product [[4, 3], [2, 1]], as for the list literal [[3, 4], [1, 2]]. A lazy collection of vectors or matrices is read as the tensor of its elements: Scan(L, Add, 0)·M over a list of matrices now stays unevaluated (a tensor of rank 3 beside a matrix), as the same list literal does, where it gave a value. A lazy collection whose elements have no known type (Map(Reverse, L)) is read from its values when a matrix is beside it; two such collections keep the product of each entry, as compiled code computes it. A point in such a collection stays a point.

  • A list literal with an absent cell had no dimensions (ROADMAP CE-389). [[2, Missing], [3, 4]] was typed list<list<integer | missing>>, while [[2, 3], [3, 4]] is a matrix<integer^(2x2)>. So it could not be assigned to a symbol declared matrix<(number | missing)^(2x2)>, Shape and Rank of it were () and 0, Multiply of two such matrices paired their rows, and Determinant and Inverse were an incompatible-type error. A literal whose cells are numbers that may be absent now has the dimensions of its shape (matrix<(integer | missing)^(2x2)>, Shape (2, 2)), and an absent cell is read as NaN where a number is needed, as for an absent operand: [[2, Missing], [3, 4]]·[[1, 0], [0, 1]] is [[NaN, NaN], [3, 4]] (the value compiled code gives), its Determinant is NaN, and its Trace, which reads the diagonal only, is 6. Transpose, Flatten and the other operators that move cells keep the absent cell. The type of such a literal, and of a broadcast over it, now carries its length: [1, Missing] is typed list<(integer | missing)^2>, and Sin([Missing, 1]) vector<2>.

0.162.0 2026-10-23​

Breaking Changes​

  • Multiply of two matrices is the matrix product, however the factors are written (ROADMAP CE-98). A product of two matrix values is now the matrix product, as MatrixMultiply, also when the factors are symbols typed tensor<number>, list<list<number>>, list, any, broadcastable<number> or number | matrix, and under .N(). Before, a product of two such symbols multiplied each entry (and .N() did so even for matrix<number> symbols), while a literal or computed factor gave the matrix product; so p·p now equals p^2. Migration: use HadamardProduct(p, q) for the product of each entry. Unchanged: a vector or a plain list times a vector or a plain list multiplies each entry, and a number times a matrix scales each entry. Related changes:

    • The canonical form keeps the written order of factors that may be matrices (q·p stays q·p; p·q − q·p is no longer 0), and isSame() and the hash tell them apart. simplify(), Expand, Factor and D keep that order: (A·B)^2 is no longer A^2·B^2, the product rule of D keeps each factor in place, and D(f^n) for a matrix-valued f uses the matrix rules (D(f^-1) = -f^-1·f'·f^-1). A sum with a term that may be a number beside a term that may be a matrix is not expanded, because a number added to a matrix is added to each entry.
    • Matrices whose dimensions do not agree give Error("incompatible-dimensions", …) (the product stayed unevaluated), and the result type of a product of matrices has the dimensions of the matrix product (matrix<2x3>·matrix<3x4> is matrix<2x4>).
    • Two tensors of rank 3 of the same length multiply each pair of matrices, as Power does; a tensor of rank 3 beside a matrix or a vector stays unevaluated; a number times a tensor of rank 3 scales every cell; a Range beside a matrix is read as a vector.
    • Compiled JavaScript: matrix<…> operands call the matrix product; tensor<number>, list<list<number>> and broadcastable<number> choose by the shape of the values when the code runs. Python uses np.matmul for matrix types. interval-js throws (its result is then entire) for a list of lists times another list. Types that may hold points (bare list, list<unknown>, any, list<tuple<…>>) keep the product of each entry, because compiled code stores a list of points and a matrix as the same array (ROADMAP CE-216.1); their compiled operand order now follows the written order. A list whose rows have different lengths, or that mixes numbers and lists ([[1], [2, 3]]), is not a matrix: its elements are paired with the elements of the other factors, as in the interpreter ([[1], [2, 3]]·[[4], [5, 6]] is [[4], [10, 18]]; it was null or wrong values). Two tensors of rank 3 multiply each pair of matrices, as in the interpreter (it threw, and a compiled Product gave NaN entries); a tensor of rank 3 beside a matrix or a vector throws when the code runs. Where the interpreter gives an incompatible-dimensions error, compiled code gives NaN. A compiled Multiply fold (Product, Reduce(L, Multiply, 1), Scan) over elements of several shapes (numbers beside lists, a matrix beside a row, rows of different lengths) compiles and multiplies each step as the interpreter does; it was refused, or threw "the elements have incompatible dimensions" for a matrix beside a row. A compiled Sum still checks that its elements have one shape.
    • A product boxed while its symbols are unknown is still sorted: declare a matrix-capable type for the written order to be kept. Divide(p, q) of two matrices still divides each entry (p·q^-1 is the matrix product).
    • The Derivative of a function declared with codomain any keeps that signature (it was typed (any*) -> number), so expressions built on it are typed any too.

  • has() on a dictionary is the symbol test; the key test is hasKey(). has(v) asks whether the symbol (or function operator) v occurs in an expression, and a dictionary now answers that over the values of its entries, as every other expression does. Before, a dictionary replaced it with a key test: ce.box({ dict: { a: { sym: 'u' } } }).has('u') was false and .has('a') was true; now .has('u') is true, .has('a') is false (a key is a string, not a symbol, unless a also occurs in a value), and .has('Dictionary') is true. The key test moves to the new method hasKey(key) of DictionaryInterface (records included). Migration: replace dict.has(key) with dict.hasKey(key) wherever you test whether a dictionary or a record has a key. A call dict.has(key) still compiles, because has() exists on every expression, and now returns a different answer. The other symbol queries read dictionary values too: .symbols, .unknowns, .freeVariables, .subexpressions, .errors and the references of a dictionary, or of an expression that holds one, now include what its values hold (.errors of {"a" -> Error("oops")} lists the error, though the dictionary stays valid). has(), .subexpressions and these queries visit a value shared by several entries once.

  • A declared type is a contract on every value the symbol takes. s: string now refuses Missing and Undefined as it refuses 5, on the engine's assignment route and in Epsil (static check and run time alike); a declared element contract is checked too, so xs: list<string> refuses ["a", Missing]. An author who wants absence writes it: string | missing, list<string | missing>, or a refining declaration (list, list<unknown>). A number declaration still admits NaN, the numeric absence marker, so a numeric restriction such as 3 {a > 0} (typed integer | nan) binds to n: number as before; a restricted non-numeric value such as (1, 2) {a > 0} (typed missing | tuple<integer, integer>) needs tuple<number, number> | missing. This reverses the rule of 2026-09-09 under which a declared type described the successes only and a symbol declared string could report string while holding Missing. Decision P1 and P1b of docs/plans/2026-10-21-presence-contracts-and-assertion.md.

  • One default for an absent argument at a library parameter that excludes absence: it is refused. An operator with no absence behavior of its own now answers an incompatible-type error naming the parameter when an absent value (Missing, Undefined) reaches a parameter typed as data that excludes absence (string, boolean, value, a color, …), as a user function does for the same argument. Before, the handler received the marker and answered as it happened to: Parse(Missing) and IsSquareMatrix(Missing) computed a value from it, ToUpperCase(Missing) was already an error. Unchanged: numeric and collection operators answer the marker of their result (Sin(Missing) is NaN, Reverse(Missing) is Missing), operators that own their absence semantics (Length, Equal, the reducers, Coalesce, IsMissing), operators that hold their operands (Expand, Integrate, ForAll), and a parameter typed expression, symbol, any or unknown. Decision P2.

  • A list type with no dimensions is read by its elements. A vector, a matrix and a tensor are read by their cells. list<T> and set<T> now read T as the type of the elements, the values that indexing returns. A matrix of integers is a list<vector<integer>> and a list<list<integer>>. It is no longer a list<integer>. Before, the subtype relation also read T as the type of the cells (a list type with no dimensions "admitted any shape"), while indexing, the library and the compiler read T as the element type. The two readings together let a wrong value through: with L: list<number>, the assignment L := [[1, 2], [3, 4]] was accepted, L[1] + 1 was typed number and gave [2, 3], Mean(L) was accepted and failed at run time, and a compiled Sum(L) gave the string "01,23,4". Now the assignment is refused: a value of type matrix<integer^(2x2)> is not compatible with list<number>. list<integer> and list<list<integer>> are not related. Their meet is list<never>, the type of the empty list [], which is a value of both. For the same reason couldMatch() and typesOverlap() answer true for two lists with no dimensions, whatever their elements.

    vector<U>, matrix<U>, tensor<U> and list<U^dims> read U as the type of the cells, the values at the depth of the rank. The elements of a matrix are its rows: matrix<integer> is a list<vector<integer>>. A list<vector<integer>> is not a matrix, because its rows can have different lengths. A list has elements and may have a length (list<T^n>); vector, matrix and tensor have cells and may have a shape, written in one place: two rows of three integers are matrix<integer^(2x3)>, and a 2×3×4 array is tensor<integer^(2x3x4)>. Two spellings are now parse errors:

    • A list with two or more axes: list<integer^(2x3)>, list<integer^2x3>, list<boolean^(2x?)>, list<T^(MxN)>, list<2x3>. The message names the spelling to use: list<boolean^(2x2)> gives "A list type has one axis at most, its length (list<T^n>), but this type has 2 axes. Write matrix<boolean^(2x2)> instead". list<U^n> with one axis is valid.
    • A list with a length, a vector, a matrix or a tensor whose cells are lists: list<list<integer>^2>, list<vector<integer^3>^2>, list<list^2>, matrix<list<integer>>, tensor<list<integer>>. The message names the spelling with one shape (list<list<integer^3>^2> gives "Write matrix<integer^(2x3)>, with the shape in one place"); write list<list<integer>> for rows of any lengths.

    vector, matrix and tensor accept every cell type that is not a list: matrix<boolean>, matrix<string^(2x2)>, vector<string^2> (printed list<string^2>), tensor<boolean> and tensor<tuple<number, number>> are valid. Before, a vector or a matrix cell had to be able to hold a number, so matrix<boolean> was a parse error while matrix<any> was not. The bare names vector, matrix and tensor still mean number cells, so the linear-algebra operators, whose signatures use the bare names, still refuse a matrix of booleans. A printed type takes its head from its rank: rank 1 is vector<…> when the cells can hold a number and list<E^n> otherwise, rank 2 is matrix<…>, rank 3 or more is tensor<U^(…)>, and an unknown rank is tensor<U>. The types themselves do not change, only their spelling:

    ValueBeforeNow
    [True, False]list<boolean^2>list<boolean^2> (same)
    [[1, 2], [3, 4]]matrix<integer^(2x2)>matrix<integer^(2x2)> (same)
    M < 3, with M := [[1, 2], [3, 4]]list<boolean^(2x2)>matrix<boolean^(2x2)>
    (1, 2) * Mlist<tuple<integer, integer>^(2x2)>matrix<tuple<integer, integer>^(2x2)>
    [["a", "b"], ["c", "d"]]list<string^(2x2)>matrix<string^(2x2)>
    a 2×3×4 array of integerslist<integer^(2x3x4)>tensor<integer^(2x3x4)>
    Determinant of a matrix of booleansrefusedrefused (same)

    [(1, 2), (3, 4)] is still list<tuple<integer, integer>^2>, and Sin(M) is matrix<2x2>.

    tensor<U> is an array of any rank (1 or more) with cells of type U, and bare tensor is a numeric array of any rank. Before, tensor<U> meant list<U> (tensor<boolean> was list<boolean>, which does not hold a matrix of booleans), and bare tensor meant list<number>. The element type of a tensor<U> is U | tensor<U>: a cell, or a tensor of a lower rank. A matrix of integers matches tensor<integer>, but not list<integer>. A list<U> with a number type U and a vector<U> denote the same values: list<integer> matches vector<integer>, and vector<integer> matches list<integer>.

    broadcastable<T> is T | tensor<T> for a T that cannot hold a list (a number type, boolean, string, a tuple, integer | missing). A matrix of numbers matches broadcastable<number>, a matrix of integers matches broadcastable<integer | missing>, and a list<list<number>> does not match broadcastable<number> (its rows can have different lengths). broadcastable<boolean> is boolean | tensor<boolean>, so the matrix of booleans that a comparison over a matrix gives is one of its values, and broadcastable<tuple<number, number>> is a point or an array of points of any rank. broadcastable<T> no longer matches T | list<T>: to accept a number or a numeric array of any rank, write number | tensor, and for booleans boolean | tensor<boolean>.

    The relation is covariant again: vector<value> matches vector<any>, and list<expression^3> matches list<any^3>. They did not match before. The meet of two lists with no dimensions is the list of the meet of their elements: list<integer> & list<string> is list<never>. A meet of two list types is never only when their shapes cannot be the same: vector<integer^2> & vector<integer^3> is never.

    Some result types change:

    • A broadcast over operands of different ranks, over an operand whose type is a union of ranks, or over a tensor of unknown rank, is typed tensor<R>, for a result R that cannot hold a list. With U: list<integer> | matrix<integer>, U + 1 is tensor<integer> (it was list<integer | vector<integer>>). With T: tensor<integer>, T < 3 is tensor<boolean>. With an operator declared broadcastable: true and the signature (number, number) -> number, the call with [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and [10, 20] is tensor (it was list<number>).
    • Map over a matrix whose function keeps the length of the rows keeps the shape of the matrix: with h: (real) -> real, map(x ↦ h(x), [[1,2],[3,4]]) is matrix<real^(2x2)> (it was list<vector<real^2>^2>, a spelling that is now a parse error).
    • A generic function literal over a matrix keeps the shape of the operand: with g the literal (x: T) -> tuple<T, T> where T with the body (x, x), g([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) is matrix<tuple<integer, integer>^(2x2)> (it was list<tuple<integer, integer>>). Over a ragged list, see Resolved Issues.
    • A conditional protocol conformance type list<T> is P where … binds T to the elements of the receiver, as the generic solver does. For a matrix, the elements are the rows. With type list<T> is Named where T: number, name([1, 2]) uses the conformance as before, but name([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) now gives a protocol-implementation-missing error: T is vector<integer^2>, which is not a number (before, T was the cell type integer).
    • A cell pattern vector<T> or list<T^N> in a generic signature binds T to the cells of a tensor of rank 1, and a matrix no longer matches it: first: (x: list<T^N>) -> T where T, N applied to [[1, 2], [3, 4]] is an incompatible-type error (it was typed vector<integer^2>). A plain pattern list<T> binds T to the rows of the matrix.
    • Norm and Trace spell their tensor parameter tensor and accept a matrix as before. The result of Integrate spells its array arm tensor. Mean and the other statistics functions still accept a matrix when the expression is boxed, and refuse it when it is evaluated.
    • A broadcast over an operand that may hold a list of any depth is typed so. With b: broadcastable<number> holding a list, -b is tensor (it was list<number>, which does not hold a matrix value of b); with no value, it is broadcastable<number> as before. With C: indexed_collection, C < 2 is list<boolean | list<any>> (it was list<boolean>): an element of C may be a list, which the comparison maps at its leaves.
    • A generic function applied to a union whose options the broadcast reads differently is typed one option at a time. With f: (x: T) -> tuple<T, T> where T and u: list<integer> | set<integer>, f(u) is list<tuple<integer, integer>> | tuple<set<integer>, set<integer>> (it was list<tuple<list<integer> | set<integer>, …>>, which holds neither value). An operand of type collection<integer>, which may be mapped or passed whole, gets both answers.
    • PointX, PointY and PointZ of a list of points have the type of the coordinate: PointX of a list<tuple<string, number>> is list<string> (it was list<number>), and of a list<tuple<integer, integer>> it is list<integer>. Over rows of points whose first row is empty, PointX([[], [(1, 2), (3, 4)]]) is [[], [1, 3]] (it was [Missing, (1, 2)]). The compiled JavaScript refuses a point accessor over points whose coordinates may not be numbers, and throws a RangeError at run time on a value whose shape its type does not decide (numbers of rank 3 or more beside points).

    This entry replaces these entries of 0.160.0, where they describe the reading of a list type:

    • "The type broadcastable<T> is now T | list<T>": for a T that cannot hold a list, the collection part is now tensor<T>. Every subtype of list<T> is still a broadcastable<T>, and a tuple is still not a broadcastable<number>.
    • "The meet (intersection) of two collection types of different kinds is the narrower kind with the meet of the elements": list<number> and collection<list<integer>> no longer share a matrix. The type reducer now gives list<never> for their meet.
    • "The overlap test of types (typesOverlap())": two lists with no dimensions now always overlap, because the empty list is a value of both. list<list<list<real>>> and list<number> still overlap, but only through the empty list: they no longer share a tensor of rank 3.
    • "A list with dimensions whose element type is a top type (vector<unknown>, …) holds scalars, not lists": list<list^2> and list<list<integer>^2> are now parse errors. A matrix is still not a vector<unknown>, because the ranks are different.
    • "The meet of two collection types of the same kind no longer drops values that are in both": list<number> & list<list<integer>> is list<never> again, since no matrix is a list<number>, and the example matrix<number^(2x2)> & list<list<integer>^2> is now a parse error.
    • "The subtype relation of lists now reads a value in every way it can be read": the nested spelling read as its flat shape, the removal of outer axes by collection<E>, and list<vector<integer^3>> as a list<integer> are removed. matrix<string> and vector<collection> are now parse errors, list<vector<integer^1>^2> is a parse error, and list<vector<integer^3>> is not a list<integer>.
    • In Resolved Issues, "Subtype relation: matrix<T> is a subtype of broadcastable<T>": still true. couldMatch() still answers true for list<integer> and list<list<integer>>, but the reason is now the empty list: a matrix is not a value of list<integer>.

    The rules are in docs/TYPE-SYSTEM.md, section "Lists, tensors and broadcastable".

New Features​

  • FixedPoint(f, x) applies f from x until two successive values are the same. It was declared but did nothing: a call stayed unevaluated. FixedPoint(x => (x + 2/x)/2, 1.0) is 1.414213562373095…, and FixedPoint(Cos, 1.0) is 0.739085133…, correct to the working precision. Two values are the same when they are identical, when they are numbers, one of them a float, that agree to the working precision, or when they are lists or tuples whose elements are the same. An optional third argument is the maximum number of applications (the engine iteration limit by default); when it is reached, the last value is returned. Without a maximum, a call that cannot converge stays unevaluated: FixedPoint(Cos, 1) (Cos(1) is exact, and each step nests it) and an exact iteration whose terms gain digits; N gives their numeric fixed point. The result type is the result type of f.

  • The presence assertion x?! (AssertPresent(x) in MathJSON, ⁈ is an alias): the value of x, or an expected-present error naming the operand when x is absent (Missing, Undefined, NaN, Indeterminate, the set isMissing recognizes). Nothing passes through, an error operand propagates. Its type is the present part of the operand's type: xs[i]?! with xs: list<string> is a string, so f(xs[i]?!) is accepted at a parameter that excludes absence, and let y: string = xs[i]?! too. It is a postfix operator at the factorial's precedence and must abut its operand; as for 3! + 1, write x?! + 1, not x?!+1. Compiled: JavaScript, the interval JavaScript target and Python raise with the message expected-present: <operand> is absent; the check is omitted when the operand's type already excludes absence (a declared length and a literal index, a type without nan); a shader target compiles the identity and does not read the assertion as a proof, so a later absence test on the value keeps its own rule (decision P5). Decision P4.

  • The Epsil static check narrows a symbol an isMissing guard proves present. if isMissing(v) { "none" } else { f(v) }, if !isMissing(v) && v != "b" { f(v) } and isMissing(v) || f(v) == "a" are no longer reported at a parameter that excludes absence. A reassignment inside the region ends it; a function literal in the region is not entered.

  • The Epsil static check reports a possibly absent value wherever the run time refuses it: at a library parameter that excludes absence (trim(xs[i]), as it already did at a function's annotated parameter) and as the initializer of a declaration that excludes absence (let y: string = xs[i]). The discharges are the same everywhere: xs[i]?!, xs[i] ?? fallback, a guard, or a type that admits absence. Decision P3. A numeric read at a real, integer or complex declaration is reported too, since these types exclude NaN: let r: real = zs[i] for zs: list<real> (typed nan | real) was refused only when the program ran; write zs[i]?!, zs[i] ?? 0, or declare real | nan. A value with another type outside the declaration, such as a / b (infinity | nan | real), is not reported.

Improvements​

  • A Gaussian with a symbolic coefficient integrates to an error function (Tycho row 428). ∫ exp(−z²/(2s²)) dz is now √(π/2)·√(s²)·Erf(z/(√2·√(s²))), and ∫ exp(z²/(2s²)) dz the same form with Erfi; before, only a numeric coefficient (∫ e^{−3z²} dz) had a closed form. The sign of the coefficient is read as written when what remains after the sign is positive wherever it is defined, for every real value of the symbols (1/(2s²), e^a): ∫ e^{−a z²} dz with a bare a stays unevaluated, because at a < 0 the Erf form needs an imaginary argument, which the compile targets do not have, and so do ∫ e^{−s² z²} dz and ∫ e^{−|a| z²} dz, whose closed form is 0/0 at s = 0 or a = 0 while the integrand is 1. A symbol declared complex disqualifies the reading. A definite integral with an infinite bound carries the condition the way ∫₀^∞ e^{−cx} dx is 1/c {0 < c}: ∫_{−∞}^{∞} exp(−z²/(2s²)) dz is √(2π)·√(s²) {0 < √(s⁻²)}, and the normal distribution function 1/(√(2π)s) ∫_{−∞}^{x} exp(−½ z²/s²) dz, with or without a mean, is a guarded closed form in Erf. Its compiled JavaScript calls erf instead of running a numerical quadrature at every call: 2 469 calls take 2 ms instead of 3.2 s, with the same values to 2e-15.

  • More operators have a precise static result type. A type handler now derives the result from the operand types, where the declared result was a bare dictionary, tuple, list, matrix, value or unknown. Each type contains every value the operator can return for operands of those types; when the operand types do not decide it, the declared result stays.

    • FindRoot and FindFit are typed as their result record: FindRoot(x^2 - 2, [(x, 1)]) is record{parameters: record{x: real}, converged: boolean, residualNorm: nan | real | signed_infinity, iterations: integer, stationary: boolean} (FindFit has no stationary). So the Epsil static check reports let c: string = r.converged.
    • The linear-algebra operators Shape, PseudoInverse, LinearSolve, AdjugateMatrix, Kernel, MatrixMultiply, HadamardProduct, RowReduce, Diagonal, IdentityMatrix, ZeroMatrix, OnesMatrix, Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors, Eigen, LUDecomposition, QRDecomposition, CholeskyDecomposition, SingularValues and CharacteristicPolynomial carry the dimensions and the cell type of the result: PseudoInverse of a 3×2 matrix is a 2×3 matrix, and IdentityMatrix(3) is matrix<integer^(3x3)>.
    • TrigExpand, TrigToExp and TrigReduce of a numeric operand are number; TupleFrom of a list of known length is a tuple of that many components (TupleFrom([1, 2, 3]) is tuple<integer, integer, integer>).
    • A pipe whose stage is the name of a library operator is typed as the call: 16 |> Sqrt is real (it was unknown), and [3, 1, 2] |> Sort is list<integer>. So the static check reports let s: string = 16 |> sqrt. A stage that names a user function is not typed: a function parameter with the same name may be the function that is called.

Behavior Changes​

  • The signature of a function literal says only what its body proves about a parameter of unknown type. g := x ↦ [x] had the signature (unknown) -> vector<1>, which says that the element is a number, but g(Set(1, 2)) is [Set(1, 2)] and g("a") is ["a"]. The signature is now (unknown) -> list<unknown>: x ↦ [x, 1] and (x, y) ↦ [x, y] give list<unknown>, and x ↦ [[x]] gives list<list<unknown>>. A parameter that a use types as a number (x ↦ [x + 1]) and an annotated parameter ((x: real) ↦ [x]) keep the shape of the list. A call with a typed argument is typed from the body: with m := t ↦ [[t, 1], [2, 3]], m(2) is a matrix<integer^(2x2)> and m(r) with r: real a matrix<real^(2x2)>; a call with a free symbol is typed by the signature, list<list<unknown>>. The reading of an operand typed unknown as a number stays where an operation demands a number: x ↦ x + 1 is still (unknown) -> number. Consequences for a function with such a signature called with a free or an any-typed argument: an index into the call is typed missing | unknown (it was missing | number | vector<2>), a sum of its elements broadcastable<number>, and Dot of such an index the wide missing | value; the values are unchanged, and each type holds its value. With f(x) := (-x, x), h(a) := f([a, a]) is typed (unknown) -> list<tuple<number, number>> as before (the call maps f over the list), and an integral over a list integrand keeps its shape (∫₀¹ [x, 2x] dx is a vector<2>: the integration variable is a real). Compiled code that cannot tell whether an element of unknown type is a number declines in eight cases that compiled before: Trace(g(x)) + 1 with g := t ↦ [[t, 1], [2, 3]] and a free x in the complex lane, Sum(1 + v(x)[2], …) with v := s ↦ [s, k] on the JavaScript and GLSL targets, Product(Rest(g(x))) and Max(At(m(x), 1)). The workaround is a declaration, x: number or g: (number) -> matrix; ROADMAP CE-377 records the compiler change that removes the declines. ROADMAP CE-25; the rationale is in docs/TYPE-SYSTEM.md, "The inferred signature of a function literal".

  • The type of a list or set literal that holds an error value describes its other elements. A type describes the successful values, so an element whose type is error (an Error expression, or a failed application such as 1/"a") is left out of the element type when another element of the same level succeeded. [1, 1/"a", 3] is now typed vector<integer^3>, as [1, 2, 3] is; it was list<unknown>. [[1, 1/"a"], [3, 4]] is matrix<integer^(2x2)> (it was list<list<unknown>>), and Set(1, 1/"a") is set<integer> (it was set<unknown>). A level whose elements all failed keeps its type: [1/"a", 1/"a"] is still list<unknown>, and a set whose elements all failed is still set<unknown>. The error is still in the expression: isValid is false and errors lists it. As a result, the value of an element-wise If or Which with at least one successful cell matches the static type of the expression: If([True, Missing, False], 1, 0) is typed list<integer> and evaluates to [1, Error(…), 0], typed vector<integer^3>; that value was typed list<unknown>. A tuple is unchanged: (1, 1/"a") is still typed error.

    A variable with a declared type still refuses a collection that holds an error element, at any depth (also inside a tuple slot or a dictionary value, and through a symbol that holds the collection), unless the declared element type admits error (any, unknown, or an explicit error arm). With s: list<number>, s := [1, Error("oops")] throws, and the Assign and Declare operators give an incompatible-type error. The message now names the failed element ("The value holds the failed element Error("oops")…"), and it no longer states the type of the value when that type matches the declared type. A declared union is read arm by arm: list<number> | set<any> refuses [1, Error("oops")]. list<number | error> now admits that value; it was refused, because the value was typed list<unknown>. A parameter binding does not refuse it: a function whose parameter is declared list<number> runs when called with [1, Error("oops")], as before. A symbol without a declared type takes the value, as before.

  • An applied function literal is typed by its body (Tycho row 426). Apply(literal, args), and xs |> literal when the literal takes its argument whole, are now typed as the body with each parameter set to the argument's type, as a call of a named function already was: with M: list<real> and p(n) = s·n, Apply(a ↦ Map(p, a), M) is list<number> (it was collection<unknown>), and 'abc' |> (s ↦ s) is string. The derivation stops (and keeps the literal's own result type) for a body with an early Return, a loop, an assignment that is not at the top of the body, or a nested function that reads an outer parameter. A call of a named function whose body passes an inline callback (Map(u ↦ 2u, a)) is also refined. Other type changes in the same area:

    • A function literal's result type includes its early Return values, and Nothing when it can return nothing (Return(), or a final empty Block): x ↦ Block(If(x > 1, Return('big')), 2x) is -> number | string.
    • A Sum or Product index with the same name as a parameter no longer sets that parameter's type.
    • Map with a callback whose result type is unknown has elements of type unknown: Map(u ↦ Q, M) is list<unknown> (it was list<real>).

  • Inside a function or a Block, a stored value takes the current values of the variables it names; a closure keeps the variable. When Assign, Declare with a value, or a destructuring stores a value that names a parameter or a block local, those names are replaced by their values at that moment: with f := x ↦ Block(Declare(r), Assign(r, If(x > y, x, 0)), Assign(x, 100), r), f(3) is If(y < 3, 3, 0), and a block local no longer escapes its block unbound (it gave If(y < 3, b, 0)). A destructuring reads every variable as it was before the statement. A function literal in the value is not changed: it reads the variable when it is called, so a closure returned after a parameter is reassigned sees the last value (u ↦ u + 10, it was u ↦ u + 3), as closures over globals and block locals already did. When a function reassigns a parameter, a result that still names it uses its last value: a ↦ Block(Assign(a, [7, 8]), Map(u ↦ 2u, a)) gives [14, 16] (it mapped the original argument), and Filter likewise.

  • Compiled Power of a value whose depth is not known follows the interpreter's matrix power. For a base typed tensor<number>, tensor, list<list<number>> or broadcastable<number>, the compiled JavaScript checks the value's shape when it runs: a square matrix with an exact integer exponent gives the matrix power ([[1, 2], [3, -4]]^2 is [[7, -6], [-9, 22]]; it was [[1, 4], [9, 16]]), also for each matrix of a tensor of rank 3 or more, and a vector or a float exponent keeps the power of each entry. A non-square matrix to an integer power other than 1 throws expected-square-matrix, as the interpreter answers; this now also holds for MatrixPower, Inverse and Power over matrix<…>, which returned NaN. When compiled code cannot tell whether the exponent is exact (for example p^(2x) with x: real, or a float within 1e-12 of an integer, such as √n·√n), it throws instead of guessing. A base that may hold points (bare list, list<unknown>, any, list<tuple<…>>) keeps the power of each entry, unchanged, because compiled code stores a list of points and a matrix as the same array. A function the caller maps with functions takes precedence, as before.

  • An index into a broadcastable<T> whose T is a tuple, a string, a record or a dictionary is typed by what it can return. With p: broadcastable<tuple<number, number>> holding (1, 2), At(p, 1) is 1, but it was typed missing | tensor<tuple<number, number>> | tuple<number, number>, and Take(p, 1) is [1], but it was typed list<tuple<number, number>>. With p: broadcastable<string> holding "abc", At(p, 1) is the character "a", but it was typed missing | string | tensor<string>. The element readers (At, First, Second, Third, Last) and the selectors (Take, Drop, Rest, Most, Slice) now also include what an index into one value of T returns: the slots of a tuple (a nothing slot included), character for a string, the field types of a record (an unknown field included) and the value type of a dictionary, also for such an arm of a union T. At(p, 1) is now typed missing | number | tensor<tuple<number, number>> | tuple<number, number>, and a selector over broadcastable<string> is typed list<string | tensor<string>> | string, which holds the rows of a 2-D array of strings. A tuple and a string are still one cell for broadcasting, and the aggregates (Sum, Max, Reduce) read the elements as before.

    Compiled code: the JavaScript At(p, 3) of the one point (1, 2) gave Missing; it now gives NaN, as the interpreter does. The JavaScript and Python element readers and selectors of an operand that may be a string without proof that it is a list (broadcastable<string>, a broadcastable of one, an alias of one, string | list<string> on Python) now decline, so the fallback option decides: they read a string by UTF-16 code unit or by code point, so At(p, 1) of "abc" gave undefined (JavaScript) or NaN (Python), and First(p) of "😀b" half of a surrogate pair. Such an operand that holds a list of strings, which compiled correctly, now declines too. JavaScript First, Second and Third of an operand typed any, value or broadcastable<any> decline, as At and Last already did.

  • An index into a broadcastable<T> value is typed by what it can return (Tycho row 425). With g(t) = [t, 2t] and x: any, g(x) is typed broadcastable<vector<2>>: a number x gives a vector, a list x a list of vectors. g(x)[1] is now typed missing | number | vector<2> (it was missing | vector<2>, which does not hold the number that g(3)[1] gives), so Repeat(0, g(x)[1]) is valid. The same reading applies to First, Second, Third, Last and At with a list of indices, and to the elements of Take, Drop, Rest, Most and Slice of such a value. Other changes that follow:

    • Sum, Product, and Reduce with Add and 0 or Multiply and 1, over elements that may be numbers or rows are typed as a number or a row (Sum(Rest(m(x))) with m(t) = [[t, 2t], [3t, 4t]] is integer | matrix<2x2> | vector<2>; it was number), with nan when the operand may be absent.
    • Arithmetic on a union of lists with dimensions maps over the list: 2·vv for vv: vector<2> | vector<3> is list<number> (it was number).
    • Product, Reduce and Fold with Multiply over elements that are matrices or vectors are accepted (they were incompatible-type).
    • PointX/PointY and Dot of a union of numbers and vectors are typed from the vector arms; PointX of string | list<string> reads the character or element at the position.
    • Compiled JavaScript At, First, Second, Third and Last over elements that may be numbers or lists choose the out-of-range value from the value read, as the interpreter does: NaN for a list of numbers, Missing otherwise. Last([]) of a list that is not of numbers (a matrix included) is now Missing (it was NaN).
    • Compiled Sum and Reduce with Add over elements that may differ in shape throw when two elements have different shapes, as the interpreter answers incompatible-dimensions; compiled Product over such elements declines.
    • Compiled Repeat throws when its count is not an integer when the code runs (it rounded the count, or returned []).
    • Compiled JavaScript Max, Min, Mean, Median and Variance over elements that may be numbers or lists, or over an operand that may be absent and holds lists, decline (they gave NaN). Python Mean, Median and Variance of a tensor or broadcastable operand check the rank when the code runs and raise for a matrix; Python folds over a tensor<number> decline.

  • Element-wise If and Which over a mask of any rank. A condition that is a nested list of True/False/Missing now selects at every level. It stayed unevaluated before. With M := [[1, 2], [3, 4]]:

    • If(M < 3, M, 0) is [[1, 2], [0, 0]], typed matrix<integer^(2x2)>.
    • Which(M < 2, 10, M < 4, M, True, 0) is [[10, 2], [3, 0]].
    • The mask may be uneven: If([[True], [False, True]], 7, 0) is [[7], [0, 7]].

    At each level, a list condition and a list arm must have the same length, and a scalar is used at every position. A position decided by a scalar condition takes the arm's value there whole. Results for a mask of rank 1 do not change.

    An arm of lower rank than the mask is refused, as Add refuses it: If(M < 3, [10, 20], 0) is Error("incompatible-dimensions", "2x2 vs 2").

    The compiled JavaScript gives the same values. Before, it compiled, and then threw Condition must evaluate to "True" or "False" at run time. Under a mask of rank 2 or more, compiled code cannot tell a point from a row of numbers, so an arm whose type does not say where its points are (list, list<any>, tensor<tuple<…>>) throws a RangeError at run time when a nested mask meets an array element. Declare such an arm matrix or list<tuple<…>> to avoid it. A mask that is flat at run time is not affected.

  • The types of If and Which hold every value they can give.

    • A condition of unknown rank types the result list<C | list<any>>, where C joins the arms: Which(C < 2, 1, True, 0) with C: indexed_collection is list<integer | list<any>> (it was list<integer>).
    • A broadcastable<T> arm contributes T: with B: broadcastable<number>, If(B < 0, -B, B) is broadcastable<number> | list<list<any> | number>. It was broadcastable<broadcastable<number>>, a type with no meaning. The list option holds the uneven value of a mask of lower rank than an arm ([[1, 2], 0]).
    • A condition typed boolean | list<boolean> types the result like a condition that may be a mask: it typed as a scalar before.

  • The Python and interval-JavaScript targets refuse a condition that may be a list in If, Which and When, so the fallback option decides. With B: broadcastable<number>, Python emitted 0 if np.less(B, 0) else B, which raises for an array of two or more elements, and the interval target gave empty for If(B < 0, 0, B). The compile of B < 0 on its own on Python no longer overflows the stack. GLSL and WGSL do not change. On JavaScript, When(v, B < 0) with B: broadcastable<number> now restricts element by element when B holds a list: it compiled as one scalar test and gave v for B = [-1, 2], where the interpreter gives [v, NaN].

  • The derivative of an element selector, and of a list with a constant point (follow-up of Tycho row 424). First, Second, Third, Last, Rest, Most, Reverse, Take, Drop, DeleteAt, RotateLeft, RotateRight, Slice and At (also with several indices) are linear in their container for a fixed selection, as PointX/PointY/PointZ already were: the derivative is the selector applied to the derivative of the container. This holds when the selection does not depend on the variable or is constant between its jumps (\lceil u\rceil); a selection that varies with the variable declines. D(Last(h(u)), u) over a path of 29 pieces is a closed form in about 0.1 s (it declined after about 1.1 s). A selector that reads by value (Sort, Filter, Unique, Max, …) is not linear and keeps the generic rule. In the derivative of a list, a tuple or a piecewise branch, a constant element that is a point now gets the zero point of its arity, not the scalar 0: with Q := (1, 2), D([(t, t^2), Q], t) is [(1, 2t), (0, 0)] (it was [(1, 2t), 0]). A selection of a constant container gives the zero of the selection's shape (D(Take([1,2,3], 2), u) is [0, 0]), an absent element stays absent (Missing), and an index past the end gives the same value as the original selection.

  • A call of a user function that shadows a library operator compiles (Tycho row 423; the fix is under Resolved Issues). On the javascript, interval-js, GLSL and WGSL targets, a call bound to a user definition with a library name (Gamma := x ↦ (x-1)!, Sin, Sqrt, Square) compiles as a call of that user function, where compile() declined and the interpreter ran it. Before the target compiles, such a call is renamed to a private name declared in a temporary scope, so no part of the compiler reads it as the library operator (the angular-unit rewrite, sign rules, scalar facts, derivative recurrences, lazy streams). Decline messages still name the user's function. These keep the decline and run interpreted: a user definition of an operator the language builds by name (Add, Less, And, If, Sum, …), a multi-clause function, a definition with its own compile handler, stated derivative, lazy, broadcastable or declared effects, a node bound to the library operator, and every user function on the Python target. A declaration in a scratch scope of a name that no binding outside the scratch scopes holds now advances no state version, so such a compile leaves the engine's type, sign and memo caches as they were.

  • A numerical integral answers NaN at once when its integrand has no real value on part of the range (Tycho row 422; the fix is under Resolved Issues).
