The adaptive quadrature, on both the interpreted and the compiled route, stops with NaN when a panel and both of its halves have a majority of NaN samples, and the integrand next to the NaN set is not of rounding size, so the integrand has no real value there: the Monte-Carlo fallback is not run. \int_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{x}\,dx on the compiled real route was 0.6667 (the part below 0 was left out) and is now NaN, as the interpreter's real route is. Removable points no longer stop the quadrature: \int_0^{64}\frac{u}{u}dx with u = x - \lfloor x\rfloor gives 64, where the quadrature gave NaN and only the Monte-Carlo fallback gave an approximate value. An integrand that overflows to NaN in a tail it has decayed in (the logistic density on [0, ∞)) keeps its earlier result.

  • A D that has no closed form is not worked out again (Tycho row 424; the fix is under Resolved Issues). When the derivative of a D node gives no closed form, the node is returned as it is, and the attempt is recorded: evaluating the same node again, or reading a parameter that holds it, does not differentiate again. A write to a symbol the derivative reads (a value, a type, a definition of a function it calls), a change of the type of the variable, an assumption, or a change of the configuration makes the record invalid. A decline made inside another differentiation, under a temporary precision or angular unit, or for a node that is not pure, is not recorded.

  • A Sum or Product bound may be a type that could be a number (Tycho row 421; the fix is under Resolved Issues). A bound whose type is a union with a number arm (number | string, broadcastable<number | tuple>) or a top type (value, expression) is now accepted, where it was an incompatible-type error; string, boolean, a list or a tuple type, and a literal string, NaN or Missing, are still refused. Such a bound gets no closed form and no fold of two equal bounds, so the operator evaluates only when its value is a number: with y: number | tuple holding (3, 4), \prod_{n=1}^{y} n stays unevaluated, where a closed form would have given Factorial((3, 4)), a tuple. Its javascript compile answers NaN for a value that is not a number, where Math.floor read the string "3" as 3 and true as 1; a bound typed as a number, unknown or any compiles as before.

  • A numerical derivative narrows its window until the value settles (Tycho row 420; the fix is under Resolved Issues). The numerical derivative of an expression that stays symbolic (its javascript compile, ND, and a derivative of a function with no closed form under N()) is an 8th-order centered stencil whose samples reach 0.4 on each side of the point. It now halves its step until the values of successive steps agree (to 10⁻⁶ at order 1, a looser part at higher orders) or converge at the rate of the stencil, and is NaN when they never do, at a jump of the function. A smooth function keeps its value bit for bit, and the compiled and interpreted values stay identical. Other values change: ND of \cos(20x) at 0.05 is −16.829419, the derivative, where it was −14.55; ND of \sqrt{x} at 0.05 is 2.236068 where a sample below 0 made it NaN; ND of x\lfloor x\rfloor at 2, a jump, stays unevaluated where it was 14.19. A smooth function costs 12 calls of the function at order 1 instead of 8, fewer than before at orders 2 to 4 (44, 67 and 154 instead of 64, 512 and 4096), and a point at a jump up to 72 at order 1.

  • FindRoot polishes a steep equation to its root (Tycho row 419; the fix is under Resolved Issues). A root solve whose accepted step was below the relative step tolerance stopped there, even when the step had removed most of the residual: on a steep equation the step to the root is that small relative to the parameter. It now goes on while its steps more than halve the sum of squared residuals. a^2 = 10^{12} from a = 1 ends at a = 10^6 exactly (it stopped at a residual of 0.14), and \sin(10^8 a) = 0.5 at a residual of 6e-9 instead of 3e-5. FindFit is unchanged.

  • FindFit and FindRoot stop polishing at the tolerance's precision (Tycho row 418; the fix is under Resolved Issues). A solve within its tolerance ends once an accepted step moves every parameter by less than tolerance · max(1, |θ_j|) while the cost is at its rounding floor, where it went on to the gradient test or to the iteration cap: a badly scaled exact fit takes 5 iterations instead of 200, and its stationary key can be true without the gradient test. The converged key of a FindFit record now reads the engine's tolerance (ce.tolerance, never below 64 machine epsilons), which it ignored before: a fit whose every residual is within the tolerance of the terms its row computes is converged, stationary or not. Setting a looser engine tolerance makes more fits exact.

Resolved Issues​

  • Collection fixes listed for 0.160.0 were not in the 0.160.0 and 0.161.0 packages. A later change removed them before 0.160.0 was published, and they are back in this release:

    • Dedup, Filter and TakeWhile of a string held by a symbol of a wider type give a string: with c: list<integer> | string holding "aab", Dedup(c) is "ab", not ["a", "b"], and so is Dedup(Filter(c, p)).
    • Filter and Dedup over a dictionary give a Dictionary, not a Set of entry tuples, also when the dictionary is an arm of a union type and through nested Filter and Dedup views. A view over a dictionary of more than five entries prints as written (Dedup(d)).
    • The preview of Map(x ↦ x + 10, c), with c declared missing | list<integer>, is the list [11, 12], not Set(11, 12).
    • Map of a function literal whose parameter is annotated as a scalar ((x: integer) ↦ x + 1) over a list of lists is refused when it is boxed; it was typed list<integer> and gave an error for each row.
    • Map(Sqrt, [[1, 4], [9]]) is typed list<vector<1> | vector<2>>; it was list<list<number>>.
    • The types of FlatMap over a source with absent cells, of Map of an operator whose declared result is any (First, PointX), of Map over an alias of a tuple (list<number>, was collection<number>), and of Map over a dictionary arm of a union hold their values again.

  • The type of a Map did not hold its value in two cases. Map(x ↦ If(x = 1, "x", x), [1, 2]) was typed list<integer | string^2>, and its value ["x", 2] is a list<integer | string>: a list whose elements are a union that is not a number type now states no length, as a list literal does. Map(First, [[], [3]]) was typed list<integer | nan> for the value ["Missing", 3]: First([]) is Missing, since the element [] states no element type, and the type is now list<integer | missing | nan>.

  • A sum with an infinite term of unknown sign folded to that infinity. ∞·c + 1 evaluated to +∞ for a c with no known sign: the sum read the coefficient ∞ of the term and ignored c, although the sum is −∞ at c < 0 and 0·∞ at c = 0. Such a term now stays in the sum, also beside a pure infinity (∞·c + ∞ is ∞ − ∞ at c < 0), ∞·c − ∞·c is Indeterminate, and a term whose cofactor has a known sign still folds (−∞·3 + 1 is −∞). Found while fixing Tycho row 428: the value of ∫_{−∞}^{x} exp(−(z−m)²/(2s²)) dz at its lower bound, Erf(−∞·√(s⁻²) − m·√(s⁻²)), folded to −1 and lost the condition √(s⁻²) > 0 that the same integral carries at m = 0.

  • A use of a call at a typed parameter rewrote the signature of the called function. With g := t ↦ [[t, 1], [2, 3]], whose signature is (unknown) -> list<list<unknown>>, boxing Trace(g(2)) (the parameter of Trace is number | tensor) widened the result of g to list<list<unknown>> | number | tensor, and Determinant(g(x)) + 1 then declined to compile ("operand is not an indexed collection"). A use now refines only a result that the body leaves unknown (k := x ↦ x used in k(1) + 2 gets the result real, as before); a result that the body states, and that may fit the parameter, is kept.

  • D of the inverse of a matrix function stayed unevaluated. With f: (real) -> tensor<number> and f := x ↦ [[1, x], [x, 2]], the call f(x) is now typed matrix<real^(2x2)> from the body, so f(x)^{-1} canonicalizes to Inverse(f(x)), and D(f(x)^{-1}, x) was an unevaluated derivative of Inverse (it was differentiated as a negative matrix power while the call was typed tensor). D(Inverse(f), x) is now -Inverse(f) · f' · Inverse(f), and agrees with a finite difference.

  • At and First refused an operand that may be absent or of unknown type, and PointX of such an operand was typed missing. With g: (unknown) -> list<unknown> and x: any, g(x)[1][2] was an incompatible-type error (at x = [1, 2] its value is 2), and PointX(g(x)[1]) was typed missing, as if always absent; it is missing | unknown.

  • Compiled Sum, Product and Reduce over a list of elements of unknown type gave null or a string when the elements are lists. With L: list<unknown> and L = [[0, 1], [2, 3], [4]], the compiled Sum(L) was the string "01,23,4" (the interpreter gives an incompatible-dimensions error: the rows have different lengths), and with L = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] the compiled Product(L) was null (the interpreter gives [3, 8]). The fold now dispatches on each element: Sum(L) is [6, 9] for [[0, 1], [2, 3], [4, 5]] and throws for rows of different shapes, and Product(L) is the product of the elements, [3, 8], [17, 39] for a matrix beside a row (the matrix product), and [[4], [10, 18]] for ragged rows. A Multiply fold over elements typed as lists of cells of unknown type (list<unknown> | unknown, the elements of Rest(g(x))) still declines (ROADMAP CE-98.3).

  • The compiled statistics over a list<unknown> read each row as a number. With L: list<unknown> and L = [[1, 2], [3, 4]], the compiled Max(L) was NaN (the interpreter gives 4). Max, Min, Mean, Median and the other statistics now decline such an operand, as they decline a bare list and a list<any>, and the interpreter evaluates it.

  • Product, Reduce and Map over a list of ragged lists that hold matrices were an incompatible-type error. With L: list<unknown> and L = [[M, [5]], [N, [2]]] (M, N 2×2 matrices), the elements of L are typed list<matrix<integer^(2x2)> | vector<integer^1>>, and the check of the callback refused Multiply and Negate for them, so Product(L) was Reduce(L, Error(incompatible-type), 1), while the product of the two elements written as p·q had a value. A union of tensors and numbers below one or more list levels of an element is now read arm by arm, as a union at the top of the element already was: Product(L) is [M·N, [10]].

  • An element of a list<unknown> result was read as a number. With g: (unknown) -> list<unknown> and x: any, the element g(x)[1] is typed missing | unknown, and it is a list when x is a list. Compiled g(x)[1] + 1 gave the string "1,21" at x = [1, 2], a product gave NaN, g(x)[1] < 1 gave one false, and Sin(g(x)[1]) was typed number, so Sin(g(x)[1]) + 1 also joined strings. A value typed by unknown, any or value beside missing or nothing only is now read as that type, both when typing and when compiling: Sin(g(x)[1]) is typed broadcastable<number> | missing, and compiled arithmetic, the cell functions (Sin, Sqrt, Abs, Floor, …), the comparisons, an If that selects the element, and a Block local that holds it broadcast at run time, as they already did for a g declared (unknown) -> list. They give the interpreter's values: [2, 3] and [false, false]. A Block local that holds the element is read the same way, also inside a cell function: Block(Assign(y, g(x)[1]), Sin(y) + 1) gave a string, and Sin(y) was typed number. A symbol the user declared any, a global with an assigned value and a free variable stay scalar code, as before. A number x gives the same values as before. The cost: an index into a list whose elements are typed unknown | missing (L[i] + 1 with L: list<unknown | missing>) now compiles to the run-time broadcast _SYS.bcast, as an index into a list<unknown> or a list<any> already did. An index into a list of numbers stays scalar code.

  • A call of a function literal over a list had a different type inside the body of another function. With f := x ↦ (-x, x), the call f(L) for a list L evaluates to a list of pairs and is typed list<tuple<number, number>>. The same call typed from the types of its arguments, which is how the engine types a call in the body of another function and how a custom type handler derives a call (context.derive), was typed tuple<number, number>, the type of one element. Both now give the same type, for a list, a matrix (each cell is mapped), a broadcastable<number> argument and a function with a declared signature such as (real) -> real; a scalar argument and a parameter typed as a collection are not mapped, as before. A call with fewer arguments than parameters is now typed as the function of the remaining parameters in both cases. Some inferred types become narrower: with h := a ↦ f([a, a]), h(1) is typed list<tuple<integer, integer>> (it was list<tuple<number, number>>), and with g: (T) -> T where T (or where T: number), Map(g, rows) over a list<list<integer>> is typed list<list<integer>>. A generic function whose type variable has a bound no longer takes its result from a list element that breaks the bound: with g: (T) -> T where T: number and a list of strings L, g(L) was typed list<string>; each element of its value is an incompatible-type error, and the call is now typed list<number>, and so is the list option of an argument typed number | list<string> (the call is typed list<number> | number).

  • Sum of elements that may be lists was typed number. With g(t) = [t, 2t] declared (unknown) -> list<unknown> and x declared any, Sum(Rest(g(x))) was typed number, but at x = [1, 2] it is [2, 4]. Sum and Product now give a type that holds a list when their terms may be lists: broadcastable<number> for terms typed unknown (the type Add gives for such operands), as in Sum(L) for L: list<unknown> or L: list; any for terms that have an any option, as with g declared (unknown) -> list; list<any> | number for rows whose cells are not typed, as in Sum(M) for M: list<list<unknown>>; and number | vector<2> for Sum(g(x)) when g(x) is typed broadcastable<vector<2>>. This applies to the Sum(body, limits) form too: Sum(L[k], k, 1, 2). Terms typed as numbers, points or rows of numbers keep their type. A compiled Sum(g(x)) or Product(g(x)) over such a g now compiles to the interpreter's value (it declined before), and a compiled Sum(L) + 1 for L: list<unknown> now declines (it gave null for a list of rows).

  • Arithmetic over a cell of unknown type took the tier of the other operand. With u: broadcastable<unknown>, 2 · u and 2 + u were typed broadcastable<integer> and 0.9 · u broadcastable<real>, although a cell of u may be any number. They are now typed broadcastable<number>, and so are [1, 2] · u, [1, 2] + u and [1, 2] - u (they were vector<integer^2>, but u may hold a matrix). A free symbol in a list literal is now narrowed to number, as the same symbol in a scalar product is: 2 · [y] is typed vector<1> and y is inferred number (they were vector<real^1> and real). With w := x ↦ 2 · [x], w(i) was typed vector<real^1> with the value [2i].

  • The complex compile mode did not reach the cells of a list input. With mode: 'complex', a scalar input declared number used complex arithmetic, but a list<number>, tensor<number>, matrix<number> or list<unknown> input did not: Add(p, 1) with a cell 1 + i gave the string "[object Object]1". Element-wise arithmetic, cell functions and the orderings over such inputs now use complex arithmetic in that mode (an ordering of a non-real cell is false). The default and strict modes emit the same code as before.

  • Compiled statistics of complex data gave NaN. Compiled Mean, Variance, StandardDeviation, PopulationVariance and PopulationStandardDeviation over complex data now give the interpreter's values in the default and complex modes: Mean([3, 4i]) is 1.5 + 2i, and the variance family is real. The strict mode still declines. Real data gives the same bits as before in every mode.

  • The variance of large values of opposite signs overflowed. In compiled code and in the interpreter at machine precision, Variance([1e308, -1e308]) was -Infinity; it is now +Infinity, and StandardDeviation([1e200, -1e200]) is 1.414e200 (it was +Infinity). Ordinary data gives the same bits as before.

  • Compiled folds and reads over elements that mix numbers and lists gave wrong values. For a list whose elements may be numbers or vectors (list<number | vector<2>>, a tensor, or the selectors of a broadcastable<vector<2>>), compiled Sum, and Reduce with Add or Multiply, joined the rows as strings ("01,22,43,6") or gave NaN; they now combine element by element, as the interpreter does. Compiled Max, Mean and Reduce(…, Max) over such elements gave NaN or compared rows as strings; they now decline. Python Max/Min of an operand that may be absent or a list returned the operand itself; they now reduce it, and give NaN for an absent or empty operand.

  • HadamardProduct, and the element-wise sum, difference, quotient and power of two tensors, gave undefined cells when the two tensors had different data types. HadamardProduct([[0.5, 1], [1, 3]], [[1, 2], [3, 4]]) threw a TypeError when the type of the result was read. The operation was taken from the first tensor's arithmetic before the two tensors were converted to a common data type; it is now taken after. The product is [[0.5, 2], [3, 12]].

  • TrigExpand, TrigToExp and TrigReduce bind their operand when they are canonicalized, as the other operators do. The operand is still not evaluated before the rewrite. So Nothing is removed from the argument list: TrigExpand(Nothing) is the error of a missing argument, as Sin(Nothing) is (it was Nothing, and TrigReduce(Nothing) was 0).

  • A FindFit evaluated with evaluateAsync and cut short by the deadline while its data was evaluated reported no parameters (parameters: {}). It reports the parameters at their starts, as the synchronous route does. On that route a malformed parameter spec is now an error before the data is evaluated, and a start such as Random() is evaluated once, as on the synchronous route (it was evaluated twice).

  • An index that occurred only in a dictionary value was left in a Sum or Product. Every check of the form "does this expression mention k?" asked a dictionary for a key named k (see the has()/hasKey() entry under Breaking Changes), so \sum_{k=1}^{2} \mathrm{If}(x<1, \{"v"\to k\}, 0) evaluated to 2 \cdot \mathrm{If}(x<1, \{"v"\to k\}, 0) with the bound k left in, and simplify() gave 3\,\mathrm{If}(\dots k \dots) for the sum to 3 and \mathrm{If}(\dots k \dots)^3 for the product. The terms are now evaluated one by one, and simplify() keeps the sum. The compiler checks that look for a function literal or a Return now see one in a dictionary value.

  • The compiler declined a call of a user function that shadows a library operator (Tycho row 423). A Desmos document defines its own Gamma, \Gamma(x)=(x-1)!; with Gamma := x ↦ x + 100, the interpreter gave \Gamma(0.5) = 100.5, and the javascript and interval-js compiles of any expression that called it failed ("a user definition shadows the library operator Gamma"), while the same function named G compiled. Both declare(name, "function") and declare(name, { signature }) followed by assign now compile \Gamma(\frac{1}{2}) + x to 101.5 at x = 1.

  • A numerical integral took 0.5 to 2 s to answer NaN (Tycho row 422). The chi-square tail \int_{x}^{\infty}\frac{y^{\frac{k}{2}-1}e^{-\frac{y}{2}}}{2^{\frac{k}{2}}\Gamma(\frac{k}{2})}dy with k = 1 has no real value at x < 0, where the integrand is not real on [x, 0). The adaptive quadrature bisected the NaN panels until its budget of 1500 panels was spent, and then each route drew 10⁷ Monte-Carlo samples, whose mean was NaN again. Now x = −0.2 and x = −1 answer NaN in under 15 ms on both routes, and x = 1 still gives 0.3173105. Written with the number -\frac{1}{2} as the exponent, the interpreted value at x = −0.2 is the complex 1.0000 − 0.3691i (the principal value, which the interpreter integrates in two parts) and the compiled real value is NaN; that is not changed.

  • A compiled numerical integral of a divergent integrand took 200 to 400 ms and answered an arbitrary finite number (Tycho row 427). The absolute moment of the normal distribution \int_{-50}^{50}|t|^{x}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{1}{2}t^2}dt diverges at t = 0 for x ≤ −1. The interpreter answered +∞, because it finds the pole from the expression with the value of x, but the compiled function gave a different number at each call (647, 708, 7249 at x = −1.5), and \int_{-1}^{2}\frac{1}{(t-x)^2}dt at x = 0.3 gave 8.9e16. The adaptive quadrature looked for a divergence only at the two bounds. When its bisection goes deep at a point inside the interval, it now finds the singular point and splits the interval there, so that each half has the singularity at a bound. The compiled function now answers NaN in under 5 ms for x = −1, −1.5 and −2.5, and the interpreter still answers +∞. A convergent moment is also more accurate: at x = −0.9 the error was 5.7e-10, and it is now 2.6e-12. A smooth integrand, a kink, a jump and a narrow peak are not split.

  • D(PointY(h(u)), u) took seconds, and was worked out again at each evaluation (Tycho row 424). With h a path joined from 29 linear pieces, the derivative went through the generic chain rule, which reads PointY as an unknown scalar function and multiplied by the derivative of the path, a list of 29 points, until a size limit declined: 0.6 to 3.6 s, paid again at each evaluation and at each read of a parameter holding the value (9 reads: 30 s). PointX, PointY, PointZ and At (with an index that does not depend on the variable, or that is constant between its jumps, such as \lceil u\rceil) are now differentiated as linear accessors: the accessor of the derivative of the container, with a constant point element of a list given the zero point. The derivative of the row is a closed form in 60 ms, and 9 reads cost what 1 does. The generic rule gave wrong values too: with g := t ↦ (t, t^2), D(PointY(g(u)), u) was a tuple, and is now 2u. PointZ of a list of 2-D points whose elements may be absent reports the dimension error, as for present points.

  • Two typing defects of 0.161.0, fixed by the change to the reading of list types (see Breaking Changes). A symbol declared (broadcastable<unknown>) -> unknown refused the function literal (x) => (x, x): ce.assign threw a type error, because provablyAdmits('nothing', 'broadcastable<unknown>') answered true, as if the type stated that a Nothing value is possible. A broadcastable<T> is now read as the union of its two parts, so broadcastable<unknown> states nothing about Nothing, as unknown does not, and the assignment is accepted. A generic function literal over a ragged list gave a type that does not hold the value: with g the literal (x: T) -> tuple<T, T> where T with the body (x, x), g([[1], [2, 3]]) was typed list<tuple<vector<integer^1> | vector<integer^2>, vector<integer^1> | vector<integer^2>>>, and its value is [[(1, 1)], [(2, 2), (3, 3)]]. It is now typed list<list<tuple<integer, integer>>>, which holds the value.

  • A Sum or Product bound refused a union type with a number arm (Tycho row 421). With x declared broadcastable<number | tuple>, \sum_{n=1}^{x} n^2, \sum_{n=x}^{5} n and \prod_{n=1}^{x} n were invalid, so a function such as s(a) = \sum_{k=1}^{a} k over that declaration never registered, while the bound of an integral and the operands of Mod and Max accepted the same declaration. The check of a bound said it refuses only a bound that cannot be a number, but it accepted only a type below number. Now s(3) is 6 and s([1, 2, 3]) is [1, 3, 6], as over a parameter declared any.

  • The derivative of a sum whose bound is ⌊x⌋ (Tycho row 420). D(Sum(Cos(i x), Limits(i, 1, Floor(x))), x) stayed unevaluated, because a bound that depends on the variable declined the rule for a sum, and the numerical derivative of its compile read across the jumps of the sum at the integers: −5.308 at x = 1.9, where the derivative is −0.946. A bound of a Sum whose derivative is 0, a step of the variable (Floor, Ceil, Round, Truncate or Sign of it, also through a call of a function), now keeps the rule: between two jumps the set of terms is fixed, and the derivative is Σ_{i=1}^{⌊x⌋} −i sin(i x), which compiles to javascript and interval-js; the derivative of order 2 closes too. At a jump the result is the value of that sum, as D(⌊x⌋) is 0 at an integer. A bound that is not a step (x) or not pure keeps the derivative unevaluated. A Product with such a bound still stays unevaluated, and its numerical derivative is now right between the jumps and NaN at them (the change under Behavior Changes): D(Product(x + i, Limits(i, 1, Floor(x))), x) at 1.9 is 1, where it was 57.3. D(Truncate(x), x) is 0, as for Floor; it stayed unevaluated.

  • FindRoot reports converged: false far from a root of a steep equation (Tycho row 419). The root test of 0.161.0 allows each residual tolerance · (1 + Σ_j |J_ij| · max(1, |θ_j|)). Its Jacobian part is a first-order claim, that a zero lies within a relative change of tolerance of the parameters, and it had no check: 2 - \sin(10^{18} a) = 0 has no real root, and its Jacobian, up to 10^18, let a residual of 1 to 3 pass at every point (converged: true from a = 1, from a = 0 and under the bound a \le 0). An equation whose residual is above tolerance is now a root only when the residual confirms the claim. Each parameter is moved by ±2 · tolerance · max(1, |θ_j|) toward and away from the zero. The central difference of the residual must be the change the Jacobian predicts to within half, and the parabola through the three values must reach tolerance, change sign, or touch 0 to within the rounding of the parameters (a root of even multiplicity, such as 10^{24}(a^2-2)^2 = 0). At a bound, the side inside the bounds is checked and a zero just past the bound is accepted. Over 100 starts, 2 - \sin(10^{18} a) = 0, \sin(10^{12} a) = 0.5 and \sin(10^{10} a) = 0.5, which oscillate faster than the tolerance can resolve, go from 100, 100 and 93 starts reported converged to none; \sin(10^8 a) = 0.5, a^3 - 2a = 10^9, 10^{12} a = 1 and e^a = 10^{30} stay converged. The check costs at most two residual evaluations per equation, at the points where the solve would stop.

  • FindFit reports converged: true at an exact fit (Tycho row 418). A degree-10 polynomial through 11 points is an exact interpolation whose constant term is 0. The fit reached the rounding floor (a residual norm of 3e-10) and reported converged: false after 200 iterations, since the record of a fit read converged from the solver's stationarity tests alone, and neither can pass on a problem scaled that badly: the Jacobian columns reach 10^10, so a residual at the rounding floor still has a gradient far above the absolute gradient tolerance, and the constant term, whose true value is 0, never takes a step that is small relative to itself (the per-component stall test of 0.161.0; the whole-vector stall test it replaced reported this fit converged after one iteration). A fit whose every residual is within the engine's tolerance of the terms its row computes, |r_i| ≤ tolerance · (1 + Σ_j |J_ij · θ_j|), is now converged, whatever the gradient and the parameters' magnitudes; a fit with a misfit is converged at a stationary point as before. The scale is the model's terms, not the max(1, |θ_j|) of the root test of FindRoot, under which a degree-10 polynomial over x in [10, 20] would tolerate a residual of 1 at data of magnitude 1. A root solve or a fit within its tolerance stops polishing once an accepted step moves every parameter by less than the tolerance of its own scale (tolerance · max(1, |θ_j|), the precision to which the tolerance test says the parameters are determined) while the cost is at its rounding floor, so the same fit now takes 5 iterations from the exact coefficients and 44 from a start of 1, and the stacked FindRoot form 4 and 39 instead of 20 and 92; a point whose residual is still dropping (1 + (10^{12} a)^2 = 0 from a = 10^{-11}, within the root tolerance of its steep equation at a residual of 101) goes on to its minimum as before. A solve cut short by a deadline reports converged: false beside timedOut: true, as the record's contract says; a root solve that timed out while polishing a root reported both true. The FindFit record still has no stationary key.

0.161.0 2026-10-21​

New Features​

  • FindRoot takes the options dictionary of FindFit (Tycho row 408). A third argument {global: {b: [lo, hi]}} searches the named parameters (at most two) over the range for the lowest sum of squared residuals of the whole system, equations included, as FindFit does for a model over data: the separable scan when the system is linear in the other parameters, a multi-start otherwise, with [lo, hi, step] for a caller-given grid step. A stacked system of fit rows next to a plain equation (a cos(b x_i + c) + d x_i + e = y_i for each data point, and d = 0) is searched for its best frequency; the constant phase coefficients of the equations (3.22 in cos(3.22 b + c)) space the grid as the span of a variable does for a fit, so a point falls in every basin of the residual. An equation built from a row at x = 0 reads a cos(0 · b + c) + 0 · d, which canonicalization keeps; such a parameter is no longer read as a step function of the system, which turned the scan into the coarse multi-start. The record is the usual one (see the stationary entry below). With a kernel pool on the engine (ce.workers), evaluateAsync() scans the grid on the workers, as FindFit does.

  • Parser.binderSymbol() and Parser.rebindSubscripts() are public, for a custom LaTeX dictionary entry that binds a name (a with clause, a loop form). Since 0.160.0 a subscripted name in a binder position is a new name also when its base is declared as a list (n_{0} with n: list<number> is At(n, 0) elsewhere); the two parser methods that the built-in binders use for that were internal, so a custom clause could not: with n a list, n_{0} + 1 \operatorname{with} n_{0} = 2 through a custom infix entry that read the binder with parseSymbol() was a parse error. binderSymbol(expr) gives the name that an expression declares in a binder position (n_0 for the At(n, 0) that the symbol parser made from n_{0}; a symbol is its own name; null otherwise), and rebindSubscripts(expr, names) rewrites those element accesses in a body, including a body parsed before the clause. See "Binding a Name in a Custom Entry" in the LaTeX syntax guide.

Improvements​

  • Factor uses certified univariate factorization over the rationals, including nonlinear factors such as Factor(x^4+4) = (x^2-2x+2)(x^2+2x+2). The numerics entry point exposes factorRationalPolynomial and its types for structured exact factors, multiplicities and explicit incomplete results when resource limits or certificate checks prevent completion.

  • .N() of Power, Exp, Ln and the other numeric heads of a number operand is about 1.6x faster at ce.precision = 30: the check for a collection operand no longer runs a type match on a number literal (#465, contributed by enumeratio).

  • GammaLn of a complex argument is the principal logarithm of Γ(z) in every region, as documented, and LogGamma stays the continuous branch (#463, contributed by enumeratio). GammaLn(0.5 - 11i) was -16.3598 - 15.3806i, the continuous value (the principal log is -16.3598 - 2.8143i), while GammaLn(-2.5 + 0.1i) was already principal, -0.1031 - 3.0313i. The imaginary part is now reduced to (-π, π], so GammaLn(-7.3 + 2i) is -13.3277 - 1.5238i (it was -13.3277 - 20.3734i), and GammaLn(25.5 - 40i) is 31.7745 - 1.2258i (it was 31.7745 - 139.4559i). Real arguments are unchanged: GammaLn(-2.5) is still ln|Γ(-2.5)|.

  • Compiled GammaLn of a negative real is ln|Γ(x)| on JavaScript and the shader targets, as the interpreter gives (#463, contributed by enumeratio). GammaLn(-2.5) compiled to JavaScript gave NaN; it is now -0.0562, and GammaLn(-7.3) is -7.7791. A pole (0, -1, -4) is +Infinity. The GLSL and WGSL _gpu_gammaln used the Stirling series, which is meaningless for x < 0; it now reflects (ln π - ln|sin πx| - ln Γ(1 - x)) and answers +Infinity at a pole, as _gpu_gamma does.

Behavior Changes​

  • unknown is an inference marker, not a content type. Every type is now a subtype of unknown, the absence markers, error and any included: ce.type("missing").matches("unknown") and ce.type("any").matches("unknown") are true, and list<integer | missing> matches list<unknown>. unknown still proves no contract: it matches only any and itself. Bare list, list<unknown> and list<any> denote one set of values and differ as declarations: the bare name and the explicit <unknown> ask inference to refine the element type from each assignment (xs: list<unknown> := [1, Missing] reports list<integer | missing>, where it stayed list<unknown>), list<any> is a contract that never moves. Bare tuple and record refine their slots and fields the same way (t: tuple := (1, Missing) reports tuple<integer, missing>), and a transparent alias of a bare name (type L = list) carries the instruction. A type derived from a value keeps an unresolved cell: ListJoin(fs, [2]) with fs: list<unknown> is list<unknown> (it was list<integer> for a value that could hold an error), and Filter(tu, p) over tu: tuple<unknown, missing> is list<missing | unknown> (it was list<missing> for the value [1]). A union keeps an absence arm beside unknown (missing | unknown) and absorbs a value arm (integer | unknown is unknown); a union with an error arm reduces to error, as before. An incompatible-type diagnostic shows a generic parameter whose variable got no bound by the variable's name, indexed_collection<T>, instead of indexed_collection<unknown>. A lambda whose parameters are not inferred yet, (unknown) -> number, still does not satisfy (any) -> number. expression and value are the contracts that exclude the immediate markers. Design and decisions: docs/plans/2026-10-21-unknown-inference-marker.md.

  • FindRoot reports converged only at a root (Tycho row 414). FindRoot(a^2 + 1 = 0, a) gave converged: True with residualNorm: 1: the solver's stop test is a stationary point of the sum of squared residuals, which is a minimum of the misfit for a fit but a root only when the residual is zero. converged is now true only when every residual is within the engine's tolerance scaled by its own equation, |r_i| ≤ tolerance · (1 + Σ_j |J_ij| · max(1, |θ_j|)) with J the Jacobian and θ the parameters: an absolute part for a residual that is zero to within the tolerance, a relative part that says the parameters the equation reads are determined to that relative precision (a^2 = 10^{12} from a = 1 is a root; a^2 + 10^{-7} = 0 is not; a steep equation or a large parameter does not hide another equation's residual). The tolerance is never below 64 machine epsilons, and a non-finite residual or Jacobian is never a root. The solver's stall test is now per component: the system a^2 = 4, b = 10^{11} stalled after one step at a = 2.5, which was reported as converged, because a step of 1 in a was negligible next to the norm of the whole parameter vector. The record gains stationary, the solver's own stop test, which is true at such a minimum too: a stacked system of data rows next to an equation, whose misfit is not zero, reads it where it read converged. The gradient test alone no longer stops a root solve: FindRoot(10^{-6} (a^2 - 4) = 0, a) from a = 1 stopped at its start point as converged, since the absolute gradient tolerance passes everywhere on a residual scaled small, and now reaches a = 2. The FindFit record and its convergence test are unchanged.

  • A call between a typed declaration with no value and the definition of the function now resolves. With let g: (integer) -> integer, then let a = String(g(2)), then function g(k) { 2k }, a was "g(2)" on the Epsil runner and on the whole-block route; it is now "4", and the call is checked against the declared signature (String(g(1.5)) gives the incompatible-type error). This also holds on each iteration of a loop body, when a block is evaluated again (with evaluate() or evaluateAsync()), and when a program runs again on the same engine. A program that stopped (time or step budget) before its definition ran no longer leaves that definition to a later program that declares the same name. Inside a function body the declared signature is still not checked (recorded in ROADMAP.md).

  • An evaluateAsync() call started by the host, or by a handler that passes no options, now runs on its own copy of the engine's evaluation-context stack, not on the engine's array. A scope that the host pushes or pops while the call is pending no longer reaches it. Example: start Block(Tick(), w + 1).evaluateAsync() with Tick() an operator that only has an evaluateAsync handler, then run ce.pushScope(); ce.declare('w', 'integer'); ce.assign('w', 5) before awaiting it. The result was 6; it is now w + 1. Pending asynchronous evaluations no longer see each other's scopes or the host's later scopes, as was already the case for scopes that an evaluation pushes itself.

Resolved Issues​

  • On the interval-js target, 0^x over an exponent interval has the value 0 (Tycho row 417). compile(ce.parse('0^{x}'), {to: 'interval-js'}) answered empty for every exponent interval, as did a declared base holding 0, so a plot that reads a row through the interval leg drew nothing for a slider at 0. The interval-exponent power read a base whose upper end is exactly 0 as a negative base. A base whose only point in the domain is 0 now answers [0, 0] for a positive exponent interval, [0, 1] for one that reaches 0 (x^0 is 1 in the interval library), a clipped enclosure for one that reaches below 0, and empty for a wholly negative one, where no point of the box is defined; the scalar-exponent power answered a clipped enclosure [+∞, +∞] there and now also answers empty. The literal bounds 0 and 1 are certified exact, so the export does not move them one ulp outward.

  • A subscripted binder is a new name in a cases block and in a set-builder whose variable appears only in the condition (the two residues of Tycho row 410). With n declared a list, the first row of \begin{cases} n_{0}\coloneq 3\\ n_{0}+1\end{cases} was read before the parser knew the environment is a block, so the target was the element access At(n, 0) and the block declared a function At; such a row of a cases, dcases or rcases environment now gets a second reading, the declaration of the local n_0, which the block swaps in for its first, middle and last rows alike (a single row, a row with a condition and a matrix keep the top-level reading). \{2n_{0} \mid n_{0}\in\Z\} read its variable as At(n, 0) because the body names no variable; a membership of the condition (v \in S, alone or in a conjunction) whose variable the body reads now names it, while a side condition on another subscript keeps its index. Both parse as with n undeclared. The parser's environmentName() gives a dictionary entry the innermost environment being read, and blockRowAlternative() the second reading of a row.

  • Solve no longer lets a called user function's global take the place of the unknown. With h := a ↦ a − k, Solve(h(k) = 1, k) gives [k + 1], and [3] with k := 2; it stayed unevaluated, and before that it gave []. The unknown is renamed in the equation and in the specs, as Integrate and Limit already rename their variable. This covers domain specs, a bundled {h(k) = 1, k ∈ 1..3}, systems and NSolve. An assumption about the unknown (assume(k ≠ −1)) and a declared or use-inferred type still restrict the solutions.

  • Solve(t·x = 1, t) gives [1/x] when t is declared real; it stayed unevaluated. The root 1/x is the pole ~oo at x = 0, but each of its finite values is real.

  • An unknown that has an assigned value is no longer restricted by the type inferred from that value. With x := 5, Solve(2x = 1, x) gives [1/2] and Solve(x^2 = 2, x) gives [√2, −√2]; both gave []. With x := 3, y := 4, Solve(2x + 4y = 1, [x, y]) is no longer sent to the integer solver, which gave []. A declared type still restricts the roots.

  • A Solve over a finite domain whose equation or predicate has a free parameter stays unevaluated: Solve(x − a = 0, x ∈ 1..5) and Solve(x > a, x ∈ 1..5) were [].

  • The bounds of a Limits clause and the collection of an Element clause of Sum, Product, Integrate and NDSolveFunction read the enclosing symbol, not the clause's own index. With k := 2, ∫₀ᵏ k dk gives 2 (was k²/2), ∏_{k=1}^{k} k gives 2 (was k!), Σ_{k=1}^{k} k gives 3 (stayed unevaluated) and Σ_{k ∈ [1, k]} k gives 3. Also Σ_{k=1}^{3} Σ_{k=1}^{k} k gives 10 on every route (was 3·Σ_{k=1}^{k} k), and ∫₀ᵏ k dk with a free k reports k as an unknown.

  • FindFit with the global option now spaces the grid of a frequency by the period of the expression its periodic function is part of, not by the period of the function alone. A square, an absolute value or a product of periodic functions of the same argument can have a shorter period: a cos(b x + c)², a |cos(b x)|, a sin(b x) cos(b x) and sin(b x) / cos(b x) have the period π, and (sin(b x) cos(b x))² has π/2. Their basins in b are half or a quarter as wide as those of a cos(b x). The grid was spaced for the period 2π, so the search could return a wrong frequency with a large residual: for example b over [0.3, 300] on 200 points over [0, 10], with the true b between two grid points. tan(b x)² keeps the period π of tan, because tan(θ + π/2) = −cot θ.

  • FindRoot did not move a parameter read through PointX of a point (Tycho row 415). On PointX(PointList(2a, 2)) = 4 the solver stopped after one iteration at the start value: the symbolic derivative of the residual was the generic chain rule's PointList(2, 0) · Apply(Derivative("PointX", 1), …), a product of a point and a number that is a type error, which compiled to a Jacobian of NaN. D now differentiates an accessor of a literal container through the operand it selects: PointX, PointY and PointZ of a Tuple or a PointList, and At of a Tuple, a PointList or a List with a literal index (D(PointY((2a, a^2)), a) is 2a, D(At([2a, a^2], -1), a) is 2a); over a PointList that zips (a component is a collection) the accessor reads the differentiated PointList, so D(At(PointList([a, 2a], 5), 1), a) is the point (1, 0); and FindFit/FindRoot take a finite difference for a derivative that is not valid.

  • Boxing nested folds whose accumulator is read by index no longer takes about three times longer for every level of nesting (#462). Since 0.158.0 such an accumulator is typed to the fixpoint of its seed and its body's result, which canonicalizes the combiner once per fixpoint step, and a fold nested in the body was refined from scratch inside each of those canonicalizations. Now a nested fold is not refined while the enclosing fold only admits its callback, and the fixpoint found for it in one step of the enclosing fold is the starting point of the next step, where one canonicalization settles it. Six nested folds of the shape reported box in 66 ms instead of 1.4 s (0.156.0: 47 ms); eight in 121 ms instead of 13 s. Types and values are unchanged, and a chain of numeric folds costs what it did.

  • A comparison with a long exact sum whose coefficients have many distinct denominators no longer throws. 0 < \sum_{k=1}^{300} \ln(-k)/k^2 evaluated by extracting the content of the sum, whose denominator (the least common multiple of k² over the terms) is past the double range; lcm gave Infinity and the next call threw RangeError: The number Infinity cannot be converted to a BigInt. rationalGcd now uses the bigint form past the safe integer range (with a non-negative denominator), and the public lcm of the numerics entry point answers NaN for a non-integer or non-finite operand, as gcd does, instead of throwing.

  • The presence test of a compiled branch condition no longer follows a global's value through a bound name of the same name. With k := 2m in the engine, \{\sum_{k=1}^{3} k > 0: 1, 0\} compiled to a test of m (_.m !== undefined), so an unsupplied m made the branch take no arm; the Sum index k is not a read of the global, and the compiled code is now (0 < 6) ? 1 : 0. The same held for a parameter of a called function literal named like a valued global. A global that the condition does read (directly, or through the body of a called function) is still tested.

  • A chain of \text{for all} or \text{there exists} clauses that have no condition, such as x_0 \text{ for all } y_0 \; x_1 \text{ for all } y_1 \; …, parsed in exponential time: 12 clauses took 10 to 30 seconds, and a ( after the chain (… + (z > 0)) made it slow too. A quantifier parsed the rest of the input up to three times, to find a ( that starts its body and then for its condition, and each parse reached the next quantifier. Now a quantifier parses its condition again only when its own ( test stopped the parse, so 12 clauses take less than 30 ms, or about 100 ms with a ( after the chain. The parse results are unchanged.

  • An aborted broadcastAsync() or FindFit.evaluateAsync() no longer keeps a worker of the kernel pool busy. Before, a slice that a worker was running when the signal aborted ran to its end, and its result was dropped. Now the pool tells the worker to stop through a cancel flag in shared memory; the worker reads it every 64 cells, or at each grid point of a FindFit scan, and is free again at once. A slice also stops within 64 cells of its deadline, so a heavy kernel keeps the cells it computed, and a slice whose deadline has passed before its turn is not sent to a worker. A worker that has not answered within the new cancelGrace option of createKernelPool() (default 250 ms, at most 2147483647; Infinity turns it off) after an abort, or after the deadline of its task, is terminated and replaced by a new one from create; the tasks that waited for it run on the new worker. Without SharedArrayBuffer (a browser page that is not cross-origin isolated), or on a host that cannot send the flag, only the termination applies.

  • Each asynchronous evaluation now has its own top-level evaluation number, carried by its evaluation-context stack. Before, all pending asynchronous evaluations of an engine shared one number. So with B(h) = Block(r := h(k), h := z ↦ 2z, r), Promise.all([B(h).evaluateAsync(), B(q).evaluateAsync()]) gave h(k) and q(k), where the same two evaluations awaited one after the other gave 2k and 2k. A synchronous evaluation of such a block while an asynchronous one was pending also gave q(k). Both now give 2k. Related fixes: when a symbol holds such a block (p), ce.symbol('p').evaluateAsync() now gives 2k, as evaluate() does; a block in an operand of a function application stays a nested block on the asynchronous route, as on the synchronous route (with f(a, b) = (a, b), f(Tick(), B(h)) gave (0, 2k) and now gives (0, h(k))); a sticky unresolved call read again after an await in one asynchronous evaluation stays unresolved (it could resolve too early); and the locals of a block are kept separately for each evaluation, so a synchronous evaluation of a block between two iterations of a pending asynchronous loop over the same block no longer removes the loop's locals (t + 2 instead of t + 3), and two evaluations whose runs of one block alternate no longer lose each other's locals (t + 1 instead of t + 3).

0.160.0 2026-10-21​

Behavior Changes​

  • A call evaluated while its function had no definition stays symbolic for the rest of the top-level evaluation that produced it, even when the name is assigned later in that evaluation. Sum(Block(If(k = 2, h := z ↦ 2z), h(k)), k, 1, 3) is 10 + h(1): the h(1) computed at k = 1 is not resolved by the assignment at k = 2 (the unreleased callable-binding change had made it 12). A later evaluation resolves the stored call as before: r = ce.parse('g(3)').evaluate(), then ce.assign('g', …), then r.evaluate() is 9. A Block evaluated directly by the host counts each statement as its own evaluation, as the Epsil runner does, so Block(r := fn(3), fn := Function(2z, z), (r, fn(3))) is still (6, 6), while the same block nested in another expression, or a do block in an Epsil statement, keeps fn(3).

  • In an Epsil program, a function statement is installed before the first statement runs when a statement before it calls the function: let a = String(g(3)) then function g(k) { k^2 } gives "9" (it gave "g(3)"; let a = g(3) gave 9 on both routes already, by resolving the stored call when a was read). The installation is skipped, and the program behaves as before, when a type statement comes before the function, when an earlier statement gives the name a value, when the body reads an earlier variable whose type cannot be read statically, or when the function is generic. An assignment of a function literal (g = (k) => k^2) takes effect when it runs, as before.

  • On the whole-block route, a let g: (integer) -> integer statement followed by function g(k) { 2k } now checks a call written before the let: g(1.5) is incompatible-type on every route (it was 3 on the block route, which ran the clause installed before the declaration).

  • The closure documentation now states what the engine does: a function literal captures the binding of a free variable, and reads the value that binding holds when the function is called; the user guides describe how a call resolves its head lexically and how a call before the definition behaves.

  • Bare list, set, dictionary, collection, and indexed_collection now admit arbitrary contents, matching their <any> forms. Bare tuple accepts every arity and slot type, including absent coordinates; tuple<any> still has one slot. Bare record covers records with absent fields. Explicit element constraints remain restrictive, and explicit <unknown> no longer collapses to the broader bare name. Numeric vector/matrix defaults are unchanged. Compiled omission-sensitive operations require evidence that raw Nothing positions cannot occur; use an explicit content constraint when the broader bare family no longer provides that evidence.

  • Raw Tabulate / Table, Scan, and Iterate results retain possible Nothing in their element types. A two-dimensional tabulation returns lazy rows: accessing a row or its count does not evaluate its cells or erase omitted positions. Shape preserves raw extents, including omitted cells and empty axes. ListFrom(row) explicitly collects and omits those entries. Compilation refuses omission-capable tabulations and scans until targets can represent omission distinctly.

  • The type broadcastable<T> is now T | list<T>. It was T or an indexed collection of T other than a tuple or a string, so the subtype relation was not transitive: tuple<integer> is an indexed_collection<integer>, which was a broadcastable<integer>, but tuple<integer> was not one. Now every subtype of list<T> (a vector, a matrix, a Range) is a broadcastable<T>, and a tuple, a string, a set and a value typed only indexed_collection<T> are not. A tuple is now provably disjoint from broadcastable<number>, as the rule that a tuple argument is passed whole requires. Evaluation does not change, with two exceptions that follow from the new meaning: ce.assign of a value typed indexed_collection<T> to a symbol declared broadcastable<T> is refused, as it is for a symbol declared list<T>; and Map(f, [(1, 2), (3, 4)]) with f: (broadcastable<number>) -> number is one incompatible-type error instead of a list of errors, one for each point.

  • The meet (intersection) of two collection types of different kinds is the narrower kind with the meet of the elements, not never: list<number> & indexed_collection<integer> is list<integer>, set<number> & collection<integer> is set<integer>, and tuple<number, number> & indexed_collection<integer> is tuple<integer, integer>. So is the meet of a list with dimensions and a list with none: list<number^2> & list<integer> is list<integer^2>. A pair that can share a matrix by different readings (list<number> & collection<list<integer>>, which an integer matrix inhabits), and a pair with two transparent aliases, are kept as written unless they are provably disjoint; a single transparent alias is met through its definition. One effect: with type alias json = list<json> | integer, Norm(j) for j: json is valid (it was refused when boxed), and with j = 5 it evaluates to 5.

  • The overlap test of types (typesOverlap()), used to admit arguments and to detect protocol conformances that collide, compares the arms of a union one by one, and two collections that share only the empty collection do not overlap at any level, as for a parameter that is not a union. So a call is refused when the argument type and a union parameter share only empty collections: f: (list<string> | string) -> integer refuses an argument typed list<integer> | integer, as f: (list<string>) -> integer refuses an argument typed list<integer>. Two collections whose elements are at different depths now overlap when a tensor can be in both: list<list<list<real>>> and list<number> share a rank-3 tensor of reals.

  • A list with dimensions whose element type is a top type (vector<unknown>, list<any^3>, list<(any | integer)^3>) holds scalars, not lists: list<list^2> and list<list<integer>^2> are no longer subtypes of vector<unknown> and list<any^2>, as list<integer^(2x2)> already was not. The relation was not transitive: list<integer^(2x2x2)> is a list<list^2>, which was a vector<unknown>, but list<integer^(2x2x2)> is not a vector<unknown>. The meet follows: list<any^3> & list<list^3> is never (it was list<list^3>), and the two types do not overlap. A list with no dimensions is unchanged: list<list^2> is a list<unknown>.

  • The meet of two collection types of the same kind no longer drops values that are in both. Two lists, two indexed collections or two collections whose elements are at different depths are kept as written: list<number> & list<list<integer>> was list<never>, although an integer matrix is in both. Two lists with different fixed shapes are met row by row: list<number^(2x2)> & list<list<integer>^2> is list<integer^(2x2)> (it was never), and list<number^2> & list<integer^-1> is list<integer^2> (it was never). A list with a fixed length and no common element is never: list<number^2> & list<string^2> was list<never^2>. A bare list is read as list<unknown>: list<any^3> & list is list<unknown^3> (it was never). The overlap test follows: list<number^(2x2)> and list<list<integer>^2> now overlap, which two protocol conformances on these types would show as a collision.

  • Two recursive aliases that can share no finite value are disjoint: with type alias A = tuple<A> | integer and type alias B = tuple<B> | string, A & B is never and the two types do not overlap (they were kept as written and overlapped). couldMatch() reads the arms of a recursive alias: with type alias json = list<json> | integer, couldMatch(number, json) is true (it was false). The test reads recursive aliases by their finite values, while the subtype relation reads them coinductively: with type alias V = tuple<V>, V is a subtype of A and of B although A & B is never. V has no value, so no value is lost.

  • A generic alias whose arguments grow at each unfold (A<T> = B<list<T>> | integer with B<T> = A<T>) no longer overflows the stack in the subtype, overlap and meet tests: past a limit on the open unfolds, the answer is the conservative one.

  • The meet, the overlap test, couldMatch() and provablyDisjoint() of types built from a chain of aliases with two branches at each level (Aₙ = list<Aₙ₋₁^2> | list<Aₙ₋₁^3>) take a time that grows with the depth of the chain. The work doubled at each level: at depth 20, the overlap test took about 7 s and the meet did not finish in 10 minutes.

  • A literal empty list at a required or optional point parameter is accepted and maps to [] without invoking the function, matching evaluation.

  • Interpreted calls and collection callbacks now use their captured lexical binding, including lazy and asynchronous evaluation. Updating that binding remains visible; an unrelated declaration with the same name cannot redirect the call. Forward calls resolve in their original lexical environment.

  • The coordinates of a point divided by a number that may be zero are typed real | infinity | nan, as a scalar quotient has been since 0.121.0: with p: tuple<integer, integer> and x: integer, p / x was typed tuple<rational, rational>, but x = 0 gives (~oo, ~oo). The same applies to a list of points and to a value typed broadcastable<vector<…>>. A divisor proven not to be zero keeps the precise type: p / 4 and p / n with n: integer<1..> are tuple<rational, rational>. Also, i / x is typed imaginary | infinity (was imaginary), and (1 + 2i) / x is typed number (was complex). An imaginary divisor is never zero, so w / j with w: complex and j: imaginary stays complex.

  • A collection divided by itself is no longer folded to 1: L / L with L: list<integer> stays L / L, and with L = [1, 2] it evaluates to [1, 1]. The fold x / x → 1 still applies to a symbol that is not declared as a collection.

  • A structural Divide(a, b, c) is typed as (a / b) / c. Only the first divisor was read: Divide(1, 2, x) was typed rational although x = 0 gives ~oo. A real numerator that may be infinite, divided by an imaginary number, is typed number (was complex): +∞ / i is ~oo.

  • Calls through callback parameters retain their lexical contracts, including inside nested lambdas such as Map(x ↦ h(x), xs). A same-named global no longer supplies the call's result type or introduces Nothing. A parameter first used as a call head now keeps its annotation and validates arguments against it. Ordinary calls and captured operators follow the same binding rule during body-based type inference. Compilation refuses a known captured function body when lowering it would substitute a different ambient binding.

  • Bare Map callbacks such as Map(h, xs) follow the callback's lexical binding. A parameter named after a global function or library operator now uses its own declared result type and argument contract. An opaque callback result stays any; a shadowed global cannot supply a narrower result or introduce Nothing into this callback's result. Reducer parameters also retain their own result type when named after a built-in arithmetic operator.

  • Corrected Map inference to retain possible nested collections and missing data when it excludes Nothing from callback inputs. Opaque any callback results remain any; they no longer copy the source element type. Positional callbacks over strings report character data. Compilation again accepts tuple mappings whose callback bodies prove they cannot return Nothing. Omission-capable sources remain refused; numeric collection annotations restore compilation for affected aggregate and predicate code. Explicit numeric callback contracts also compile for mutable local functions and callback parameters; opaque runtime callbacks remain refused.

  • Data tuples preserve Nothing coordinates: (1, Nothing, 3) has three positions. A tuple whose coordinates are all missing remains a tuple. Zip preserves these coordinates and all-missing rows, so source positions stay aligned. JavaScript and Python compiled tuples retain all-missing tuples; compilation refuses possible Nothing coordinates until targets can represent omission distinctly. Lists and TupleFrom retain their existing immediate omission behavior.

  • Numeric aggregates skip Nothing yielded by raw lazy views. Mean of a view exposing 1, Nothing, 3 now returns 2 instead of an incompatible-type error; its denominator counts only retained data. The other univariate statistics follow the same rule, and extrema such as Min now finish evaluating after an omitted datum. All-omitted input follows each operator's ordinary empty-input rule (Sum gives 0, Product gives 1). Source counts and positions are unchanged; Missing still propagates normally. Aggregate compilation refuses omission-capable source types, including collection<any>, until targets can distinguish omission from missing data.

  • Filter drops immediate Nothing inputs without calling its predicate. Filtering a raw view yielding 1, Nothing, 3 with an always-true predicate now yields 1, 3, rather than an incompatible-type error cell or a retained omission. Count(source, predicate) follows the same selection rule. Missing and nested markers still reach the predicate. Result types exclude immediate nothing; compilation refuses sources that might contain it until targets can distinguish omission from missing data.

  • Map bypasses its callback for immediate Nothing inputs and preserves their positions. A strict numeric callback over a view yielding 1, Nothing, 3 now yields its two results and Nothing, rather than an incompatible-type error cell. Multi-source maps bypass the whole row if any input is Nothing. Missing and markers nested inside a datum still reach the callback.

  • Covariance, PopulationCovariance, and Correlation skip whole aligned observations containing Nothing, instead of rejecting them. Raw source lengths must still match; all terms use the same retained observations. Compilation refuses these statistics and maps whose inputs or map results may contain Nothing until targets can preserve its distinct representation.

  • Dedup, Filter and TakeWhile of a string held by a symbol of a wider type give a string, as they do for a string literal: with c: list<integer> | string := "aab", Dedup(c) was ["a", "b"] and is now "ab"; Dedup(Filter(c, p)) is a string too.

  • Filter and Dedup over a dictionary give a Dictionary (also when the dictionary is an arm of a union type, through nested Filter/Dedup views, and for a bare record); they gave a Set of entry tuples (Set(("a", 1))). Filter over a record is typed dictionary<any>.

  • Map of a user function with scalar parameters over a list of lists is typed with lists as elements (Map(f, pr) with f: (number) -> number is list<list<number>>, was list<number>), as the call broadcasts over each row; a polymorphic callback with one parameter ((T) -> T where T) is typed the same way (list<list<integer>>). Map of a function literal written in place whose parameter is annotated as a scalar ((x: integer) ↦ x + 1) over a list of lists is refused when it is boxed; it was admitted and gave an error for each row. Over a source that can hold Missing, such a literal is typed with the NaN it gives for an absent cell: Map((x: integer) ↦ x + 1, [1, Missing]) is list<number> (was list<integer>, value [2, NaN]). A Missing that the body returns for a present cell stays in the type, also for several sources of an abstract collection type.

  • A view whose source can be absent (Map(x ↦ x + 10, c) with c: missing | list<integer>) previews as a list; it previewed as a Set. The preview, and a bounded materialization, of Dedup, Filter, Join or Append over more than five dictionary entries show the expression as written (Dedup(d)); they showed an incompatible-type error.

  • Two mutually recursive aliases that describe the same values are subtypes of each other: with a = list<b> and b = list<a>, a <: b is now true (it was false, a conservative cutoff). A self-referential alias such as R = list<R> is a subtype of list, list<unknown>, list<list<unknown>> and value; J = list<J> | missing is still not a subtype of unknown.

  • Dedup, Filter and Map accept a source typed missing | string (typed missing | string or list<character> | missing); it was an incompatible-type error. Map of a broadcastable operator over ragged rows (Map(Sqrt, [[1, 4], [9]])) gives list<vector<1> | vector<2>>; it was an incompatible-type error.

  • A comparison with an undefined operand is false in a branch condition too, as in Desmos and IEEE 754. An ordered comparison (<, ≤, >, ≥) or an equality (=) whose operand is NaN or Indeterminate already evaluated to False on its own; an If or a Which on it now takes the next arm (the else arm) instead of no arm. This holds in the interpreter and on the javascript, python and interval-js targets. Before and after:

    • \left\{\frac{0}{0}>0:1,0\right\} (also with <, ≤, ≥, =), and If(0/0 > 0, 1, 0): Missing before, 0 now.
    • \left\{x > 0: 1, 0\right\} compiled to JavaScript and run at {x: NaN}: NaN before, 0 now. The same on the Python target. The compiled guard no longer tests the operand for NaN (_.x === _.x); it still tests for a variable the caller did not supply (_.x !== undefined), which still gives NaN, also through arithmetic (2x > 0). The guard tests a variable of any type (p.x > 0 tests p), and a variable read through an assigned value (a := \sin x, then \cos a > 0) or through the body of a called user function. It does not test a variable read only by an arm of a nested If, Which or When: If(If(x > 0, y, 1) > 0, 1, 0) at x = -1 is 1 with y not supplied.
    • 0 < \sqrt{x} compiled to interval-js at x = [-1, -1], where the root has no value (empty): 'maybe' before, 'false' now. The same for ≤, >, ≥ and =.
    • On interval-js, a comparison with an operand that has a value over only part of the cell (partial) is now at most 'maybe': \sqrt{x} \ge 0 at x = [-1, 1] was 'true'. 0 < \sqrt{x} there stays 'maybe'.
    • A sum of such a piecewise, \sum_{n=0}^{10000} M(n) with M(n) := \{K(n) > 0: 1, 0\} and K(0) undefined, is now 10000 instead of NaN.

    Not changed: ≠ keeps its behavior (\mathrm{NaN} \ne 0 is True, and a branch on a ≠ with a NaN operand still takes no arm: Missing in the interpreter, NaN on javascript and python, 'maybe' on interval-js). Missing keeps its Kleene reading (Less(Missing, 1) is Missing): a comparison with a nested else-less If or default-less Which that selects no arm still takes no arm (If(If(c > 0, 1) > 0, 1, 0) at c = -1 is NaN compiled), and on interval-js that value is an empty with a missing flag, so Which(x > 5, 1) > 0 over x = [0, 1] stays 'maybe'. A comparison of two collections with an absent cell still takes no arm. The GPU targets (glsl, wgsl) already took the else arm. This reverses the rule of 2026-09-03, under which a NaN operand of any comparison made the branch take no arm (docs/ERROR-MODEL.md).

  • A value that has no order also makes a comparison false: the pole ComplexInfinity (~oo, the value of 1/0) and a number that is not real (i, \sqrt{-1}, \ln(-1), any value with a nonzero imaginary part). An ordered comparison (<, ≤, >, ≥) with such an operand is now False, alone and in the condition of an If or a Which, which then takes its next arm. +∞ and −∞ are real and keep their order. An equality with the pole is False (the pole has no value, as NaN has none), but an equality with a complex number keeps its meaning. An exact constant such as \ln(-1) is approximated to find its imaginary part (not when it holds an infinite Sum or Product or a Limit), and the imaginary part of a number literal is read exactly (1 + 10^{-800}i is not real). A comparison stays unevaluated only when its operands are free symbols or forms that depend on one (0 < x, 0 < ix): a value with no order decides False also next to a free symbol (x < i, x < \frac{1}{0}), as NaN does. A chain stops at its first pair that is False. Before and after:

    • 0 < \frac{1}{0}, 0 < i, 0 < \ln(-1), \pi + i < 4 + i, x < i: unevaluated before, False now.
    • \frac{1}{0} = \frac{1}{0} and \ln(-1) \le \ln(-1): True before, False now.
    • 0 < i < \mathrm{Missing}: Missing before, False now.
    • \int_0^1 x^{i\pi} dx: \frac{1}{1+i\pi} with the condition 0 < 1 + i\pi before, \frac{1}{1+i\pi} now (the convergence condition is on the real part of the exponent), and the same for the other convergent integrals of a power or an exponential with a complex exponent.
    • \log_{1+i}(x) = 2: the root 2i with the condition 0 < 1 + i before, 2i now (a base that is not real has the conditions b \ne 0 and b \ne 1).
    • \left\{\frac{1}{0} > 0: 1, 0\right\} and \left\{\sqrt{-1} > 0: 1, 0\right\}: a held Which before, 0 now.
    • \sum_{n=0}^{10} M(n) with M(n) := \left\{\frac{1}{n} > 0: 1, 0\right\}: a held expression before, 10 now.

    Not changed: \frac{1}{0} = 0 is False, i = i is True, i = 0 is False, \frac{1}{0} \ne 0 is True (≠ is not part of the decision), 0 < \infty and \infty = \infty are True, and Missing keeps its Kleene reading. The methods isLess(), isGreater() and the others still answer undefined for a complex operand.

    Compiled code: the arithmetic does not change, so a pole computed at run time is the IEEE Infinity, which has an order. \left\{\frac{1}{x} > 0: 1, 0\right\} at x = 0 gives 1 on javascript and on python (with a NumPy x; a plain Python float raises ZeroDivisionError), where the interpreter gives 0; \frac{1}{x} = \frac{1}{x} at x = 0 is true there. On interval-js, \frac{1}{x} over the point [0, 0] is empty, so that branch already gives 0. A non-real value at run time already gave false (\left\{\sqrt{x} > 0: 1, 0\right\} at x = -1 is 0). A closed comparison with such an operand now folds to the value of the interpreter on javascript, glsl, wgsl and python, with or without constantFold: \left\{\frac{1}{0} > 0: 1, 0\right\} compiles to 0 (it was 1), and 0 < \frac{1}{0} and \frac{1}{0} = \frac{1}{0} to false (they were true). i < 2 compiles to false (it was a compile-time decline; i < x still is one). interval-js does not fold a comparison: 0 < \frac{1}{0} and \frac{1}{0} = \frac{1}{0} there are still 'true'. The constant pole next to a variable is the IEEE Infinity: x < \frac{1}{0} at x = 1 is true on javascript, python and interval-js, where the interpreter gives False.

  • The subtype relation of lists now reads a value in every way it can be read, so the relation is transitive and a union or a meet of list types no longer drops values. Three rules changed. The rows of a list with dimensions are read whether or not its scalar element matches the target's element: matrix<string> is a vector<collection> as matrix<integer> always was (a string is a collection, so only its rank was read before), and matrix<integer> is a vector<integer | list>; the elements of a vector<unknown> or vector<any> stay scalars, and matrix<unknown> is not a vector<unknown>. A list declared in the nested spelling answers as its flat spelling toward every target: list<vector<integer^1>^2> is a list<number>, a collection<number> and an indexed_collection<real>, as list<integer^(2x1)> is (it was a matrix only). collection<E> and indexed_collection<E> peel any number of outer axes, as list<E> does: list<boolean^(2x2x2)> is a collection<vector<boolean^2>>. The meet follows: list<string> & vector<collection> keeps the string matrices (it was vector<string>). An outer list with no dimensions admits any shape of its rows, so its flat spelling has no dimensions: list<vector<integer^3>> is a list<integer> and a collection<integer> but not a matrix<integer> (its missing length was read as one axis of any length, which made it a matrix although it holds a 2×2 arrangement of 3-vectors), and at a matrix<T^(MxN)> parameter it pins no length (it pinned N). A random check of 72,000 pairs of list and collection types against concrete values finds no loss (it found 18).

Resolved Issues​

  • Factor merges equal factors into a power and finds every copy of a repeated root:

  • Factor((x^2-1)(x+1)) is (x-1)(x+1)^2; it was (x-1)(x+1)(x+1).

  • Factor(x^3+3x^2+3x+1) is (x+1)^3; it was (x+1)(x+1)(x+1).

  • Factor(x^5-x^4-2x^3+2x^2+x-1) is (x-1)^3(x+1)^2; it was (x^3-x^2-x+1)(x-1)(x+1).

  • Factor(x^4-2x^2+1) is (x-1)^2(x+1)^2; it was (x^2-1)^2.

  • A rational root is used in lowest terms, so Factor(4x^4+12x^3+x^2-12x+4) is (2x-1)^2(x+2)^2; it was (x+2)(x-\frac{1}{2})(2x-1)(2x+4).

With A and B matrices, Factor(A·B·A) keeps the product as written: matrix factors are not merged. PartialFraction now decomposes these denominators when they are given expanded, also with a negative leading coefficient (1/(-x^3+3x-2)). Before, it returned them unchanged.

  • A Multiply declared not commutative (ce.declare('Multiply', { commutative: false }, { extend: true })) removes its factors 1: a·1·b is a·b, and Factor(a·b·a) is a·b·a. They were kept, and Factor(a·b·a) gave a·1·b·1·a·1. No other operand moves, and no other simplification is applied to such a product.

  • Result types of broadcast arithmetic over nested lists hold their values. Rows of different lengths are no longer typed matrix: Sin(L) with L: list<list<integer>> := [[1, 2], [3]], and Sin([[1, 2], [3]]), are list<list<number>> (they were matrix and list<number>). A nested list of points plus a number (L + 0.5 with L: list<list<tuple<integer, integer>>>) is refused as an error, as a flat list of points is. Rows of points beside numbers keep point cells for Divide, Power, Mod, Root, Log, Round, Remainder and Arctan2, with the rank of the deepest operand (Power(NQ, V) is list<list<tuple<number, number>>>, was list<number>), also when the numbers can be absent; a divisor cell that may be zero gives number coordinates. On the derive route, Subtract of a nested list is no longer one level too deep, and Divide of a nested list of points keeps its points.

  • Subtype relation: matrix<T> is a subtype of broadcastable<T>, and couldMatch no longer answers false for pairs that share a subtype (tuples with an any slot against indexed_collection, tuple against tuple<any>, record{a: any} against dictionary<integer>, a flat list against a nested list such as list<integer> against list<list<integer>>, which a matrix matches both, and others). An operand typed with an alias is unfolded before the type variables are solved: Sort(a) with a: L, L an alias of list<integer | missing>, is list<integer | missing>; it was list<unknown>. A self-referential alias (cyc = cyc | list<integer>) no longer overflows the stack.

  • Total no longer builds the union any | unknown. Zip([1, Undefined], [2, Undefined]) is typed with missing elements, as with Missing.

  • Collection operator types: FlatMap over a source with absent cells keeps the absent cell (FlatMap(l, x ↦ [x, x]) with l: list<integer | missing> is list<integer | missing>, was list<number>; with an annotated parameter, the NaN of an absent cell is in the type; a callback that can answer a list or Missing is spliced arm by arm, so FlatMap([[1, 2], Missing], x ↦ Reverse(x)) is list<integer | missing>). couldMatch of a record against a collection of entries compares each required field with its own key (record{a: integer} cannot match collection<tuple<"b", integer>>). Map over an alias is a list (was collection<number>). Map of an operator whose declared result is any (Map(PointX, ["a", "b"])) is list<any^2>, not a copy of the source type. Map of a function literal over any elements whose body can return a collection (x ↦ Sqrt(x)) allows a collection element. Map over mixed non-numeric elements no longer states a length. A Map over a union with a dictionary or record arm types that arm as a collection of entries.

  • The derivative of a Sum no longer reads a global symbol as the index of the sum when a function called in the sum reads a symbol with the name of the index. With k := 2 and g := a ↦ a·k·x, Σ_{k=1}^{5} g(k) is 30x, but its derivative in x was 55 (the sum of k², the global k read as the index): it is now 30, as it is for the same sum with the index j. When k has no value, the derivative was 55 too: it is now 15k. When this occurs, the derivative renames the index to a fresh name, such as k_1: the derivative of Σ_{k=1}^{n} g(k) is Σ_{k_1=1}^{n} k·k_1.

  • \int \sin x + 1 parsed to Integrate(0) + sin(x) + 1: the integrand was lost. It now parses to Integrate(sin(x) + 1). A differential inside one term of a sum or a difference now ends the integrand at that term, and the terms after it keep their sign: \int \frac{x\,dx}{2} - 1 parses to Integrate(x/2, x) - 1 (it was Integrate(x/2, x) + 1), and \int 1 - \frac{dx}{x} to Integrate(1 - 1/x, x) (the dx stayed in the integrand). A parenthesized term in such a sum (\int (\sin x\,dx) + 1) no longer becomes a tuple, and with diagnostics: true the variable of the integration is no longer reported as undeclared in the integrand of such a sum.

  • A subscripted name in a binder position is a new name, also when its base is a list. With n declared as list<number>, a subscript on n is an index: n_{0} is At(n, 0). The parser read a binder spelled that way the same way, so \sum_{n_{0}=1}^{3}n_{0} was ["Sum", ["At", "n", 0], ["Tuple", "Nothing", 1, 3]] (a sum with no index) and it evaluated to 3·At(n, 0). It is now ["Sum", "n_0", ["Tuple", "n_0", 1, 3]] and evaluates to 6, as when n is not declared. The same applies to a product index, a comprehension variable ([n_{0}^2 \operatorname{for} n_{0} = [1,2,3]]), a local of a where clause or of a ; block (n_{0} \coloneq 3; n_{0}+1 is 4, not an assignment to a function named At), a function parameter (n_{0} \mapsto n_{0}^2, f(n_{0}) \coloneq n_{0}^2, which were a parse error and an invalid function), a for … from … to … do index, a limit variable, a quantified variable, the variable of a set-builder (\{n_{0} \mid n_{0}>0\}), an integration variable (dn_{0}) and a differentiation variable (\frac{d}{dn_{0}}, \partial n_{0} in a denominator). The occurrences of the binder in its scope are the new name too. Elsewhere, a subscript on a list is still an index: in \sum_{k=1}^{3}n_{k}, the body is At(n, k), and in \frac{\partial n_{0}}{\partial x}, the differentiand is At(n, 0). A top-level assignment n_{0} \coloneq 3 is not a binder: it is still the error expected-a-symbol, as before.

  • The variable of Integrate and Limit no longer reads a symbol of the same name inside a called user function. With k := 2 and g := a ↦ a·k·x, \int_0^1 g(k)\,dk was x/3 and is now x, the value of \int_0^1 g(t)\,dt; \lim_{k\to 1} g(k) was x and is now 2x; \int g(k)\,dk was -x k^3/6 + k x k^2/2 and is now x k^2. When k has no value, \lim_{k\to 1} g(k) is now k x (it was x) and \int_0^1 g(k)\,dk is k x/2 (it was x/3). These operators inline the body of g and select the variable by its name, so the k of the body became the variable. The variable is now renamed to a fresh name first. The fresh name is not a name of the expression and not the name of a declared symbol, with or without a value. The bounds of the integral and the point of the limit keep their symbols: \sum_{k=1}^{2} \int_0^k g(k)\,dk is 5x (the bound is the index of the sum), and \int_0^{k_1} g(k)\,dk is x k_1^2. An indefinite integral whose result also holds the global k keeps the fresh name, and the printed result shows it: \int g(k)\,dk is \frac{1}{2}k x k_1^2 when k has no value (k_2 when k_1 is declared). That result is correct: the k of g and the variable of the antiderivative are different symbols. Sum and Product already gave these answers. Solve(g(k) = 1, k) and Solve(\{g(k) = 1, k \in 1..3\}) had the same capture and answered [] (no solution); they now stay unsolved.

  • Integrate and Solve inline a function that is declared with a function type and then assigned (g: (real) -> real, then g := a ↦ a·x), as they do for a function that is only assigned. \int_0^1 g(t)\,dt stayed unevaluated and is now x/2. With g := a ↦ 2a + x, Solve(g(t) = 1, t) stayed unevaluated and is now [(1 − x)/2].

  • A recursive user function is no longer inlined by Integrate, Limit and Solve. With r(x) := r(x − 1) + 1, \int_0^1 x^2 + r(3)\,dx ran for about 11 seconds and ended with a stack overflow (RangeError). The call now stays as it is, and its evaluation stops at the recursion limit with a CancellationError at once, as it already did for a function declared with a function type.
