  • An element read over a collection whose element type is any, or over a symbol declared any or value, is typed any. It was unknown, and arithmetic reads an unknown operand as a number: with P: any (or P: list<any>), P[i] was unknown and P[i] - P[j] was broadcastable<number>, although P can hold points and (3, 4) - (1, 1) is (2, 3). Now P[i] and P[i] - P[j] are any. This applies to At (a single index, a gather, several indices, a dictionary key, a dynamic index into a tuple or a record with an any field), First, Second, Third, Last and Field (D.a with D: dictionary<any> is any, was unknown). A function of such a read is any too: Sqrt(P[i]), Sin(P[i]) and h(P[i]) with h: (number) -> number were broadcastable<number>. A symbol whose type is inferred from its uses is not changed: with P undeclared, P[i] is still unknown and P[i] - P[j] still makes P an indexed_collection<number> (and a read of Rest(P), Take(P, 2), Sort(P), … is unknown as well). A bare list (a synonym of list<unknown>) still gives unknown. A tuple of such reads still compiles: (P[1], P[2]) with P: list<any> or P: collection<any> | tuple compiles to JavaScript, since a list element is never Nothing.

  • Sum and Product of terms typed any or value are typed any. They were number: with P: any := [(3, 4), (1, 1), (0, 0)], Sum(P[k], k, 1, 3) and Sum(P) evaluate to the point (4, 5).

  • A read of Take(P, 2), Rest(P), Drop(P, 2), Most(P) or Reverse(P) with P undeclared is unknown. It was character | missing, the element of the string option of the type list<unknown> | string, so Rest(P)[i] + 1 was an incompatible-type error.

New Features​

  • broadcast() and broadcastAsync() of a javascript result take shared inputs and write several values per cell (Tycho row 416). Two additions, for a kernel that reads the field values around a cell and writes several numbers per cell (the corners and edges of a 3-D implicit surface):

    • A shared input is bound once for the whole batch and read by index in the expression: with F: list<number> and i: integer, F_{i+1} over { i: Float64Array [0, 1, 2], F: [1, 2, 3, 4] } gives [1, 2, 3]. A variable whose declared type is a list is shared; the new shared option names any other one ({ shared: ['G'] }). A shared input is a plain array of numbers or a Float64Array, is not a column of the cells layout and not an axis of the grid layout, and goes to each worker of the pool once per broadcastAsync() call instead of once per slice. A variable read as a list was refused before ("cannot be broadcast"); a plain array for any other variable throws.
    • An expression whose type is a tuple of two or more elements that can be numbers (an element typed unknown, such as an undeclared symbol, counts) writes that many values per cell into one output array: (i, 2i) over { i: Float64Array [1, 2, 3] } gives [1, 2, 2, 4, 3, 6]. The result reports the count as broadcastOutputs, which a stored result keeps for createJavaScriptRuntime().loadBroadcast() and the pool's workers; the new outputs option overrides it. An element missing from an array answer is NaN, and a non-array answer or a thrown cell is NaN in every slot. done of broadcastAsync() is still a count of cells.

    An interval-js result throws a TypeError for either option.

  • The grid of the global option of FindFit now has a point in every basin of a frequency (Tycho row 407). The search sampled a searched parameter at a fixed number of points (400 for one parameter, 40 × 40 for two), so a wide range for a frequency found the best fit only when a point fell near it by chance. With a cos(b x + c) + d x + e on 200 points over x ∈ [0, 10] (true b = 2.2), b over [0.3, 120] and c over [0, 2π] gave a sum of squared residuals of 390 at b = 0.3; it now finds b = 2.2 (about 1e-27). Three changes:

    • A parameter that multiplies a variable inside Sin, Cos, Tan, Cot, Sec or Csc (b in cos(b x + c)) gets grid points π / (rate · span of x) apart (half that for Tan and Cot), up to 4,000 points, in every angular unit (ce.angularUnit). A parameter whose phase rate is not a constant (cos(b² x)) and a non-periodic model keep the previous grid.
    • A phase that is only added to the argument of a Sin or Cos multiplied by a linear amplitude (c in a cos(b x + c)), searched over at least one period, is solved by least squares with the linear parameters, since a cos(b x + c) = p cos(b x) + q sin(b x). It is then no longer sampled, and the search over b and c costs as much as a search over b alone. The fitted phase is in its range. Otherwise two searched parameters share a budget of 8,000 grid points.
    • A range can give the grid step as a third element: {global: {b: [0.3, 120, 0.05]}}. It sets the grid of the scan that solves the linear parameters; when the model is not linear in the other parameters, the solver still runs from each point of the coarse grid (24 points, or 6 × 6). A step on a phase keeps that phase on the grid instead of solving it by least squares. A step that is not a finite positive number is an unexpected-argument error, as is a pair of steps that asks for more than 8,000 points of the grid of that scan.

    With more than 300 data rows, the grid is scanned on a stratified sample of 300 rows (the same rows for the same data, not a regular sub-grid, so that an alias of the true frequency does not fit the sample), the 24 best grid points are solved again on every row, and the 6 best of those are refined on every row. When the deadline of the evaluation expires during the scan of the sample, the record (timedOut: True) has the best scanned parameters and residualNorm: NaN, since their residual over every row was not computed. On 1,000 rows with b over [0.3, 628] the search took about 410 ms and missed the fit (residual sum 1,947); it now takes about 260 to 330 ms and finds it. On 200 rows the deciding cases take about 45 to 70 ms (they took about 90 to 100 ms).

  • FindFit with the global option runs its grid scan on the engine's worker pool on the asynchronous route. When the engine has a kernel pool (ce.workers, see createKernelPool()), expr.evaluateAsync() sends the grid points of the scan to the workers in one slice per worker; the refinements by the solver stay on the calling thread. Each worker solves its points with the code the calling thread uses, on the same numbers, so the record is the record of evaluate(). The pool is used only when the model and the derivatives the scan reads compile to JavaScript that a worker can run (a model with a function that does not compile, such as LogGamma, runs on the calling thread), and only for a model that is linear in the parameters that are not searched (otherwise each grid point is a solver run, on the calling thread). A worker that fails or refuses the problem is replaced by the calling thread for its points, with the same result. The engine's iterationLimit applies on the workers too. An abort of the signal of evaluateAsync() rejects the evaluation with a CancellationError, whatever the reason given to abort(); the fit on the calling thread stops within a data row, and a slice that a worker runs finishes there and its result is dropped. On the asynchronous route, with or without a pool, the data operand is evaluated with evaluateAsync(), so data from an operator that has only an asynchronous handler is read. evaluate() does not use the pool. Measured with a cos(b x + c) + d x + e (benchmarks/workers/fit-parallel.mts, load average 6 on 18 cores): 1,000 rows with b over [0.3, 628] take 62 ms with 8 workers and 76 ms with 4, against 230 ms for evaluate(); the 200-row cases take 13 to 23 ms with 8 workers, against 34 to 42 ms.

0.159.0 2026-10-20​

Behavior Changes​

  • Absence checks treat both numeric markers alike: IsMissing(Indeterminate) is now True, and Indeterminate ?? 5 returns 5, as for NaN. Exact arithmetic and reducers still produce Indeterminate where they did before. Nothing passes through fallbacks and is not missing data.

  • Coalesce(x, RuntimeError("absent")) retains the successful type of x instead of becoming never. Coalescing removes only whole-value absence: a list's missing cells and a possible Nothing result remain in its type. Compilation refuses absence tests that might confuse Nothing with missing data until the target can represent that distinction.

  • LaTeX: an authored \mathrm{Nothing} (or \operatorname{Nothing}, also in braces or in \smash{…}) is an operand. Before, the parser skipped it, as it skips a presentational command, which lost the argument and broke the comma list around it: \mathrm{If}(x > 1, \mathrm{Nothing}, x) was If(Error(incompatible-type), x) and is now If(x > 1, Nothing, x), as on the ce.box route. f(a, \mathrm{Nothing}, b) gives the same arguments as f(a,,b).

  • LaTeX: a style switch (\displaystyle, \large, …), \color{…}, a strut or an invisible box (\phantom{…}, \vphantom{…}, \hphantom{…}) between an operand and an infix operator no longer changes the expression: x \displaystyle + 1 was the product x·1 and is now x + 1; x\vphantom{y} + 1 was x·1 and is now x + 1; a \cdot b \displaystyle + c is ab + c. The style of such a switch is not kept. The body of a switch now ends where the expression that holds it ends: x \displaystyle y + 1 was x·(y + 1) and is now x·y + 1, and 2 \displaystyle \frac{1}{2} + 1 was 3 and is now 2. A switch at the start of a group still applies to the whole group ({\displaystyle x+y}).

  • LaTeX: \smash{x} gives x; before, its content was discarded (\smash{x}+1 was 1). The option of \smash[b]{…} and of \placeholder[…]{…} is read as text, not as math.

  • LaTeX: an element of a comma list or a matrix cell that holds only a presentational command (f(a, \phantom{x}, b), \begin{pmatrix} a & \phantom{0} \\ c & d\end{pmatrix}) is an empty element. Before, the list ended there (f((a,), b)), and the matrix lost its row break. \phantom{y} x, with a space, was an unexpected-token error and is now x.

  • LaTeX: a keyword that does not apply is text, as a word that is not a keyword is. x \text{where} (no binding after where), x \text{for} y (no comprehension or condition after for) and x \text{if} (no then) were a Sequence of x and an unexpected-operator error; they are now x followed by the text, as x \text{hello} is. \operatorname{where} and \mathrm{for} that do not apply are symbols, as \operatorname{foo} is. Such a keyword in a group no longer breaks the group: \{x \text{where}\} is a set and \frac{x \text{ where }}{2} a fraction. A statement keyword that applies after an operand starts another expression for the \text spelling too: x \text{return} y was an error and is now x followed by Return(y), as x \operatorname{return} y already was. The input after such a statement is read too: a \text{return} b \text{return} c was a followed by Return(b), without c, and x \operatorname{break} y lost y. The same applies after a prefix operator that ends an operand: x \neg y \neg z lost Not(z), and x \lnot y ) dropped the ) with no error; it now reports an unexpected-delimiter error, so that input is no longer valid.

  • LaTeX: a keyword operator with nothing after it has a missing right operand, as the symbol operators have: x \text{and} is And(x, Error("missing")), as x \land is. The right operand was Nothing, so x \text{and} became And(x) and the error was lost. The same applies to or, iff, if and only if and such that.

Resolved Issues​

  • Compiled GammaRegularized(a, z) is correct for a non-positive order a, as .N() is (#457, contributed by enumeratio). With a and z declared real, compile(GammaRegularized(a, z)).run({a: -1.5, z: 0.001}) was NaN and is now 8894.8453395772…. At a non-positive integer a the compiled value is 0 for z > 0 and NaN at z = 0, as the interpreter answers; at z = 0 and a negative non-integer a it is ±Infinity by the sign of Γ(a). The kernel works in logarithms at a large negative order, so GammaRegularized(-150.5, 120) is -7.65e-105, not 0. A value outside the double range is ±Infinity, or a signed 0, as the IEEE rules give it. The machine kernels were also made more accurate in related places, each checked against mpmath:

    • The Python target gives the same values. GammaRegularized(a, z) lowered to scipy.special.gammaincc, which is nan for every a < 0, and the two-operand Gamma(s, z) refused to compile for a constant s ≤ 0. Both now use a helper that keeps SciPy for a positive order and computes a non-positive order itself; the helper also fixes Gamma(200, 1000), which overflowed to inf (its value is 6.3e162). compileLambda() cannot hold the helper, as for Power. A lambda keeps the inline lowering only where it is correct: GammaRegularized with a constant order of at least 1e-20, and Gamma(s, z) with a constant order from 2.5e-4 to 7.5. Any other order fails with "use compileFunction"; before, such a lambda gave nan or a wrong value.
    • Gamma, Digamma, Trigamma and ln|Γ| near a negative integer: the reflection formula now takes the sine of the exact remainder, so Gamma(-10.000000001) has at least 12 correct digits instead of 7. The interval enclosure of Gamma(-1.000001) is under 1e-12 wide (relative), not 3.5e-9.
    • GammaRegularized(a, z) for |a| ≤ 1/2 and Gamma(s, z) for -1 < s < 1/2 and a small z: GammaRegularized(1e-9, 0.99) had five correct digits, and Gamma(-0.9999, 0.001) was NaN.
    • Binomial(n, k) for an n close to a negative integer: Binomial(-51.999999999999986, 87) was 0 (its interval enclosure was [0, 0], which did not hold the true value -2.1e38), and Binomial(-426.1545291590769, 635.8454312348206) was -Infinity, not -1.18e305.

  • Log(1, base) threads over a list of bases instead of folding to the scalar 0: Log(1, [-10, e, 27]) was 0 and is now [0, 0, 0], as Log(8, [2, 4]) is [3, 3/2]. The Log(1, b) = 0 fold now applies only to a base that cannot be a collection, so a symbol declared real | list<real> is not folded either. A tuple base threads, as it already did for Log(8, (2, 3)): Log(1, (2, 3)) is (0, 0). A set base is an incompatible-type error, as it already was for Log(8, Set(2, 3)), where it was the scalar 0 before (#455, contributed by enumeratio).

  • LaTeX: a chain of \text keyword operators such as a \cdot b \text{and} a \cdot b \text{and} … took time that grows exponentially with the number of keywords (14 keywords: about 0.2 s; each two more: about 3.4 times longer). The parser now compares the braced text with the keywords instead of parsing the right operand to find out whether the keyword matches.

  • LaTeX: a chain of \text{ for } or \text{ where } clauses that do not apply (x_0 \text{ for } y_0 \; x_1 \text{ for } y_1 …) took time that doubles with each clause (12 clauses: about 0.3 s). Two dictionary entries read \text{for}, and each one parsed the rest of the input. The parser now calls the handler of a keyword once at each position, and keeps the result when it declines; 64 clauses take about 0.5 s. A chain of \text{for} clauses with \text{from} … \text{to} … \text{do} … at its end took about 3.7 s for 16 clauses (each four more: about 15 times longer); it takes about 0.06 s for 16 clauses and 0.5 s for 32. A chain of \text{for all} clauses is faster too (10 clauses: 1.7 s, was 21 s), but still grows exponentially.

  • The derivative of a Sum follows a call in a term or a bound into the body of the called function (Tycho ledger row 405). With g := a ↦ a·x, D(Sum(g(k), Limits(k, 1, 5)), x) was 0: the rule read only the names written in the term, and x is not one of them. It is now 15, the value that the derivative of each call (D(g(2), x) is 2) gives. A bound that calls a function whose body reads the variable (N := a ↦ ⌊a·x⌋, Limits(i, 1, N(1))) depends on the variable, so the derivative stays unevaluated, as for the bound ⌊x⌋; it was differentiated term by term. A function passed as an argument (G(h, k) with h a function) is followed too. A call of a function that is not pure (its body draws a random number) is not evaluated to find its body, and a call of a function whose body is not known that way is taken to depend on the variable: a bound with such a call keeps the derivative unevaluated.

  • The derivative of a call of a user function no longer reads an assigned value of its variable. With h := a ↦ a·x² and x := 5, D(h(k), x) was 0: the body of h was found by evaluating h, which gave 25k. The body is now taken from the function literal, with the arguments in place of the parameters, and is not evaluated, so D(h(k), x) is 2kx with and without a value of x. The derivative follows the name of its variable into the body of a called function in both cases; Integrate, Limit, Solve and Sum keep the rule of 2026-09-21, under which their variable does not reach into a called function. A free symbol of the body that is not the variable still reads its value: the derivative of q in its parameter, with q(a) := a x² and x := 5, is 25.

  • A parameter used as the name of a called function now takes a function argument in a derivative. With G := (f, a) ↦ f(a), D(G(h, k), x) stayed unevaluated, because the body of G applied to wildcards was an Error; it is now the derivative of h(k). D(G(Sin, x), x) is cos(x), and a function literal argument is applied: D(G(t ↦ t·x, k), x) is k. The derivative of Apply(t ↦ t·x, k) is k; it was t * Apply(Derivative("Apply", 1, 0), (t) => t * x, k), with the parameter t free in it. A recursive function (f(x) := x·f(x−1), or two functions that call each other) is not expanded: its derivative stays Apply(Derivative(f, 1), x), as before. A function composed with itself is expanded: with h := a ↦ a·x², D(h(h(x)), x) is 5x⁴. A call in an argument is never taken for the parameter (G(h, f(x)) is h(f(x))), and a function with no body passed as an argument keeps its own name (D(G(u, x), x) is u′(x)).

  • The derivative of a power, an exponential and the other operators sees a variable that a call reads in the body of the called function. With g := t ↦ t·x, D(g(k)², x) and D(e^{g(k)}, x) were 0: the rules tested only the names written in the operand. They are now 2k²x and k·e^{kx}.

  • On the interval-js target, a negative base under a float exponent that the interpreter reads as a rational with an odd denominator, but that is not the double nearest to that rational, has its real root (Tycho ledger row 406). x^{0.4545454545454545} (16 digits, read as 5/11) over [−1.1, −0.9] was empty, while evaluate() and the javascript target give −1 at x = −1; it is now [−1.0443, −0.9532]. The same holds for x^{0.6000000000000001}, a negative such exponent, and a root index such as \sqrt[2.2000000000000006]{x}. The new routine _IA.powRealBranch(x, e, oddNumerator) encloses ±|x|^e with the float e, the value the interpreter computes. An exponent that is the double of its rational (0.4, 1/2.2) still uses _IA.powRational.

  • A tuple with an absent slot is accepted as the source of Map, Filter, Reduce, Fold, Scan, TakeWhile, DropWhile, FlatMap, Any, All, MaxBy, MinBy, ArgMax, ArgMin, Dedup and Differences, as a list with an absent element already was. Map(x ↦ x + 10, t) with t: tuple<integer, missing> was an incompatible-type error; it is now typed list<number>. An alias of list<integer | missing> is accepted there too. The result of these operators and of Take, Reverse, Sort and Unique over a source that can be absent as a whole keeps its absent elements in its type: with w: missing | list<integer | missing>, Dedup(w) was typed list<number> | missing and is now list<integer | missing> | missing, and MaxBy(w, …) is missing | number. Dedup over a tuple or a list with a stated length is typed list<…>: Dedup([1, 1, 2]) was typed vector<integer^3>, which does not hold its value [1, 2].

New Features​

  • Batch evaluation of compiled functions. A javascript or interval-js compilation result has broadcast(inputs, options): the inputs of every cell at once, one Float64Array per free variable (a lo, hi pair per cell for interval-js) or one number for every cell, and one Float64Array of results: one value per cell, or a lo, hi, kind triple per cell with the INTERVAL_KIND codes (interval, empty, entire, singularPole, singularJump, partial, boolTrue, boolFalse, boolMaybe, error). A grid layout takes the arrays as the axes of a regular grid, and out is a caller-owned output array. Cell for cell, the value is the one run() gives; the conversions run once per batch instead of once per cell, which measured 20 % faster than run() per cell on the main thread.

  • Worker threads. broadcastAsync(inputs, options) runs a batch on a pool of worker threads when the host gives the engine one (ce.workers = createKernelPool({ create, size, prewarm })), and inline in slices between yields to the event loop otherwise or when the batch is too small to pay for the transfer. It takes a signal, a deadline in milliseconds and a chunk size, and resolves to { out, done }, the output and the number of leading cells that are valid. The worker is the new entry @cortex-js/compute-engine/kernel-worker, one self-contained file that holds the compiled-code runtime and the interval runtime and no engine; it rebuilds each compiled function from its text and runs the same loop as the main thread. Measured on an 18-core machine: an implicit plot of 512×512 interval cells takes 175 ms inline and 34 ms on 8 workers. The engine creates no worker on its own. Design and measurements: docs/plans/2026-10-20-worker-kernel-pool.md.

  • The interval runtime. createIntervalRuntime() from @cortex-js/compute-engine/interval rebuilds a stored interval-js compilation result with no engine behind it, as createJavaScriptRuntime() does for javascript code; the result now carries runtimeVersion, preambleOnce and preamblePerCall. Both runtimes gain loadBroadcast().

0.158.0 2026-10-20​

Behavior Changes​

  • A read past the end of a declared numeric list that holds no element is NaN, taken from the declared element type. With E: list<integer> assigned [], First(E), Last(E), At(E, 5) and E[1] were Missing, which their type integer | nan does not hold; they are now NaN, as a read past the end of a non-empty numeric list already was. A list of strings, an undeclared E := [] and the literal First([]) stay Missing.

  • A lazy view keeps a Nothing result in its own display, and erases it when it becomes a list. With m = Map(x ↦ If(x > 1, Nothing, x), [1, 2]), m.toString() was [1] while m counted 2 elements and m.at(2) was Nothing; it now prints [1, Nothing]. The same holds for Tabulate, Table, Scan and Iterate. A list built from the view erases Nothing as a list literal does, and its count agrees: ListFrom(m), m.evaluate({ materialization: true }), [...m, 9], ListJoin(m, [9]), Sort(m) and Tally(m) hold only 1, and Length(Sort(m)) is 1 (it was 3). A set-kind view does not count Nothing: Map(x ↦ If(x > 1, Nothing, x), Set(1, 2, 3)) has 1 element.

  • An overloaded function now accepts a symbol declared error that has no value, as a function with one signature does. With ce.declare('e', 'error') and ov declared ((number) -> number) & ((string) -> string), ov(e) is valid, typed number | string, and evaluates to ov(e). Before, it was the error "expected number | string, got error", while g(e) with g declared (number) -> number was valid. The same applies to a call typed error only by its declared result type (h(2) with h declared (number) -> error), and to an overload with a generic arm (((string) -> string) & ((T) -> T where T: number), also typed number | string). An arm whose parameter is a collection (list, tuple<…>) or a function still refuses such an argument. A function with several clauses selects no clause for it: with f(a: number) = a + 1 and f(a: string) = "s", f(e) stays f(e); it was the no-matching-clause error. A clause whose parameter is typed error or any is still selected for it. The library operators that have a string form as well as a collection form (Reverse, Sort, Take, Drop, Slice, Unique, Most, Rest, RotateLeft, RotateRight, Permutations, Combinations, SlidingWindow, RandomSample, RandomShuffle, DeleteAt, StringSplit, Chunk) now accept such an argument through their string form: Reverse(e) is valid, typed string, and evaluates to Reverse(e); it was refused. A parameter typed unknown now accepts such an argument on every route: a library operator with the signature (unknown) -> unknown and a function literal (a: unknown) ↦ a refused it.

  • A valid call of an overloaded function where no arm is selected is typed by the arms that the call can take at run time. With r declared real and G declared ((T) -> T where T: integer) & ((string) -> string), G(r) is typed integer, as with the ground form ((integer) -> integer) & ((string) -> string). It was typed string.

  • A sum or a product written with no bounds (\sum_k f, \prod_k f) runs over k = 1, 2, 3, … with every method: evaluate(), N(), simplify() and the derivative give the same result as for \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} f. Only N() did this before; evaluate() and simplify() kept the sum as it was. Now \sum_k \frac{1}{k^2} evaluates to \frac{\pi^2}{6}, \sum_k x^k to \frac{x}{1-x} when |x| < 1, \sum_k \frac{x^k}{k!} to e^x - 1, \sum_k k to \infty and \prod_k (1 + \frac{1}{k^2}) to \frac{\sinh(\pi)}{\pi}. \sum_k y stays as it is under evaluate() and simplify(), as \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} y does: its value depends on the sign of y. The derivative of \sum_k x^k is \frac{1}{(1-x)^2} when |x| < 1. The expression keeps its form with no bounds (\sum_{k}y is still written \sum_{k}y). A sum or a product with one bound only (\sum_{k=1} f) still stays unevaluated with every method.

  • A symbol whose name has a superscript part (__) is written in \operatorname{}, and reads back as the same symbol. Before, x__a was written x^{a}, which reads back as the power Power(x, a), and aleph__plus was written \aleph^{+}, which reads back as PseudoInverse(aleph). Now x__a is \operatorname{x^{a}} and aleph__plus is \operatorname{\aleph^{+}}. The superscripts and the subscripts are written in the order of the name, with a brace group where the order or valid LaTeX needs one: x__a_1 is \operatorname{x^{a}_1}, x_1__a is \operatorname{{x_1}^{a}} (it was x^{a}_1, the same as x__a_1), and two superscripts are nested, R_doublestruck__0__plus is \operatorname{{\mathbb{R}^0}^{+}} (it was \mathbb{R^{0,+}}, which does not parse). A style on the base stays on the base: x_bold__a is \operatorname{\mathbf{x}^{a}} (it was \mathbf{x^{a}}, which reads back as x__a_bold). A name with a base of more than one letter is written in \operatorname{} too: mass__earth is \operatorname{mass^{earth}} (it was \mathrm{mass^{earth}}, which also read back).

  • A wildcard name with a style or an accent reads back as the same name: the \_ is inside the style. _x_bold is \operatorname{\mathbf{\_x}} and _x_hat is \operatorname{\hat{\_x}} (they were \operatorname{\_\mathbf{x}} and \operatorname{\_\hat{x}}, which do not parse), and _x_1_bold is \operatorname{\mathbf{\_x_1}} (it was \operatorname{\_x_{\mathbf{1}}}, which reads back as _x_one_bold).

  • A name with a style on its base and a style after a subscript of digits reads back: x_bold_1_bold is \mathbf{\mathbf{x}_1} (it was \mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{1}}, which reads back as x_bold_one_bold). A name with two such subscripts is written in \operatorname{}: x_1_bold_1_bold is \operatorname{\mathbf{\mathbf{x_1}_1}}.

  • A symbol whose name has a subscript part that is a symbol (plus, minus, star, dag, circle, …) is written in \operatorname{}, and reads back as the same symbol. Before, x_plus was written x_{+}, which reads back as Subplus(x); x_1_plus was {x_1}_{+} (Subplus(x_1)), and x_a_dag was {x_{a}}_{\dag}, which is a parse error. Now they are \operatorname{x_{+}}, \operatorname{{x_1}_{+}} and \operatorname{{x_{a}}_{\dag}}. x_star is \operatorname{x_{\star}} (it was x_{\star}, which also read back). The operators do not change: Subplus(x) is still x_+. The parser reads \circ in a name as circle, so x_{\circ} is the symbol x_circle (it was a parse error).

  • A unicode escape in a symbol name stays in the part where it is: x_a____002012 (the parse of x_{a\unicode{"2012}}) is written x_{a\unicode{"2012}}. It was \operatorname{x\unicode{"2012}_{a}}, which reads back as x____002012_a. A subscript that starts with an escape, x_____002012, is written x_{\unicode{"2012}} (it was x^{,}_{002012}, which does not parse).

  • A name with the deg accent reads back: the parser reads \degree in the body of \mathrm{} or \operatorname{} as the accent, so \mathrm{x\degree} is the symbol x_deg (it was a parse error). Outside of a name, x\degree is still Degrees(x).

  • A subscript of digits with only the upright style is written without the style: x_1_upright is written x_1 (it was x_{\mathrm{1}}, which reads back as x_one). No spelling reads back as x_1_upright, and x_1 is the nearest name.

  • The term of Table is a function body: a name that a branch of the term assigns is read-before-declaration in a cell where the branch did not run (Table(Block(If(k = 2, h ≔ (z ↦ 2z)), h(k)), (k, 1, 3)) is [Error(…), 4, Error(…)]; it was [h(1), 4, h(3)]). The term of Sum and Product keeps its value from one index to the next, as before.

  • An assignment to a loop variable in the loop body changes it for the rest of that iteration only, and is no longer the scope effect: function g() { s = 0; for k in 1..2 { k = k * 10; s = s + k }; s } gives 30 (it was refused). Compiled code does not compile such a loop.

  • Compiled JavaScript and interval code throws read-before-declaration when a function-body local is read before any assignment gave it a value (after a branch that did not run), as the interpreter reports; it gave undefined. A read that follows an assignment on every path compiles without a check, and other targets refuse such a body.

  • In an Epsil function body, an assignment to a name that no enclosing scope declares makes a local of the whole body, also when the assignment is in a branch of an if, a loop body or a do block, as in Python: function g(c) { if c { t = 1 }; t } gives 1 for g(true) and the read-before-declaration error for g(false) (both gave the symbol t). A let in a nested block still declares a local of that block only, and a function literal owns the names of its own body. epsil check reports a read before the first assignment in a nested block, and does not report a read after an if that assigns in only one branch.

  • In a program evaluated as one block, a let of a library constant name (i, e, Pi, ExponentialE, …) shadows the constant only from its statement on: with function g() { i + 1 }, then let i = 2, g() gives 1 + i on every route (the block and compiled routes gave 3). A later let of a name that is not a constant is still visible to a function defined before it.

  • A negative integer power of an operand that can be a matrix stays a power: g(x)^{-1}, with g a function that was not declared, is Power(g(x), -1). It was the quotient 1/g(x), which is the element-wise reciprocal when g(x) is a matrix. When g(x) has a matrix value, the power is now the matrix inverse: with g returning [[2, 1], [1, 1]], g(x)^{-1} is [[1, -1], [-1, 2]] (it was [[1/2, 1], [1, 1]]). This applies to the call of a function that was not declared or that returns any, to a symbol declared any, and to a value of a type such as number | matrix. In a product with a matrix the power keeps its position: A·g(x)^{-1}·A stays as it is. The negative power of a scalar (x^{-1} for an undeclared symbol or a real symbol, \sin(x)^{-1}) and of a list of numbers is still a quotient (1/x), and the negative power of a matrix is still Inverse(M) or MatrixPower(M, -n). evaluate() and simplify() of a product keep the power: 2g(x)^{-1} stays 2g(x)^{-1} (it was 2/g(x)), and with the value above it is [[2, -2], [-2, 4]]. The quotient 1/g(x) is still a quotient. The LaTeX of the power is g(x)^{-1}, which reads back as the same power: y g(x)^{-1} is written yg(x)^{-1}, not \frac{y}{g(x)}. simplify() combines the integer powers of such an operand as evaluate() does: in a product with no matrix, f(x)^2 f(x)^{-1} is f(x) and f(x)^{-1} f(x)^{-1} is f(x)^{-2}; in a product with a matrix, only adjacent powers with exponents of the same sign are combined.

  • A power with the exponent 1 is its base for any base: g(x)^1 is g(x), and (f(x)^{-1})^{-1} is f(x) (it was f(x)^1, which evaluated to \sqrt[1]{f(x)}).

  • A sum of quantities where at least one operand is a temperature with an offset (degC or degF) now converts each operand to kelvin, with its offset, and adds the values in kelvin. The result is in K. Before, the result had the unit with the largest scale and the sum was wrong: Quantity(0, degC) + Quantity(0, degF) gave -17.78 degC; it is now 47567/90 K (273.15 K + 255.372… K = 528.522… K). An exact magnitude stays exact. The rule also applies when all the operands are in degC: 10 degC + 10 degC was 20 degC and is now 566.3 K (283.15 K + 283.15 K). A difference of two temperatures is the difference of their values in kelvin: 20 degC - 10 degC was 10 degC (which reads as 283.15 K) and is now 10 K; 20 degC - 10 degF was -3.33 degC and is now 290/9 K (32.22 K). A sum of temperatures with no offset (10 K + 10 K) does not change. A scalar multiple (2 · 10 degC) and a negation (-(10 degC)) are not changed: they keep the unit degC. So 20 degC - 2 · 10 degC is 20 degC - 20 degC, that is 0 K.

  • \sum_k y and \prod_k y, a sum or a product with no bounds whose body does not use the index, now keep their indexing clause in the canonical form: Sum(y, Limits(k, Nothing, Nothing)). They were y.

  • An Epsil program that is compiled, or evaluated as one Block, follows the order of its top-level statements for the names a function body owns: in function g(k) { t = k + 1; t }, then let t = 0, then [g(1), g(2), t], every route gives [2, 3, 0]. The compiled program gave [2, 3, 3], and the block evaluation gave the scope effect error. A read of a later name, and the order of declarations inside a nested block, do not change.

  • In a function body, a read of a name before the first assignment that makes it a local of the body is the read-before-declaration error, as for a let local read before its let: function g(k) { t = t + 1; t } gave t + 1 for g(1). Each call starts with no value for such a local, a loop body keeps the local from one turn to the next within a call, and a closure reads the local when it is called. epsil check reports the read before the program runs when the order is certain from the source. A block outside every function (a host Block, or a top-level do block or loop body) is not changed: Block(x ≔ x + 1; 2x) is still 2(x + 1). A call of a local that has no value yet is the same error: function g() { u = h(1); h = (x) => x; u } gave 1. A for loop whose collection evaluates to an error stops, and the error is its value (the loop ran no turn and the error was lost). epsil check also reports a let local used before its let when the order is certain from the source, and the run does not report the same use a second time.

  • A quantity with a dimensionless unit (percent, ppm, rad, deg, grad, turn, arcmin, arcsec) compares with a number as a value: 6 percent = 0.06, 180 deg = π and 30 deg = π/6 are True, and 6 percent < 0.07 is True (they stayed unevaluated). Two exact values are compared exactly, and a float within the tolerance. isEqual(), is(), isIdenticallyEqual(), the order methods, Equal, NotEqual, Less and the other relations, Max, Min, Sort and Clamp agree (Max(6 percent, 0.05) is 6 percent). A quantity with a logarithmic unit (dB, Np) is not compared with a number.

  • In LaTeX, a numeric constant expression written before a unit is a quantity: \pi\,\mathrm{rad} is Quantity(Pi, rad) (it was a product), and so are 10^{-30}\,\mathrm{rad}, \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{m}, \sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{m} and 2\pi\,\mathrm{rad}. A magnitude with a variable (x\,\mathrm{m}) is still a product.

  • The reciprocal and factor fraction styles no longer put a symbol, a number or a function in parentheses. a/b was a\times(b)^{-1} and \frac{1}{b}(a); it is now a\times b^{-1} and \frac{1}{b}a. In the reciprocal style the denominator gets parentheses where the base of a power does (a sum, a product, a power: a\times(2b)^{-1}). In the factor style the numerator gets parentheses where a factor of a product does (a sum, a negative value: \frac{1}{b}(a+c), \frac{1}{b}(-a)), and a numerator that starts with a digit gets an explicit \times (\frac{1}{3}\times2). A numerator 1 is no longer written in the factor style (\frac{1}{b}, not \frac{1}{b}(1)). The default style uses the factor style for a long numerator over a short denominator, so the default output changes too: \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{StieltjesGamma}(2)(x-1)^2. Every output parses back to the same value.

  • In Epsil, an assignment in a function body to a name that no enclosing scope declares when the function is defined makes a local of the function, with a new binding at each call. function g(k) { t = k + 1; t } then [g(1), g(2)] gives [2, 3]; the definition was refused with "writes outside a function require a declared scope effect". A declaration of the same name made later is not written: with let t = 0 after the function, [g(1), t] is [2, 0], also when t is declared by a later program on the same engine or with ce.assign(). An assignment to a name declared before the function (a top-level let or assignment, a parameter or a local of an enclosing function) still writes that binding and is the scope effect. A function defined before a top-level const does not write the constant, and epsil check does not report it; a function defined before a const of the same block is still reported.

  • Or, And, Nand, Nor, Implies, Any and All do not depend on the order of their operands when an operand fails. A True operand of Or or Nor, a False operand of And or Nand, a False antecedent or a True consequent of Implies, and a deciding element of Any or All decide the answer wherever they are, also after a failed operand: Or(1/"a" > 0, True) is True, as Or(True, 1/"a" > 0) already was, And(1, False) is False, and Any([1, 1/"a", 3], u ↦ u > 2) is True (they were the error). When no operand decides, the answer is the error of the first failed operand. Evaluation still stops at the first deciding operand, but the operands after a failed operand are now evaluated, with their side effects (also Epsil && and ||). Xor and Equivalent need every operand and are not changed. ForAll, Exists and ExistsUnique over a finite domain follow the same rule: Exists(x ∈ [1, 2], …) whose body fails at x = 2 and is False at x = 1 gives the error (it was False), Exists(x ∈ [1, 2], x > n) stays unevaluated (it was False), and ForAll over {1, 2, 3} and over [3, 2, 1] give the same answer.

  • Any and All over a source that is not known to be finite (Range(1, +oo), Repeat(5)) read at most iterationLimit elements (1024 by default) and then stay unevaluated, as IndexOf does. Before, a walk with no decision did not end; a decision after the limit, such as Any(Range(1, +oo), u ↦ u > 5000), was found after a long walk and now needs a larger ce.iterationLimit. A source known to be finite is still read to its end.

  • Two quantities whose units have different physical dimensions are not equal: 6 W = 6 m and 0 m = 0 s are False, 6 W ≠ 6 m is True, and isEqual() and isIdenticallyEqual() return false (they stayed unevaluated or gave undefined). A quantity with a dimension and a number are not equal either: 6 m = 6 is False, and a quantity is never equal to a string or a boolean (6 m = "a" and 6 percent = True are False). Order has no meaning across dimensions, so Less, isLess(), Max, Min, Sort and Clamp stay unevaluated for such operands. A unit that is not in the unit table, and a dimensionless quantity compared with a number (6 percent = 0.06), stay undecided.

  • In a block written in LaTeX, k \coloneq v still declares a local k. A new keyword, let (\operatorname{let}, \text{let}), writes a declaration with a type, \operatorname{let} s\colon integer\coloneq 1, and a declaration with no value, \operatorname{let} s. A bare Assign in a block, which changes a k outside the block, is written \mathrm{Assign}(k, v) and reads back without a Declare: it was written k\coloneq v, which read back as a local, so a LaTeX round trip left the outer k unchanged. A typed Declare in a block was dropped and is written with let. let also works in a where clause and in a row of a one-column cases block. A function defined as f(x)\coloneq\left(j\coloneq x; j\right) has the block as its body; the body was a block inside a block. \mathrm{let} is now a keyword, so a symbol named let is read as one, as if and where already are. After let, = is also the assignment, as in Epsil (\operatorname{let} k = 2), and a type that is not one (\operatorname{let} s\colon\mathbb{Z}) is an invalid-type error. A name is declared once per block: x\coloneq 1; x\coloneq x+1; x is 2 (it was a variable-redeclaration error). The rows of a one-column cases block are read as a ; list is, so a k\coloneq v row declares a local k (it changed the k outside).

  • Assigning a value to a constant has a stable error code, and epsil check reports it. ce.assign() and the Assign operator still throw Cannot assign a value to the constant "c", and the error now has code: 'constant-assignment' and constantName. In Epsil, const c = 1 then c = 2 is reported before the program runs, as a static error with the code constant-assignment and a note on the const; before, epsil check reported nothing and the run reported a runtime-error whose code was the message text. The check covers a const of the program at any depth and each name of a destructuring const, wherever the assignment is, also in the body of a function defined before the const. A let, a parameter or a loop variable that shadows the constant is not reported. The run reports each assignment once: it does not repeat an assignment that the check reported, and it reports an assignment that the check could not see, such as an assignment to a library constant (Pi) or to a constant of an earlier program. The error value is ["Error", ["ErrorCode", "constant-assignment", "c"]].

  • A unit has one canonical form: its unit symbols with exact exponents, those with a positive exponent over those with a negative exponent, in the canonical order. Quantity arithmetic, Quantity, UnitConvert and the LaTeX parser give this form, so an evaluated quantity and the parse of its LaTeX are the same expression: (4 m)^(-1/2) is Quantity(1/2, Divide(1, Sqrt(m))) (it was Power(Power(m, 1/2), -1)), (m/s)^2 is m^2/s^2, and m^(2/3)·m^(2/3) is m^(4/3) (it was m^1.3333333333333333). The unit of AvogadroConstant is Divide(1, mol), and the text form writes a reciprocal unit with a negative exponent (3 m^-1).

  • Quantity arithmetic keeps the units it combines and no longer replaces them with a named derived unit: (2 V)·(3 A) is 6 A·V (it was 6 W), (2 N)·(3 m) is 6 N·m (it was 6 J), and (1 J)/(1 kg) stays J/kg. UnitSimplify still gives the named unit (UnitSimplify(6 A·V) is 6 W), and equality is not changed: 6 A·V equals 6 W.

  • A List or Set literal that keeps a failed cell ([1, Error(…), 3]) is typed list<unknown> (it was error, so a variable that held it was a scalar): with fs := [Error(…)], ListJoin(fs, [2]) is [Error(…), 2] (it was [[Error(…)], 2]), and a variable declared list accepts the value. An absent cell keeps its arm: [Error(…), Missing] is typed list<unknown | missing>.

  • A List or Set that holds a failed cell can be iterated. In Epsil, with g(x) = 1/x and xs = [1, g("a"), 3], a for loop runs one turn for each cell, and Map, Filter, a comprehension and an arithmetic broadcast give the failed cell to the body as the value of that element: map((u) => u + 1, xs) is [2, Error(…), 4]. Before, the loop ran no turn, Map returned the list unchanged, and the comprehension stayed unevaluated. Length and Count give the number of cells (3), and First, At, Reverse and Take keep the failed cell in its position. An operator that needs the value of every cell gives the error of the failed cell: Sum, Product, Max, Min, Mean and the other statistics, Sort, ArgMax and MaxBy. A comprehension guard that fails on an element keeps the error in that position, as Filter does; before, the element was removed. The same rules apply when the failed cell is a list that holds the error: Mean([[1, 1/"a"], 2]) is the error, and Map(u ↦ 1, [[1, 1/"a"], [3]]) is [1, 1]. Membership and equality give the error when the answer depends on a failed cell: 2 ∈ [1, 1/"a"] and [1, 1/"a"] = [1, 1/"a"] are the error, while 1 ∈ [1, 1/"a"] is True and [1, 1/"a"] = [2, 1/"a"] is False. The equality of two collections first checks the facts that decide the equality of valid collections (a set and a list, different counts, a finite and an infinite collection), then reads the cells only as far as needed, so [1, 1/"a"] = Range(1, 10^12) is False. IndexOf, Count with a value, Union, Intersection, SetMinus and SymmetricDifference follow the same rule. Unique, Tally and Dedup follow it when there is another element to compare: Dedup([1, 1/"a", 1]) is the error, because whether a neighbor is a duplicate depends on the value of the failed cell, while Unique([1/"a"]) is [1/"a"]. The list still carries its error (isValid is false), and it still does not compile. A Tuple or Dictionary with a failed cell is not changed.

  • A point divided by a matrix is the matrix of the point divided by each cell, as a point times a matrix is: (1, 2) / [[1, 2], [3, 4]] is [[(1, 2), (1/2, 1)], [(1/3, 2/3), (1/4, 1/2)]] (it stayed unevaluated and was typed number).

  • isGreater, isGreaterEqual, isLess, isLessEqual and the operators Greater, GreaterEqual, Less, LessEqual read the range of a declared type: with p: integer<0..>, p.isGreaterEqual(0) and p ≥ 0 are true (they were undefined). A float within the tolerance of a number is not ordered strictly against it: ce.number(1e-12).isGreater(0) is false, as isEqual(0) is true (it was true); an exact value is still ordered exactly (10^{-30} > 0).

Resolved Issues​

  • A Table whose term assigns a variable gives its list in a function body too: Apply(Function(Block(Table(Block(Assign(a, k), a), (k, 1, 3))))) gave an unevaluated Tabulate(…), and gives [1, 2, 3], as at the top level.

  • A closure created in a branch or a loop body of a function, whose own body assigns a name, is no longer refused with the scope effect error: its body keeps its own locals.

  • A numeric type with an excluded bound excludes it when a value is checked: with g declared (real<0<..>) -> real, g(0) is an incompatible-type error (it gave a value), on evaluate(), .N() and a symbol holding 0; the compiled JavaScript call gives NaN and the interval call gives empty.

  • A compiled call of a function whose parameter has a declared type agrees with the interpreter. With let g: (integer) -> integer then function g(k) { k + 1 } (or g = (k) => k + 1), the compiled g(1.5) gave 2.5 where the interpreter gives an incompatible-type error, and g(x) with x = 1.5 did the same. An argument that cannot be of the declared type now fails the compilation. An argument whose type is not proven is tested when the code runs: the JavaScript call gives NaN and the interval call gives empty for a value outside the type. The GLSL, WGSL and Python targets, which have no such test, refuse the call when the type allows only some real numbers (an integer type, a bounded real type, rational). An argument whose type is declared, or a constant, compiles with no test.

  • A product of a number and a number to a negative integer power, such as 3·10^-30, (3/7)·10^-30 or 3·2^-3, is written so that it parses back to the same expression (3\times(10^{-30}), \frac{3}{7}\times10^{-30}, 3\times2^{-3}). It was written \frac{3}{10^{30}}, which parses back as a rational.

  • A product nested in a product that has a matrix keeps the order of its factors. With A a matrix and g, k functions that were not declared, ['Multiply', 'A', ['Multiply', g(x), k(x), g(x)]], A\cdot(g(x)\cdot k(x)\cdot g(x)) and A(g(x)k(x)g(x)) were A·k(x)·g(x)·g(x), because the nested product was sorted on its own before the matrix was seen. They are now A·g(x)·k(x)·g(x), like the product written without the nesting. A negation of a nested product and a nested product divided by an integer are spliced too: A\cdot(-g(x)k(x)) is -(A·g(x)·k(x)). A product with no factor that can be a matrix has the same canonical form as before, and a juxtaposition in parentheses that is not a product (a mixed number such as A(2\frac{1}{3}), an imaginary number such as A(2i)) is read as before.

  • Parsing a nested juxtaposition in parentheses takes a time proportional to its depth. (g(x)(g(x)(…)A)A)A with 8 levels took about 7 seconds, because each level was made canonical several times.

  • The empty numerator of a product whose factors are all negative powers is written 1: x^{-1}y^{-1} in raw form is \frac{1}{xy}, not \frac{}{xy}.

  • On the glsl and wgsl targets, the product of the imaginary unit and a complex value is a rotation of that value: iz with z complex compiles to vec2(-z.y, z.x), i\tanh(z) to _gpu_cmul(vec2(0.0, 1.0), _gpu_ctanh(z)) and t + i\tanh(z) adds the two complex terms. They compiled to vec2(0.0, z), vec2(0.0, _gpu_ctanh(z)) and vec2(t, _gpu_ctanh(z)), and a shader vec2 constructor reads only the first component of a vec2 argument, so the value was (0, Re w) where i·w is (−Im w, Re w). The product with a real value (it is vec2(0.0, t)) is unchanged.

  • A negative base under a decimal exponent, or a decimal root degree, that reads as a rational with an odd denominator compiles to the real signed root on every target, as it evaluates: x^{\frac{1}{2.2}} (5/11) at x = −1 is −1 on javascript, interval-js (_IA.powRational(x, 5, 11); it answered an empty interval), glsl, wgsl and python, and \sqrt[2.2]{x} gives the same (it compiled to Math.pow, NaN for a negative x), and \sqrt[2.5]{x} (x^0.4, an even numerator) compiles to the positive real |x|^{0.4}. The compiled code uses the exponent reading of the interpreter, so an exponent such as 0.3 keeps its complex value. On interval-js the rational power is used only when the literal is the double of that rational (0.6, 1/2.2); a literal that is not (0.6000000000000001) keeps the previous lowering. In the interpreter, Root of a negative radicand under a non-integer degree is a^(1/b) as Power reads it: Root(-8, 0.5) is 64 (it was −64), Root(-8, 2.5) is (-8)^{2/5} = 2.297 (it was −2.297) and Root(-8, 2.4) is the complex principal value.

  • At with a NaN, indeterminate or infinite member in a list index gives the hole in that member's slot and reads the other members: At([10, 20, 30], [NaN, 1]) is [NaN, 10] and At([(1, 2), (3, 4)], [NaN, 1]) is [Missing, (1, 2)], the same hole an out-of-range member gives. The call stayed unevaluated. The compiled javascript _SYS.at agrees (it gave a whole-result NaN).

  • A compiled Epsil program checks a function definition against the effects that an earlier declaration of its name states: with let g: (integer) pure -> real then function g(k) { Random() }, the compilation is refused, as the interpreter refuses the definition (incompatible-type). The compiled program ran the definition.

  • A call argument that is a symbol declared without a value in the caller's scope keeps that declaration when the function body is evaluated: with g := a ↦ a·x and c := 5 in the global scope, after pushScope() and declare("c", "real"), g(c) is c·x (it was 5x), and with declare("i", "real") in the pushed scope, g(i) is i·x (it was ImaginaryUnit·x). A call frame's parent is the scope that defined the function, so the body's read of the argument found the outer c or the library i by name. A free symbol of the body still reads the definition scope, and a loop or sum index still reads by name.

  • A symbol with two or more subscripts is written with nested subscripts, so it reads back as the same symbol. The symbol x_1_2 (the parse of x_1_2, of {x_1}_2, and the canonical form of Subscript(Subscript(x, 1), 2)) is now written {x_1}_2; it was x_{1,2}, which reads back as Subscript(x, Sequence(1, 2)). Three subscripts give {{x_1}_2}_3. A name with an upright base keeps the second subscript outside the \mathrm{}: speed_1_2 is {\mathrm{speed_1}}_2 (it was \mathrm{speed_{1,2}}, which did not parse). A name with digits before a subscript keeps them in the name: x1_2 is \mathrm{x1_2} (it was x_{1,2}). A single subscript (x_1, x_{12}), a subscript with a comma list typed as x_{1,2}, and a matrix element (M[1, 2]) are written as before. A name whose base is an indexed collection does not read back in either spelling: with A a matrix, the symbol A_1_2 is written {A_1}_2, which reads back as Subscript(At(A, 1), 2) (A_{1,2} read back as At(A, 1, 2)).

  • A symbol with a style and a subscript reads back as the same symbol. \mathbf{x}_1 (the symbol x_bold_1) was written \mathbf{x_1}, which reads back as the different symbol x_1_bold; it is now written \mathbf{x}_1, and x_bold_1_2 is written {\mathbf{x}_1}_2. The parse of \mathbf{x_1}, the symbol x_1_bold, was written x_{\mathbf{1}}, which reads back as x_one_bold; it is now written \mathbf{x_1}, and x_1_2_bold is written \mathbf{{x_1}_2}. The other styles work the same way (\mathit, \mathbb, \mathcal, …). The upright style is the exception for a style after a digit subscript: x_1_upright is still written x_{\mathrm{1}}, which does not read back.

  • Two braced subscripts inside \mathrm{}, \mathbf{} or \operatorname{} are two parts of the name: \mathrm{x_{1}_{2}} is the symbol x_1_2, as x_{1}_{2} is. It was x_12. The body of such a command can also start with a brace group that has its own subscripts: \mathbf{{x_1}_2} is the symbol x_1_2_bold.

  • A sum or a product written with no bounds (\sum_k x^k, which is Sum(x^k, Limits(k, Nothing, Nothing))) is no longer read as a sum over the single point k = Nothing: \sum_k x^{k-1} evaluated to \frac{1}{x}, \sum_k x^k and \prod_k x^k to an error, and \sum_k y and \prod_k y became y. It runs over k = 1, 2, 3, …; see the entry about sums with no bounds under "Behavior Changes". simplify() keeps a sum or a product with one bound only as it is: \sum_{k=1} k gave \frac{1}{2}.

  • \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^k}{k!} evaluates to e^x - 1. It was e^x - x^0, which has no value at x = 0, where the sum is 0. The same applies to the sum from any lower bound above 0.

  • simplify() of a geometric series with an infinite upper bound and a free ratio keeps the sum as it is: \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} x^k simplified to \frac{x - x^{\infty}}{1 - x}, and x^{\infty} is not a value. evaluate() still gives \frac{x}{1-x} when |x| < 1. With a number ratio the closed form still applies: \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} (\frac{1}{2})^k simplifies to 2.

  • simplify() of a sum or a product over an infinite range (\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} f, or \sum_k f with no bounds) no longer puts the infinite bound into a closed form when the result depends on a symbol of unknown sign or has no value:

    • \sum_k 0 simplified to Indeterminate; it is 0, also under evaluate().
    • \sum_k y simplified to \infty \cdot y, which is wrong for y = 0; it stays as it is. A body of known sign gives \infty or -\infty (\sum_k 3 is \infty).
    • \prod_k 1 simplified to Indeterminate; it is 1. A product of a constant c is the limit of c^n: 0 for |c| < 1, \infty for c > 1. evaluate() and N() now give the same values (\prod_k \frac{1}{2} is 0; it stayed unevaluated). For c ≤ -1, and for a free body (\prod_k y simplified to y^{\infty}), the product stays as it is. The comparison with 1 uses no tolerance: an exact number is compared exactly, and a float within the engine tolerance of 1 (1.000000000001) keeps the product as it is, since the float does not tell on which side of 1 the value is. A body that is not pure (\mathrm{Random}()) is not compared, and an empty range (k from \infty to 5) is not read as an infinite one.
    • \sum_k (1 + xk) simplified to \infty, which is wrong for x < 0, and \sum_k kx to \infty \cdot x; both stay as they are. With no free symbol the closed form still applies: \sum_k (1 + 2k) is \infty.
    • \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} (-1)^k simplified to Indeterminate; it stays as it is, as under evaluate().

  • simplify() of a geometric series with an exact ratio keeps it exact: \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})^k simplified to the float 2.414…; it is now 1 + \sqrt{2}, as under evaluate(). The finite form \sum_{k=0}^{n} (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})^k keeps the exact ratio too.

  • The derivative of a sum over an infinite range is no longer the series of the derivatives when that series has no closed form: the derivative of \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{\sin(kx)}{k} was \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \cos(kx), which diverges, while the derivative is -\frac{1}{2} on (0, 2\pi). It now stays unevaluated. A sum with a closed form is differentiated through it: the derivative of \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^k}{k!} is e^x, and the derivative of \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} x^{k-1} is \frac{1}{(1-x)^2} when |x| < 1. explain('D') shows the rewrite of the sum to its closed form as a step before the steps of its derivative. A finite range is still differentiated term by term.

  • compile() of a sum or a product with no bounds reports the infinite upper bound, as for \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} f. It reported that the Nothing marker cannot be read as a variable. Both fall back to the interpreter.

  • simplify() of a sum or a product with more than one indexing clause no longer reads the second index as a free symbol and drops its clause: Sum(i·j, Limits(i, 1, 3), Limits(j, 1, 2)) gave 6j. It now stays as it is under simplify(), and evaluate() still gives 18.

  • Reading a variable whose value is an expression with no canonical form (r = Map(t, (x) => x * 2), with the arguments in the wrong order) no longer loops forever: it gives the same result as the expression written in place.

  • In a comprehension, an element that does not match a tuple pattern ([p + q for (p, q) in [(1, 2), 5, (3, 4)]]) is the incompatible-type error in its position, and the other elements are kept ([3, Error(…), 7]); the comprehension stopped at that element. A for loop still stops on it.

  • A trigonometric function of an angle quantity with an exact magnitude is exact: \sin(30\,\mathrm{deg}) evaluates to 1/2 (it was 0.4999999999999999), because the angle is converted with the exact factor of its unit (30 deg is π/6).

  • A comprehension whose domain evaluates to an error has that error as its value: Length, Count, Sum and an element read of it give the error.

  • An Epsil function declared with a type and then defined (let g: (integer) -> integer, then function g(k) { k + 1 }) compiles on JavaScript and interval-js and gives the interpreter's value; the compilation failed with Unknown operator \g``.

  • Compiled code refuses a named function definition that the interpreter refuses because of its effects: a body that writes a variable declared before the function without the scope effect, or a body whose effects are not in the stated effects (pure). With let t = 0 before function g(k) { t = k + 1; t }, the compiled program gave [2, 2] for [g(1), t]; it now fails with the interpreter's message, on every target.

  • A quantity whose compound unit cancels is the plain number of its magnitude: ["Quantity", 2, ["Divide", "m", "m"]] and 2\,\mathrm{m/m} are 2 (they were Quantity(2, 1), written \mathrm{Quantity}(2, 1)). A named unit (percent, rad) and a compound unit that does not cancel (in/ft) stay units.

  • A number raised to a negative integer is written as a power in LaTeX: 10^{-30} and 2^{-3} (they were \frac{1}{1\cdot10^{30}} and \frac{1}{8}), and the LaTeX parses back as the same expression.

  • isEqual(), is(), isIdenticallyEqual() and the order methods compare a quantity whose magnitude is an expression with no unknowns by its value, as Equal does: Quantity(2, m).isEqual(Quantity(1.5 + 0.5, m)) is true (it was undefined).

  • Quantity arithmetic and unit conversion of float magnitudes use the working precision: (π·(1 rad)).N() is 3.14159265358979323846 rad (it was 3.141592653589793 rad), and 1.1 m + 1.3 cm is 1.113 m. At precision = 'machine', machine numbers are used as before.

  • Two quantities with different logarithmic units are not equal: 1 dB = 1 Np was True, because both units have a nominal scale of 1.

  • A mixed number such as 2\frac{1}{3} is read only when the integer, the numerator and the denominator are exact integers: 2\frac{1.0}{3} and 2.0\frac{1}{3} are the inexact product 2/3, and a float numerator keeps all its digits when it is serialized.

  • Serializing a juxtaposition no longer changes its value when a factor-style fraction that ends in a digit comes before a fraction (\frac{1}{x}\times3\times\frac{1}{2}), or when a negative fraction follows another factor (2(-\frac{3}{4}); it was 2-\frac{3}{4}, which reads back as 5/4).

  • The subscript of a function application written as a name with parentheses ((g(x+1))_{k}, (\Gamma(x))_{1}), or of a base that ends in a superscript ((\exponentialE^{x})_{1}, (f^{\prime})_{1}), is written in parentheses, so it reads back as written. g(x+1)_{k} read back as g·(x+1)_k.

  • An argument whose value is an error gives that error at every parameter type. With let w = Ln("a"), function op(a: unknown) { a } and op(w) gave a new error, "expected unknown, got error at w". So did a parameter typed as a collection (list, tuple<…>) or as function, a parameter typed by a type variable with a bound (Conjugate(w), Remainder(w, 2), a function declared (T) -> T where T: number), and the condition of if and Which. A function with several clauses (op(a: number), op(a: string)) gave "expected number | string, got error". The callback of a collection operator gave "expected function, got error": Any(xs, w), All(xs, w), Filter(xs, w), Reduce(xs, w), Scan(xs, w), TakeWhile(xs, w), MaxBy(xs, w) and Map(w, xs). The call now evaluates to the error of Ln, with the frame of the call, as it already did for a parameter typed number or with no type, and for Sort(xs, w). An element read directly (Map(w, xs).at(1), a walk of Filter(xs, w)) is that error too. An operator that binds or reads such an operand as an expression is not changed: Integrate(w, Limits(w, 0, 1)) is still 1/2. An argument of the wrong type is still refused, and Map(w, f), with the arguments in the wrong order, still reports the wrong order.

  • A symbol declared error that has no value, and a call typed error only by its declared result type (g(2) with g: (number) -> error), are checked by the same rule at a parameter typed by a type variable as at a ground parameter. Neither holds an error value, so the call evaluates to itself. Conjugate(e) and a function declared (T) -> T where T: number applied to e gave "expected number, got error"; they are now valid, as Sqrt(e) and a function declared (number) -> number applied to e are. The condition of If and Which admits them too, as a parameter typed boolean does, and selects no branch. A collection parameter (list, or a type variable bounded by a collection) still refuses them, and so does an overloaded function, with ground or generic arms.

  • Map(f, xs) with a callback known to be a function with no known result type (f declared function), or with a symbol that holds an error, is typed with unknown elements: Map(f, [1, 2]) is list<unknown^2>. It was typed as the source, vector<integer^2>. A callback that is not declared still gives the type of the source.

  • An integer followed by a fraction is read as a mixed number only when the numerator and the denominator of the fraction are number literals. 2\frac{1+1}{3} was read as 2 + 2/3; it is now the product 4/3, as 2\frac{x}{3} is a product. 2\frac{1}{3} is still 7/3. A mixed number in raw form (["InvisibleOperator", 2, ["Divide", 1, 3]]) is written 2\frac{1}{3} with every fraction style; with the reciprocal style it was 2\times3^{-1}, which reads back as 2/3.

  • In a product that has a matrix, a factor that can be a matrix keeps its position. This covers the call of a function that was not declared (g(A), g(x)), a symbol declared any, and a value of a type such as number | matrix. Before, such a factor was sorted in front of the matrices, and the powers of a matrix on each side of it were merged: with A a 2×2 matrix, A·g(A)·A evaluated to A^2·g(A), and A^2·g(A)·A^3 to A^5·g(A). Both are wrong when g returns a matrix that does not commute with A. evaluate(), simplify() and Expand now keep A·g(A)·A. A quotient whose denominator can be a matrix also keeps its position, because the quotient is element-wise: (A/g(x))·A evaluated to A^2/g(x), A·(1/g(x))·g(x)·A to A^2, and, with B a matrix, (A/B)·A to A^2/B. Factors of a scalar type (real, integer, an undeclared symbol) still move to the front, and a product with no matrix is unchanged.

  • Expand does not distribute a product with a matrix over a sum that has a scalar term. The sum of a matrix and a scalar adds the scalar to each element, so A·(B + r) is not A·B + r·A: Expand(A·(B + r)) gave A·B + A·r, and now stays A·(B + r). A sum of matrices is still distributed, and each term keeps the order of its factors: Expand(A·(B + C)·g(x)) is A·B·g(x) + A·C·g(x).

  • In Epsil, the source range of an expression includes the parentheses of its operands. The range of (a) + (b) was a) + (b, and the range of the statement let v = (1) + (2) ended before the last ), so an error reported on that statement did not underline the last ). This applies to every operator, call, member access, index, if … else, is, loop collection, comprehension and pattern with a parenthesized operand. A single parenthesized expression (a) keeps the range of a.

  • In Epsil, an error in an operand of a call that canonicalization reorders is underlined on the right operand. With let w: any = "s", the statement let v = Ln(w) * 2 underlined 2, because Ln(w) * 2 is 2·Ln(w) in canonical form; it now underlines Ln(w). This also applies to a library operator such as Xor and to a user function marked commutative or associative: with w = Ln("a") and op commutative, op(z, w) underlined z. When the operand is not sure, as in Ln(w) + Ln(w), the whole call is underlined.

  • A function marked commutative or associative passes an error value through, as the same function without the word does. With w = Ln("a") and function op(a, b) commutative { [a, b] }, op(z, w) gave a new error, "expected unknown, got error", in place of the error of Ln. A parameter without a type is now checked as any at the call, as it is without the word.

  • In the unit argument of the siunitx commands \qty, \SI, \unit and \si, a . or a ~ between two units is a product of the units, as in siunitx. \qty{3}{m.s^{-1}} and \qty{3}{m~s^{-1}} are the quantity 3 m/s, the same as \qty{3}{m\cdot s^{-1}}, and \qty{3}{kg.m^2.s^{-2}} is 3 kg·m²/s². The . form gave parse errors, and the ~ form gave 3 per millisecond. A decimal point in an exponent (\qty{2}{m^{1.5}}) is not a separator, and a space is still not a product: \qty{3}{m s^{-1}} is 3 per millisecond, as LaTeX prints it.

  • A siunitx unit argument that is not a unit gives an unknown-unit error with the text of the argument: \qty{3}{foo} is ["Quantity", 3, ["Error", "'unknown-unit'", ["LatexString", "'foo'"]]]. It was an unexpected-command error on \qty, and the arguments were parsed as a list.

  • The derivative of a sum or a product is computed. It stayed unevaluated: \frac{d}{dx}\sum_{k=1}^{3} k x^k gave the same expression back, and now gives 9x^2 + 4x + 1. A sum is differentiated term by term when its bounds do not depend on the variable, also with a symbolic or infinite bound: \frac{d}{dx}\sum_{k=0}^{n} x^k is \sum_{k=0}^{n} k x^{k-1}. A product with integer bounds and at most 24 factors is expanded, then differentiated: \frac{d}{dx}\prod_{k=1}^{2} (x+k) is 2x + 3. A product with a symbolic bound or more factors stays unevaluated. When the index of the sum or product is the variable (\frac{d}{dx}\sum_{x=1}^{3} x), the derivative is 0. When a bound depends on the variable, the derivative stays unevaluated.

  • A fraction written with the nice-solidus fraction style reads back as the same division. ce.parse('x/10').toLatex({ fractionStyle: () => 'nice-solidus' }) gives {}^{x}\!\!/\!{}_{10}, and parsing this LaTeX gave Superscript(Error('missing'), x); it now gives Divide(x, 10). The parser reads only this exact shape as a division: {}^{a}, any number of \!, /, any number of \!, {}_{b}. A {}^{a} or a {}_{b} alone keeps its reading.

  • The base of a subscript is written in parentheses when it is compound, as the base of a power is, so the LaTeX reads back as the same expression. Subscript(x+1, 2) was written x+1_{2}, which reads back as x + BaseForm(1, 2); it is now written (x+1)_{2}. A product, a negation, a negative number, a power, a fraction and a factorial are also fenced: (2x)_{1}, (-2)_{k}, (x^2)_{1}, (\frac{x}{y})_{1}.

  • The limit at infinity of a difference of two radicals that grow at the same rate has a value: \lim_{t\to\infty} (\sqrt{t+1} - \sqrt{t}) is 0, and \sqrt{t^2+3t} - \sqrt{t^2+t} gives 1 (they stayed unevaluated). The same is true for a radical minus a term that grows at the same rate: \sqrt{t^2+t} - t gives 1/2 at +\infty, \sqrt{t^2+t} + t gives -1/2 at -\infty, and \sqrt[3]{t^3+t^2} - t gives 1/3. The limit code multiplies the difference by its conjugate, \sqrt{u} - \sqrt{v} = (u - v)/(\sqrt{u} + \sqrt{v}). A difference that grows without bound, such as \sqrt{2t} - \sqrt{t}, still gives +\infty. The limit of an absolute value at infinity also has a value: \sqrt{t^2+1} is +\infty (it stayed unevaluated) and |(1 - 2t)/(t + 3)| is 2. A limit at infinity whose value is a ratio of radicals is exact: \lim_{t\to\infty} \frac{\sqrt{2t^2+1}}{t} is \sqrt{2} and \lim_{t\to-\infty} \frac{\sqrt{3t^2+1}}{t+1} is -\sqrt{3} (they were the floats 1.414… and -1.732…).

  • A limit at infinity of the form x·f(c/x) is exact: \lim_{x\to\infty} x\ln(1+\frac{\pi}{x}) is π (it was the float 3.14159265356268, with wrong last digits), x\sin(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{x}) is \sqrt{2}, x^2(1-\cos(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{x})) is 3/2 (it was 1.4999999839369884), and x(e^{1/x}-1) is 1 (it stayed unevaluated). The limit code reads the value from the series of the function with x = 1/u at u = 0. evaluate() no longer returns a float for a limit whose value it cannot find exactly: the limit stays unevaluated, and .N() gives the float.

  • Whole-number powers of one matrix combine. With A declared matrix<2x2>, A^2 A^3 evaluates and simplifies to MatrixPower(A, 5), and A A^2 to MatrixPower(A, 3) (they stayed products, such as MatrixPower(A, 2) * MatrixPower(A, 3)). A^2 A^2 is MatrixPower(A, 4) (it was MatrixPower(MatrixPower(A, 2), 2)), and (A^2)^3 is MatrixPower(A, 6). Only positive whole-number exponents combine, and only for powers that no other matrix separates, because the product of matrices is not commutative: A^2 B A^3 stays as it is. A^2 A^{-1} stays as it is too, because A^2 A^{-1} = A is true only when A is invertible.

  • Solve answers an equation with a trig function of a periodic argument, such as sin(sin(x)) = 0. Such an equation is periodic, with the period of the inner trig function. Solve(sin(sin(x)) = 0, x) is [πt], ce.parse('\sin(\sin(x))=0').solve('x') is [0, π], and over [-7, 7] the roots are -2π, -π, 0, π, 2π (there was no answer since 0.148.0). An equation with no real root gives the empty list: cos(sin(x)) = 0 is [], because |sin(x)| ≤ 1 < π/2. The solver uses each period of the outer function that the inner sin or cos reaches: sin(4·sin(x)) = 0 holds for 4·sin(x) = 0, π and -π, and the roots of sin(x) = -π/4 are now in the answer. A scan of one period with an interval proof checks each list. tan(4·sin(x)) = 1 and cot(4·sin(x)) = 1 are answered the same way, with the half-turn period of tan and cot. When the inner function reaches so many periods of the outer one that more than 16 roots would be added, there is no answer, and it comes quickly (sin(200·sin(x)) = 1/3, sin(1000·sin(x)) = 0). A trig function of an argument that is not periodic (sin(x²) = 0, sin(eˣ) = 0) still gives no answer.

  • For an unknown declared real, a root written with arcsin or arccos of a constant in [-1, 1] is kept. With x declared real, sin(x) = arccos(9/10) gives [arcsin(arccos(9/10)), π − arcsin(arccos(9/10))], and cos(sin(x)) = 9/10 gives its four roots; both gave no answer, because the type of arcsin(c) is complex when it does not use the value of c. sin(x) = 2 still gives [].

  • Solve(cos(x)^2 = 1/9, x) is [πt − arccos(1/3), πt + arccos(1/3)] (it stayed unevaluated). The roots -arccos(-1/3) and arccos(1/3) − π are in the same family, but their difference did not evaluate to 0: the solver now uses arccos(-c) = π − arccos(c) to compare them.

  • expr.solve() no longer lists one root twice for a periodic equation. It gives one root of each family in one period, but sin(x) = -1 gave [-π/2, 3π/2] and 3cos(x) + 3 = 0 gave [π, -π], two roots that differ by the period 2π. They now give [-π/2] and [π]: of two roots that differ by a multiple of the period, the first one is kept. expr.explain('solve') gives the same list, with a step that names each root it removes.

  • subs() reads only the own properties of the substitution object. A symbol named like a property of a JavaScript object, such as constructor or toString, was replaced by that inherited property: ce.box(["Add", "x", "constructor"]).subs({ x: 1 }) gave "Undefined" + 1. It now gives constructor + 1.

  • A comprehension or a lazy collection that calls a parameter or a local function applies that function after it leaves the function or block that made it: function g(f) { [f(x) for x in [1, 2]] } applied to (a) => a + 1 gives [2, 3], and so does do { let f = (a) => a + 1; [f(x) for x in [1, 2]] }; both stayed unevaluated. A map or filter callback that calls a parameter works the same way, also when the collection is passed to a function that has a parameter with the same name (it used that other function). A call of a function parameter inside a Sum, a Product or a comprehension in a function body calls the parameter: (g) ↦ Σ_{k=1}^{3} g(k) applied to a ↦ a + 1 is 9 (it was g(1) + g(2) + g(3)), and Σ_{k=1}^{3} h(k) uses a function h assigned after the sum was written.

  • A comprehension over library functions or pure user functions prints its elements: [f(0) for f in [Sin, Cos]] prints [0, 1].

  • In LaTeX, a bracket pair of two function literals after \in is a list, not an interval: \prod_{q\in [a\mapsto a+1, a\mapsto 2a]} q(3) is 24.

  • In a function body, an assignment in an if branch to a local that a later statement of the body assigns writes that local: with function g(k) { if k > 1 { t = 5 }; t = t + 1; t }, g(2) is 6 (it was t + 1).

  • A function held by the index of a comprehension is applied where the index is the callback of a lazy collection operator: [Map(q, [1]) for q in [a ↦ a + 1]] is [[2]] (it was [[q(1)]]), and Filter([1, 2], q) with the same kind of index no longer throws. A call of such an index in an inner comprehension uses the function of its own element, also when the elements are read in another order. Evaluating a comprehension whose index is called like a function, such as [k(1) for k in [a ↦ 0, a ↦ 1]], no longer declares k in the global scope.

  • A view whose callback holds an error under a selection, such as Map(u ↦ If(u = 2, 1/"a", u), Range(1, 5)), is a collection whose second element is the error: Sum and Mean over it give the error, Length gives 5 and First gives 1. Before, Sum gave back the view itself and Length stayed unevaluated.

  • A pipe into Map over a list with a failed cell gives the same value as the direct call: [1, 1/"a", 3] |> Map(f, _) and Apply(z ↦ Map(f, z), [1, 1/"a", 3]) stayed an unevaluated Map, and a loop over that value ran no turn. Substituting such a list with subs() also keeps the expression bound. In Epsil, a statement whose value is a map or filter over a list literal with a failed cell, such as let ys = map((u) => u, [1, g("a"), 3]), is reported as a runtime-error; a cell with an effect is not evaluated for this check.

  • Angle quantities with exact magnitudes compare exactly. The scale of deg, grad, turn, arcmin and arcsec is a rational multiple of π, so 180 deg = π rad is True with no rounding, and 1 deg < (π/180 + 10^-30) rad is True (it was False, a tie within the tolerance). A quantity in daltons compares exactly with the value stored in the unit table (CODATA 2018). Unit conversion results do not change.

  • In Epsil, a failed cell in the collection of a for loop or comprehension header is reported. With g(x) = 1/x, for x in [1, g("a"), 3] { n = n + 1 } ran 3 turns and reported nothing, because the body does not use x and a header is not a statement. The loop still runs 3 turns, and the list gets a runtime-error with the same message and code as the statement let xs = [1, g("a"), 3]. Each header is reported once, also in a nested loop or in a function that is called more than once. A header that is a variable (for x in xs) is not reported again, because the statement that gave xs its value is. A comprehension header is reported when the program reads the list.

  • A tuple whose type has an absent slot, such as a symbol declared tuple<integer, missing>, is treated as a tuple. It was not, because the bare type tuple admits value slots only. So [...t, 5] and {...t, 5} spread it (they are now the spread-tuple error, as for any tuple), and Join(t, [3, 4]) with t := (1, Missing) had 4 elements (it now has 3, the first of which is the tuple). (1, 2) = p, with p declared tuple<integer, integer | missing> and no value, was False; it now stays undecided, as for a tuple with value slots. A union of a number and such a tuple joins with a list (Join([3, 4], s)), where it was an incompatible-type error. A compiled Dot of a tuple of such tuples is declined, as for other tuples of tuples.

  • A tuple or list literal compared with a value whose type only may be a tuple or a list stays undecided. (1, 2) = x with an undeclared x was False, and so was the comparison with a symbol declared tuple<integer, integer> | missing or integer | tuple<integer, integer>. [1, 2].isEqual(x) was false for an undeclared x or for a symbol declared list<integer> | integer; it is now undefined. A literal is still unequal to a value that cannot have its kind: [1, 2] = (1, 2) and (1, 2) = 5 are False, and so is a tuple literal compared with a value of a nominal type.

  • A type alias that names itself as an arm of its own union, such as cyc = cyc | tuple<number, number>, no longer overflows the stack. Spread, Join, arithmetic, comparisons and At of a symbol of such a type threw or logged Maximum call stack size exceeded. Such an alias is now a subtype of what its other arms are subtypes of: with cyc = cyc | 0, Norm(c) is valid and evaluates to |c|, where it was an incompatible-type error, and Join([3, 4], c) with cyc = cyc | tuple<number, number> appends c as one element. An alias that names itself inside a constructor, such as json = list<json> | integer, is unchanged.

  • The static type of a list plus or times a number contains the result when an element of the list is itself a collection. [[1, 2], 3] + 0.5 was typed list<integer | list<integer> | real>, which does not hold its value [[1.5, 2.5], 3.5]; it is now typed list<list<real> | real>. The same holds for an element whose type is an alias of a list (list<myints> + 0.5 is list<list<real>>), for a list of ranges ([1..3, 5] · 0.5), and for a list of tuples with an imaginary component times i. A sum or product that stays an integer keeps its type: [[1, 2], 3] + 1 is still list<integer | list<integer>>.
